studies.meaning: A short instruction is followed by a family line of chosen people. Four are named: the first human being, the survivor of the flood, and two families. Then one phrase ties them together, calling them offspring one from another. Early scholars read that as real descent in part and as a shared calling throughout, since Adam has no ancestors among them. The point of the list is continuity, and it prepares the account of Mary and Jesus that follows.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, where the surah is laying shared ground with communities who honour these same figures. It does that by naming them in one sequence under one act of choosing. The family of Imran appears here for the first time, and the surah takes its name from that phrase. What follows straight away is a story of a birth, a dedication and a prophecy, all set inside this frame.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to take the clear part of something, as one skims what is pure from a liquid. It implies selection for a purpose rather than preference, and the form stresses the choosing itself.
From a root tied to scattering, as seed is scattered. The word covers descendants across many generations, so it names a line stretching forward rather than a set of children.
A plural covering every category of created being, not humanity alone. Setting the chosen against that background makes the selection universal in scope rather than tribal or local.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Family line was the organising fact of Arabian life. A man's name carried his father and his grandfather. Trained reciters held the lines of whole tribes in their memory. Inheritance, marriage, alliance and blood claims all ran along those lines. So presenting the prophets as a single descent spoke the audience's own language, using the one frame everybody in the room already trusted.
studies.didYouKnow: Surah 3 takes its name from the phrase family of Imran, which occurs nowhere else in the Quran. Several surahs are named for a word that appears only once inside them. The name works as a label rather than a summary, which is how most Quranic surah names work.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Choosing is shown as continuous, not as a run of clean breaks. That shapes how you read the later prophets. Because the line is described as offspring one from another, no messenger arrives as a break with the one before him. The passage also puts all of them under a single act of choosing. So disagreements between the communities who honour them become differences inside one story.

crossReferences.why: Lists prophets from the offspring of Adam, Noah, Abraham and Israel as one continuous line.
Traces the same descent across many names, saying each was guided and chosen.
Shows Abraham handing the same religion to his sons as a thing inherited.

studies.applyIt: Say the names in these verses slowly. Notice how many belong to other people's traditions as much as to yours. That overlap is not an accident of history; the passage presents it as the design. Today, if the chance comes up, mention the shared line to someone of a different faith rather than the point where you part ways.
studies.explainEasier: God says to obey Him and His Messenger. He chose Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham and the family of Imran above everyone else. They came one from another, a single line. God hears and knows.

studies.title: A Vow Made Before Birth
studies.meaning: A woman speaks before her child is born and gives that child away in advance. She dedicates what is in her womb to God's service, attaching no condition and asking for nothing back. Her only request is that the offering be accepted. Early scholars dwell on the word she uses, which means freed from other claims. They read it as releasing the child from the ordinary duties owed to a household. The woman herself is never named.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, opening the surah's account of the family the chapter is named for. The scene belongs to an earlier community, in a sanctuary kept by dedicated servants. The Quran gives no date and names no ruler. Early scholars add details from older traditions but treat them as extras, holding to what the passage itself reports about the vow and the answer given to it.

keyTerms.note: The verb for binding yourself to give something to God. A vow in this vocabulary hands over ownership, so what is vowed leaves the giver's reach the moment the words are spoken.
A passive participle from the root for liberation. Early scholars read it as freed from service to anyone but God, so the child is dedicated by being released rather than assigned.
An intensified form of the verb to receive. It asks not merely that the gift be taken but that it be taken with favour, which is why the answer two verses later repeats the same root.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A child in the ancient world was a workforce and an old-age pension. Sons worked, defended and inherited. Daughters married into alliances that held a household's place. Promising an unborn child to a sanctuary meant giving up the return on the biggest investment a family ever made. Anyone listening in Arabia, where children counted as wealth, would have felt the size of that.
studies.didYouKnow: The woman who speaks these words is never named in the Quran, though the tradition keeps a name for her. Only one woman is named outright in the Quran: Mary, the child being given away here. Everyone else, this mother included, is known by a relationship. That makes the naming of her daughter a few verses later stand out.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A gift is offered here before anyone knows its value. Neither the child's sex nor its future is available to the woman making the vow. That makes it an act of trust rather than a trade. It also shows a woman's private words entering scripture as the opening of a prophetic history. This line starts in a room nobody witnessed, not at a public event.

crossReferences.why: Continues the scene: the child is born a daughter, and the mother responds in prayer.
Shows Abraham settling his family near the Sacred House with a prayer of dedication.
Presents another parent offering a child, and a son who consents to the offering.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you are protecting because you expect a return from it later: a child's path, a career move, a friendship you are quietly managing. Try saying, privately, that the outcome is not yours to hold. Say it once and change nothing. Then notice how much of your planning had assumed you held the deciding vote.
studies.explainEasier: Imran's wife prayed to God before her baby was born. She promised the child to Him, set apart for His service. She asked God to take her gift, and said that He hears and knows.

studies.title: I Have Delivered A Female
studies.meaning: The vow had assumed a son, since that sanctuary's dedicated service was men's work, and the child is a girl. The mother reports it to God almost as an apology. Then a clause cuts in: God knew better what she had delivered. Scholars differ over whether the words about the male not being like the female are hers or a comment on them. The two readings pull opposite ways, one conceding a shortfall and one denying it. She names the child and asks protection for her and her descendants.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, carrying on the account of the family of Imran that opens the surah's central story. The passage speaks into a world where a daughter was widely felt to be the lesser outcome. The Quran takes that attitude up directly elsewhere. Early scholars note the vow had been framed for a son, and that the answer given went past what was asked. That is what the next verse develops.

keyTerms.note: The everyday verb for setting something down, used of giving birth. The plainness matters: the mother reports the fact without ornament, and the pronoun already carries the disappointment she is naming.
A comparative from the root for knowledge, dropped in as an aside in the middle of her speech. It corrects the assumption behind her report without addressing her or rebuking her.
A passive participle from the root meaning to stone or pelt. It names the adversary by what has been done to him, driven off and chased, rather than by any power he is imagined to hold.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In much of seventh-century Arabia the birth of a daughter was met with silence. The Quran elsewhere describes a father hiding from his people at the news, weighing whether to keep the child in shame or bury her. Daughters made marriage talks harder, could not raid, and left the household when they married. A mother saying she had delivered a girl was reporting into that air.
studies.didYouKnow: Mary is the only woman called by name in the Quran, and this is where her name first appears. She is named thirty-four times, more often than in the Gospels. A whole surah carries her name. The naming happens inside her mother's own speech rather than in the narrative voice.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God's acceptance here does not match the terms of the offer. A vow was made in one shape and answered in another, and the answer turns out to be the larger of the two. The aside about God knowing better settles something else. The worth of a person is not fixed by the categories a culture hands out. That is the ground the whole story that follows stands on.

crossReferences.why: Gives the answer to this prayer: a gracious acceptance, and a growth described as beautiful.
Describes how a daughter's birth was received in that society, and judges the reaction.
Names Mary again as one who confirmed the words of her Lord and was among the devout.

studies.applyIt: Think of a time you got an outcome you had not asked for and quietly filed as second best. Give it another look now, with the distance you have since gained. The aside in this verse is short and easy to miss. God knew better what was delivered. See whether anything on your own list has turned out to be the larger answer.
studies.explainEasier: When the baby was born, the mother said she had given birth to a girl. God knew exactly what she had borne. She named the child Mary, and asked God to keep her and her children safe.

studies.title: Provision Without Reckoning
studies.meaning: Three verbs answer the mother's prayer: God received the child graciously, made her grow well, and placed her in a guardian's care. The word used for growth normally belongs to plants. Then the scene narrows to something that keeps happening. Her guardian finds food with her that he did not bring, and her answer names the source without explaining how. The closing words widen it right out: God provides beyond calculation, to whom He wills.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, inside the surah's account of the family of Imran. The passage brings in Zechariah as Mary's guardian. That sets up his own prayer for a child in the verses just after. Early scholars discuss what the provision was and differ over the details, several reporting fruit out of its season. They agree the weight of the scene falls on what the guardian sees, not on what he is told.

keyTerms.note: A verb used of God bringing plants up out of the earth. Applying it to a child's upbringing borrows the picture of cultivation: growth tended from outside and unfolding of its own accord.
A word for the innermost part of a place of prayer, and elsewhere for a raised or private room. It marks a space set apart, one you enter deliberately rather than pass through.
Literally without an account being kept. The phrase can mean without measure and also without the receiver being held to account for it, and early scholars keep both senses open.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Food came in seasons and everybody knew which. Dates arrived in late summer, grain after the rains. What you ate in a given month was steady enough to be everyday talk, and storage was small and costly. So finding fruit out of its season was no small wonder in that world. It broke a calendar that everyone planned their year around.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the sanctuary chamber turns up only a handful of times in the Quran. Two of those are in this surah, in the account of Mary and Zechariah. Another belongs to the same episode retold in a later surah. It went on to become the ordinary Arabic word for the niche in a mosque wall that marks the direction of prayer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage answers the mother's worry about her daughter without ever taking it up. It does not argue that a girl can serve; it shows the child receiving what nobody arranged for her. Provision is shown loose from the visible channels that usually carry it. That does not make those channels unreal. It only takes them out of the place of final cause, and the closing words carry this far beyond the story.

crossReferences.why: Promises provision from where one does not expect it, for whoever is mindful of God.
Shows Mary provided for again, alone beneath a palm tree, at the birth of her son.
States that provision is in the heaven, together with what is being promised.

studies.applyIt: Look back over the past year for something that arrived without your arranging it: an introduction, a piece of timing, help from someone you barely knew. Name one. Then resist explaining how it came about. The guardian in this scene asks where it came from and gets no mechanism in reply, only a source, and he takes that as an answer.
studies.explainEasier: God took Mary in and helped her grow up well. Zechariah looked after her. Every time he came in, he found food with her. She said it came from God, who gives to whoever He wants.

studies.title: The Prayer Of An Old Man
studies.meaning: The word that opens the verse means at that point. It ties the prayer to what Zechariah has just seen: food arriving for Mary from a source he cannot account for. Watching one unexplained gift, he asks for another. He asks for good offspring, and the reason he gives for asking is not his own need but God's nature, that He hears prayer. Early scholars note the prayer comes after evidence, not out of despair.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, where this sits in the surah's account of the family of Imran, which runs from the vow of Mary's mother through Mary's upbringing to the birth of John and then of Jesus. Zechariah is her guardian in the sanctuary. The passage gives no dates. Early scholars fill the story out from the wider tradition, while noting how compressed the Quran's own telling is.

keyTerms.note: A demonstrative of place that early scholars read here as also of time. It links the prayer to the moment just before it, so the request answers something he has witnessed.
The adjective means wholesome, clean and pleasant, used of food and of soil. He asks not for a child but for a particular quality of child, and early scholars highlight that precision.
A construction that makes hearing prayer a defining description rather than an occasional act. He states the ground of his request as something about God, not about himself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Having no children in a society built on family lines was a specific, public grief. A man without sons had nobody to carry his name into the records that shaped every claim. Nobody would inherit his trade. In old age he had no protection beyond the goodwill of nephews. An audience hearing an old man ask for a child heard a request about carrying on, and about safety, as much as about love.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran tells the story of Zechariah's prayer three times: here, in surah nineteen, and in surah twenty-one. Each telling brings out something different. Here it is the sanctuary and Mary; in surah nineteen it is the whisper and the frailty of his bones. Surah twenty-one gives the shortest version of all. Early scholars treat the three as filling each other out, not as repeating.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer is set off by a sign. So watching God act for someone else can be grounds for asking on your own behalf, rather than for envy. Zechariah also asks for something his body says is unlikely, and the verses around this show him surprised when it is granted. The Quran records that without criticism. Honest astonishment at an answered prayer is left standing as part of what faith looks like.

crossReferences.why: Retells the same prayer with the detail of his whispered call and his fear for his successors.
Gives the shortest version and adds that he called on God in hope and in awe.
Describes the provision found with Mary, the sign that prompts this prayer.

studies.applyIt: The next time you notice something going unexpectedly well for someone else, use it as Zechariah did and treat it as evidence. Then let it prompt your own long-abandoned request. Most people meet another's good news with comparison. Try meeting one instance of it this week with a prayer of your own instead, said at once, while the impression is fresh.
studies.explainEasier: Zechariah was old and had no children. He saw God give food to Mary out of nowhere. So he asked God for a good child of his own, because God hears people who ask.

studies.title: Called While Standing In Prayer
studies.meaning: The answer to a long prayer arrives during the prayer itself, not afterwards. Angels call out while the man is still standing there. The promised son is described in four terms: he will confirm a word from God, he will be a leader, he will be restrained, and he will be a prophet among the upright. Early scholars differ over the third of those. Some read it as self-restraint in general, others as a life lived without marriage.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, still inside the story of the family of Imran. It moves from Mary's upbringing to her guardian's own request. The scene belongs to an earlier people, in a sanctuary kept by servants who had been given to it. The guardian was old and had no children. Classical sources tell the episode more fully from older stories, but keep the Quran's order, which puts his request right after what he had been seeing.

keyTerms.note: Early scholars understand this as pointing to Jesus, whom this surah names with the same term a few verses later. An abstract noun stands for a person, which is how the passage introduces him.
From a root meaning to go in front or to take charge. It describes someone others defer to for his qualities rather than for any office, and here it is applied to a child not yet born.
An intensive form from a root meaning to confine or to besiege. Early scholars differ over whether it names control of desire in general or a life without marriage, and the word carries both.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Having no children in the ancient Near East was a social state as much as a private grief. Property passed to side branches of the family. A man's name ended with him, and nobody was left to press his family's claims. An old man with no son had already begun to fade out of his own community's arrangements. What is announced here turns around a standing, not just a disappointment.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah puts two birth announcements within a few verses of each other. One goes to a man in old age, one to a young woman. Angels deliver both, in closely similar wording. In each case the person asks how such a thing can happen, and in each case the answer comes back in the same form.
studies.theologicalSignificance: An answer can arrive inside the act of asking, and this scene shows it. That changes how a prayer and its result sit together. The passage also brings Jesus in sideways, as a word to be confirmed, before he is named at all. That order serves the surah's argument: the one who will testify to him is announced first. So his coming reads as expected, not as a break in the story.

crossReferences.why: Retells the same episode at greater length, including the prayer that preceded this announcement.
Announces the other birth in the same terms, and names the word from God directly.
Recalls the same request and answer, adding that the household was quick in good works.

studies.applyIt: Notice whether you finish your requests to God and then leave the room, mentally, to go and wait. In this scene the answer arrives while the man is still standing. The next time you ask for something that matters, stay a moment longer than feels natural. Do that before you get up and start arranging it yourself.
studies.explainEasier: While he was standing and praying, angels called out to him. They said God was giving him good news of a son called John. John would confirm a word from God. He would be a leader, and good, and a prophet.

studies.title: How Will I Have A Son
studies.meaning: The man who has just been given exactly what he asked for answers with a question about how. He is old, his wife cannot bear children, and he says both things plainly. The reply does not touch the obstacle at all. It repeats one word meaning even so, then says that God does whatever He wills. Early scholars read the question as wonder rather than doubt. He asks how and not whether, and no rebuke follows it in the text.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, inside the surah's account of the family of Imran. The episode belongs to an earlier community. It is retold at greater length in a later surah, where the same request gets more of its setting. The Quran supplies no dates. Early scholars place the prayer right after what the guardian had been seeing in the sanctuary, and that is how this surah orders the two scenes.

keyTerms.note: An interrogative covering manner and origin together. It asks by what route a thing could come about, which is why early scholars hear wonder in it rather than a challenge.
An adjective used of a woman or a man who does not conceive, and also of land that yields nothing. It states a settled condition rather than a season of waiting.
A demonstrative meaning in that manner. As an answer it declines to explain, pointing back at the promise instead of forward to a mechanism, and that refusal is the whole reply.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Age was guessed at rather than counted in Arabia. A man was old when he could no longer ride or work a season through. Not being able to bear children was named openly and carried public weight. A household with no children lost its labour, its defence and its claim on the future. Saying both facts aloud in a prayer was stating what everyone around him already knew.
studies.didYouKnow: The same question, in almost the same words, appears twice in this surah within a few verses. Once from an old man, once from a young woman. In both places the reply opens with the same pointing word. The parallel is close enough that early scholars regularly discuss the two scenes together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A prophet is allowed to ask how without the question counting against him. Asking for a mechanism is separated from doubting a promise, and the first is answered by being set aside. The reply also puts the event down to will rather than to capacity. The point is not that God can get past barrenness. It is that what He wills is simply done, which takes the obstacle out of the picture.

crossReferences.why: Retells the same exchange, adding that God had created him before when he was nothing.
Puts the same question in Mary's mouth a few verses later, and answers it the same way.
Shows Abraham's wife asking how she could bear a child in old age, and getting a like reply.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often your first response to good news is to work out how it could possibly happen. That instinct is not faithlessness; the man here has it too. But watch what it costs you in the minutes afterwards. Try receiving one piece of unexpected good news this week without immediately checking whether it is plausible.
studies.explainEasier: He asked God how he could have a son. He was old, and his wife could not have children. God told him it would happen anyway, because God does whatever He wants.

studies.title: A Sign Of Three Silent Days
studies.meaning: He asks for a sign and is given one that costs him something. For three days he will not be able to speak to people, only to gesture. Early scholars note that the limit covers speech to people, not speech to God. The same breath tells him to remember his Lord a great deal. It tells him to praise at both ends of the day. So the sign and the instruction are one thing: a tongue taken out of conversation and handed to something else.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, inside the surah's retelling of the family of Imran. The episode belongs to an earlier community. A longer version appears in a later surah, reporting the same three days and adding that he came out to his people and signalled to them. The Quran gives no place or date. Early scholars discuss the nature of the silence and mostly treat it as an inability, not a choice he made.

keyTerms.note: A word for a signal made with the eyes, lips or hand and without sound. It names talking stripped of voice, which is the sign itself: he can be understood, but not heard.
The verb covers keeping in mind and saying aloud at once. Arabic does not separate the two, so remembering God is already a spoken act, which is why it survives the ban on speaking.
A noun for the first part of the day, paired here with the late afternoon. Naming the two edges of a day is an Arabic way of saying throughout it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man's standing in seventh-century Arabia rested on his speech. He argued his claims aloud. He made contracts by word in front of witnesses. He defended his family's name in public, and poetry and speech-making were the known tools of power. Losing the use of the tongue for three days was no small private nuisance. It cut him off from every means by which men in that world acted.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the few places in the Quran where a sign, once asked for, arrives as a limit rather than a display. The three days are reported the same way in the longer retelling in a later surah. That is one of several details matching across the two accounts. The two otherwise differ a lot in length and stress.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The sign given here works by taking away. It does not show power by adding something to the world. It withdraws a power and leaves the man with only the use of it that matters. So the sign cannot be pulled apart from a discipline. Confirmation and instruction arrive as one event. It also treats speech to God and speech to people as genuinely different acts.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same sign in a fuller retelling, showing him signalling to his people afterwards.
Shows Abraham asking to be shown, and answered with an action rather than an argument.
Repeats the same instruction: remember God much, and praise Him morning and evening.

studies.applyIt: Try one meal, or one commute, without speaking and without a screen. Not as an achievement, simply as an experiment. Notice what your attention does when its usual outlet is closed. The instruction attached to these three days was not merely to be quiet but to redirect, and the second part is what most people leave out.
studies.explainEasier: He asked God for a sign. God told him he would not be able to talk to people for three days, only make signs with his hands. He was also told to remember God a lot, evening and morning.

studies.title: Chosen And Told To Bow
studies.meaning: Two announcements come, and then an instruction. The angels tell Mary she has been chosen, purified, and chosen again over the women of the world. Early scholars discuss that repeat. Most read the first choosing as her acceptance into dedicated service and the second as her selection for what is about to be announced. Then, straight after that height of honour, comes a command: be devoted, bow down, kneel with those who kneel. The honour does not excuse her from the ordinary posture.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, where these verses belong to the surah's central story and to its conversation with a community that honours Mary deeply. The passage names her choosing in strong terms, then places her among worshippers rather than above them. The Quran reports the angels' words without describing a setting. Early scholars add no occasion beyond the order of the surah itself.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to take the pure part of a thing. It is used twice in one verse of the same person, which early scholars generally read as two separate selections rather than emphasis.
An imperative from the root for sustained obedient standing, the same word used earlier in this surah of the reverent. It names a posture held over time rather than an act done once.
The verb for bending at the waist. Its command form here is addressed to a woman on her own, while the phrase right after places her among a plural group of those bowing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Standing in Arabian society came with exemptions. A chief was not expected to carry water. A man of rank sent others to do what was beneath him, and honour was measured partly by what you no longer had to do yourself. Rank meant relief from common tasks. The instruction here runs straight against that grain, tying honour to joining in rather than to being excused.
studies.didYouKnow: Mary is the only woman the Quran addresses by name in direct speech. This passage does it twice, in two verses running. The surah that carries her name is one of only a handful named after a person. And it is the one surah in the Quran named for a woman.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Being chosen and being bound are joined here, not traded against each other. Being chosen above all women is followed at once by a command to do what every worshipper does. She is to do it in company with them. That puts the highest honour the passage can name inside ordinary devotion, not beyond it. The purifying is described as done to her, so even her standing stays a gift rather than an achievement.

crossReferences.why: Names Mary again as one of the devout, using the same root as the command given here.
Places her withdrawn to an eastern place, supplying the setting this passage leaves out.
Supplies the dedication and upbringing that brought her to the point of this address.

studies.applyIt: Think of an area where you have some standing: at work, in a family, in a community. Find one ordinary task there that people at your level usually stop doing. Do it this week without announcing it. This passage attaches the highest honour it can name to bowing alongside other people rather than in front of them.
studies.explainEasier: The angels told Mary that God had chosen her and made her pure. He chose her above all the women in the world. Then they told her to worship her Lord, and to bow and kneel with the others.

studies.title: You Were Not There
studies.meaning: The story stops for a moment to speak to the one receiving it. These accounts belong to what is unseen, and the point is made with two denials. You were not there when they cast lots over who would take charge of Mary. You were not there when they quarrelled about it. Early scholars note the detail chosen. Not a miracle, but a dispute over who would take on a child. That is exactly the sort of thing an outsider would have no way of knowing.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, breaking into the account of Mary between her upbringing and the news of her son. Addresses like this appear all through the Quran wherever a story from an earlier people is retold. Here it lands inside a surah in conversation with people who held those histories themselves. So the claim being made is about where the account comes from, not about what it says.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for news that carries consequence, marked off by early Arabic dictionary writers from ordinary information. It names accounts that change something for whoever receives them.
What is absent from perception, whether hidden by time, distance or nature. The word does not mean the supernatural; a past event no witness survives is unseen in exactly this sense.
The word for a trimmed reed used in writing, and here for the marked shafts cast to settle a question. One object served both purposes, which is why the term carries so much at once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Casting marked arrows or reeds to decide a matter was familiar across Arabia before Islam. It was used at sanctuaries to settle questions nobody could otherwise resolve. Anyone hearing this verse would have known the procedure at once. It gave a decision the look of being fair to all sides, which is exactly what a group of men arguing over a costly duty would have wanted.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran often marks the edge of the Prophet's own knowledge with the phrase you were not there. It uses it of Moses at the mountain, of Joseph's brothers agreeing on their plan, and here. The formula turns up across several surahs. It always attaches to a small, checkable circumstance, never to a grand event.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The claim rests on a detail rather than on a marvel, which is a particular kind of argument. Anybody could invent a miracle. Few would think to invent a quarrel over guardianship. The passage also draws the unseen wide enough to take in the ordinary past. That puts revelation in the place of a witness rather than a reader of meaning, and it does so without running down the accounts already held nearby.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same formula: you were not with them when they agreed upon their plan.
Repeats it of Moses, saying the Prophet was not present on the mountain's western side.
Calls the account of Noah news of the unseen, revealed and not previously known.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of what you know rests on testimony rather than sight: your own birth, your grandparents' lives, nearly all of history. You already live by trusted report. Pick one thing you are certain of today and trace how you actually came to know it. The exercise makes this verse's kind of claim less foreign than it first looks.
studies.explainEasier: These stories come from things you could not have seen. You were not there when they drew lots to decide who would look after Mary. You were not there when they argued about it either.

studies.title: A Word From Him
studies.meaning: The angels choose every word with care. He is a word from God. His name comes with a title and with his mother's name, where a father's would normally stand. He is held in high regard in this world and the next, and among those brought near. Then two moments of his speaking are named: in the cradle and in grown-up years. Early scholars read a word from God to mean brought into being by God's command, and they treat the naming through his mother as part of the announcement itself.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, speaking closely to the Christian community of Najran. Classical sources report that their delegation travelled there to discuss this very question. The surah does not open with disagreement. It gives the announcement first, and gives it in terms of honour. Only later in the chapter does it take up how he is to be understood, once the story has been laid out.

keyTerms.note: A title, not a name. Its root means to wipe or to anoint. The Quran always uses it of Jesus. Early scholars discuss several possible roots for it and do not settle on one.
From the word for a face. It describes a person whose face is welcome, someone of standing whose word carries weight. The verse extends that standing to this world and the next alike.
A passive form: they are drawn close, rather than coming near by their own power. It names a rank set by nearness to God, and the verse describes that rank as given rather than earned.
The word for the age between youth and old age, roughly the middle years. Pairing it with the cradle marks the two ends of his speaking: one of them impossible, one entirely ordinary.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Names in Arabia carried fathers. A man was known as the son of his father. That chain placed him in a tribe, an inheritance and a set of duties. To name a child by his mother in a formal announcement was unusual enough to be a statement in itself. It fixed who he was in a way the audience could not mishear, and it has stayed attached to him since.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran calls Jesus the son of Mary more than twenty times, and the phrase became the standard Arabic way of naming him. Naming a man by his mother was rare in that setting. Yet the usage holds across surahs sent down years apart, in very different circumstances.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The announcement sets out his standing in the strongest terms it has, and every part of that standing is placed in what he was given. He is a word from God. He is brought near rather than approaching. He is held in regard in both worlds. So the passage places him without lowering him: it honours him fully and keeps him on the created side throughout. That is how the surah frames the discussion that comes later.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same terms of him, a word conveyed to Mary and a spirit from Him.
Reports the speech from the cradle, in which he names himself a servant of God.
Compares his creation to Adam's later in this surah, as made from dust by a command.

studies.applyIt: Read the announcement slowly and notice how much honour it gives. If you have Christian friends or family, it is worth knowing well. It is neither a put-down nor a full agreement. Saying clearly what your own book says about Jesus helps more in a conversation than a rough sense picked up from either side.
studies.explainEasier: Angels bring Mary good news. She will have a son named Jesus. God has given him a high place in this life and the next. As a baby in his crib he will speak to people.

studies.title: Be, And It Is
studies.meaning: Mary asks the same question the old man asked a few verses earlier. The reply differs in one telling word. He was told that God does what He wills; she is told that God creates what He wills. Then the answer gives a mechanism after all: a command, and the thing is. Early scholars note that this formula is used in the Quran for events with no precedent. The passage then names what the child will be taught, placing him inside a tradition of learning rather than outside it.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, in the surah's central story and its careful account of how the birth is to be understood. Classical sources link this section to a Christian delegation from Najran, then in the city. The Quran's order is deliberate. How the creation happens is stated before any disagreement is raised. The teaching of the Torah and the Gospel is named in the same breath as the miracle.

keyTerms.note: The verb for bringing something into being with a form. It replaces the broader verb used in the answer to Zechariah. Early scholars read that swap as marking a difference between the two births.
A two-letter imperative, the shortest command Arabic can make. Its brevity is the point: no process is described between the word and the thing, so nothing stands between the will and the result.
Set apart here from the Book, so it names more than a text: sound judgement about how and when to act. The root also carries restraint, as of a bridle holding a horse.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Making anything in that world took time you could watch. A garment was spun, woven and cut over weeks. A house went up course by course, and a field waited on rain and then on months. Nothing came into being without a visible process attached to it. A creation with no gap between the word and the result was, in that setting, unlike everything the audience had ever seen made.
studies.didYouKnow: The formula in which God says Be, and a thing is, occurs eight times in the Quran. It is used of the making of the heavens and the earth, of the raising of the dead, and here of one birth. The same short phrase covers events of very different scale. Early scholars treat that as deliberate, not accidental.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A unique event is set inside a general rule rather than treated as an exception. Creation by command is God's ordinary way of working. So this birth is unusual in its circumstances, not in how it happens. The teaching named right afterwards works the same way. Whatever is singular about him, his learning is described in the terms used of other prophets.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical formula of the heavens and the earth, originated with no precedent before them.
Applies the same command to Adam, created from dust, as this surah's own comparison.
States the principle in general: His command, when He wills a thing, is to say Be.

studies.applyIt: There is a difference between a question asked in order to understand and one asked in order to resist. Mary asks how, and receives an answer. Think of something you have been told is possible and have quietly filed as unrealistic. Ask honestly which of the two kinds of question you have been putting to it.
studies.explainEasier: Mary asks how she can have a baby when no man has touched her. God tells her that He makes whatever He wants. He only has to say Be, and the thing is there.

studies.title: By God's Leave
studies.meaning: A messenger describes his own signs, and each one comes with a limit attached. He shapes a bird from clay and it lives. He heals two conditions that medicine could not reach. He brings the dead back to life. He tells people what they have eaten and what they store at home. Three times the phrase by God's leave breaks into that list. Early scholars point out that he says it himself, about himself, so the limit belongs to the claim rather than being added later.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, inside the surah's account of Jesus and his mission to the Children of Israel. The signs are reported as given, with no dates attached. Early commentaries note that each one answered something the community of that time prized. They treat the pattern as general: every messenger is described as given signs the people of his own moment could recognise.

keyTerms.note: From a root that also means to hear or give ear. In Arabic, permission is granted by listening. So the phrase implies an authority present and allowing, not just a rule that permits.
A specific word for blindness present from birth, not acquired later. Naming it on its own rules out any recovery that might be credited to time or to treatment.
A noun for outward shape and appearance. It says carefully that what he makes has the form of a bird. Early scholars say this marks the line between shaping a thing and giving it life.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medicine in the ancient world mostly meant making room. A blind man was led about, and a person with a skin disease lived apart. Families built their lives around conditions nobody expected to change. Healers set bones and mixed remedies for fevers. Nothing in daily life turned back a condition a person was born with, which is why these two were the ones named.
studies.didYouKnow: The sign of the clay bird appears twice in the Quran: here, and in a later surah where God recounts the same favours directly to Jesus. Both times the phrase by God's leave is attached to it. The Quran mentions the sign nowhere else, and never once without that qualification in place.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A messenger can hold great signs and give away their source in the same sentence. That settles a tension the surah is working on. Honour and power can be given freely, as long as their origin stays clear. The limit is repeated three times inside one short speech. That repeating does the work an argument would otherwise have to do, and it does it in his own voice.

crossReferences.why: Recounts the same signs, with God addressing Jesus and repeating the same qualification each time.
Continues the same speech, ending on God as my Lord and your Lord.
Says Jesus was given clear signs and supported by the holy spirit.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you are genuinely good at, the thing people come to you for. Say aloud, once, where the capacity for it came from. Not as false modesty; the man speaking here does not understate what he can do. He simply never makes a sentence about it without naming the source, and that is a habit rather than a mood.
studies.explainEasier: Jesus tells his people about the signs God gave him. He can shape a bird from clay and make it live. He can heal the blind and raise the dead. Each time he says it happens by God's leave.

studies.title: My Lord And Your Lord
studies.meaning: The speech now turns to what it is for. He confirms the scripture they already hold. He says that some of what was forbidden is now made lawful. He points again at the sign he brought. Then the whole message shrinks to one sentence: God is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. Early scholars notice the order of the pronouns. The speaker puts himself under that lordship before he addresses anyone else. They read a straight path as naming exactly that.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, inside the surah's account of Jesus and central to its conversation with a community that honoured him. The passage reports his own words rather than describing him from outside. Classical sources link this section with a delegation from Najran. The Quran's method here is to quote, not to argue. Reported speech carries a point the surah states plainly only later.

keyTerms.note: The same participle used of the Quran at this surah's opening. Applying it to a messenger and to a book alike presents both as witnesses to what came before them, not as replacements for it.
An idiom for what lies ahead in place and behind in time, so what came earlier stands in front of a person. Arabic pictures the past as visible and the future as somewhere behind you.
A road broad enough for many to travel, paired with a participle meaning standing upright and holding its direction. The phrase names both the way and its refusal to bend away.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Roads in that world were not built; they were worn by use. A straight route between two places was rare. Paths bent around wells, rock, and land a traveller could not safely cross. A way that held its direction was the exception and was known by name. Anyone who had made a long journey knew the difference between the shortest road and the one people actually took.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase rendered a straight path occurs more than thirty times in the Quran. That includes the short surah every reciter opens with. Here it is placed in the mouth of an earlier prophet, describing his own message. It is one of several spots where the wording of that opening chapter turns up inside a story.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The speech puts the speaker and his listeners on the same side of one bond. It does that in the grammar itself, by naming his Lord before theirs. The central claim is settled without ever being set out as a plain statement. Lifting some earlier rules works the same way. It shows that revelation can change in its details while its centre holds, which is the surah's larger case for what carries over.

crossReferences.why: Reports the same sentence from him almost word for word, in a later surah's account.
Repeats it again as his own speech, adding that this is a straight path.
Asks for the same path, in the prayer that every recitation of the Quran begins with.

studies.applyIt: Notice the order of the pronouns: my Lord, then your Lord. When you next find yourself telling someone what they ought to do about faith, try putting yourself into the sentence first, and honestly. It changes what you say next. Most religious advice fails at exactly this point, before any of its content is even reached.
studies.explainEasier: Jesus tells his people that he agrees with the book they already have. He says that God is his Lord and their Lord too. So they should worship God. That, he says, is the straight path.

studies.title: Who Will Stand With Me
studies.meaning: The turn is described as something felt: he sensed disbelief. He does not press the argument any further. Instead he asks a question that makes people name themselves. The disciples answer in three parts: we are the helpers, we have believed, and bear witness that we have submitted. Early scholars note the call for witness at the end. It turns a private belief into something said aloud in front of others, which is what that moment needed.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, at the point where the surah's account of Jesus turns from his mission to how it was received. The episode is told again in a later surah, where the same word for his helpers appears. The Quran gives no setting and names no one. Early commentaries treat this as the moment the community around him split. That is why the surah places it just before a plan and a counter-plan.

keyTerms.note: A verb tied to the physical senses rather than to reasoning. It suggests he felt the change in the room before anyone said it, which is how opposition usually announces itself first.
The plural of a word for one who comes to another's aid in trouble. The same word later named the people of Medina who took in the emigrants, a link the first audience caught at once.
A term early Arabic dictionary writers connect with whiteness and with purity or sincerity. The Quran uses it only of this group, and its exact root is discussed without ever being settled.
The participle from the same root this surah uses for the religion God accepts. Placing it in the disciples' mouths ties them straight to the definition given earlier in the chapter.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a tribal society, declaring support was a formal act with consequences. Standing up for a man under pressure meant taking on his enemies as your own. It was done in the open, so everyone knew where duties now lay. A quiet well-wisher gave nothing at all. So the question here does not ask what people think; it asks who will say so.
studies.didYouKnow: The word the disciples use for helpers is the one that later gave the people of Medina their historical name. The surah's first listeners carried that name themselves. Putting it in the mouths of a much older community links the two groups across centuries, through a single choice of wording.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats faith as something that has to be sayable. Belief is stated, and then witness is asked for. The inward and the spoken are held together, and neither stands on its own. The passage also shows a prophet meeting rejection by looking for company rather than by raising the argument. What follows in the surah confirms that the answer given here was the thing that lasted.

crossReferences.why: Recalls the same exchange and calls the believers to be helpers as the disciples were.
Reports the disciples' declaration again, with God saying He inspired them to believe.
Gives their prayer immediately afterwards, asking to be recorded among the witnesses.

studies.applyIt: Support that stays private is not much use to the person who needs it. Think of someone currently taking heat for something you actually agree with. Say so to them directly this week, in a message they can keep, rather than a public post. The question in this passage asks who will stand up, and it expects a name in reply.
studies.explainEasier: Jesus could feel that people were turning against him. So he asked who would stand with him and help. His close followers said they would. They said they believed in God and had given themselves to Him.

studies.title: Count Us Among The Witnesses
studies.meaning: A short prayer is followed by a sentence that turns the whole scene around. The disciples ask to be written among those who bear witness. They have named what they believed and whom they followed. Then, with no warning, the passage says that they schemed and God schemed. The same word covers both, and early scholars explain that of God it means undoing a plot by an unseen arrangement, not deception. The contrast is between a plan made in a room and one that encloses it.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, closing the surah's account of the reception Jesus met. The Quran neither describes the plan nor names those who made it. Early scholars connect the passage to a plot against his life and to the outcome the following verses report, on which they keep more than one reading. The surah stays brief here because its concern is the pattern rather than the run of events.

keyTerms.note: The verb for recording in writing. Asking to be written among a group is asking for a place on a list, an image drawn from the registers kept of tribes, of soldiers and of shares.
Those who testify to what they have seen, and in another usage those present at an event. Both fit: they ask to be counted among people who were there and who then said so.
A verb for a plan made out of its target's sight. Of people it carries blame. Of God, early scholars explain it as the hidden overturning of a scheme, keeping the mirrored wording without the blame.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Registers mattered in the seventh century. Tribes kept lists of who was owed a share, who had ridden out on a raid, and who stood surety for a debt. Being written down was how a claim survived memory and argument. So asking God to write your name among a group reached for the most concrete image of belonging available, one everyone had watched decided in practice.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here of scheming is applied to God several times in the Quran. It always mirrors a word just used of people in the same sentence. Classical writers on style describe this as a known device, in which a term is turned back on an opponent. They note that the Quran never uses the word of God on its own.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The two verses set together say something this surah repeats elsewhere. A group states its loyalty and asks to be written down. Meanwhile a plan is already moving against them. The passage does not answer that with a promise of safety. It says the larger arrangement holds the smaller one inside it, which changes what the plan means without always stopping it from running.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same mirrored wording of a plot laid against the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him).
Shows a scheme made and its outcome reversed, using the same vocabulary throughout.
Shows others asking to be written among the witnesses, in almost identical words.

studies.applyIt: There is a difference between asking to be safe and asking to be counted. This prayer asks for the second. Think about which of the two you actually ask for, most days. Then say the disciples' request once in your own words, and notice that it contains no request for the situation to improve.
studies.explainEasier: The followers of Jesus pray to God. They ask to be counted among the people who tell the truth about what they saw. Others made a secret plan against him. But God had a plan too.

studies.title: Raising You To Me
studies.meaning: God speaks to Jesus directly and states four things: a taking, a raising, a clearing from those who refused him, and a placing of his followers above them until the Resurrection. The first word is the hard one. Scholars differ over whether it means causing to die, taking in full, or taking up as one is taken in sleep. Early scholars record that whole range and do not force a choice. Then the verse leaves every remaining dispute to God's own judgement.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, closely tied to the surah's dealings with the Christian community of Najran. Classical sources report their delegation coming to the city. The passage does not narrate the events around the end of his earthly presence. It states what God did, then leaves the disagreement open. That is the method the whole section uses: state the essentials, and leave the disputed detail to the judgement named at the close.

keyTerms.note: A participle from a root meaning to receive something in full, used both of collecting a debt and of death. Early scholars record several readings of it in this place and settle on none.
The participle for lifting up, used in the Quran of rank as well as of place. Both senses appear in the commentaries, and the word itself does not choose between them.
From the root for purity, here in the sense of separating someone from what would stain them. It concerns his standing among people rather than any condition within him.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man's name in Arabia could outlive him. Whoever told his story afterwards could repair it or ruin it. Poets were paid to praise and paid to insult. A family's standing turned on which account survived. So clearing a man of those who had wronged his name was a known act in that world, and it mattered as much as anything done to his body.
studies.didYouKnow: This verse leaves a disagreement to a later judgement rather than settling it now. The Quran makes that move often with matters disputed between communities. The wording appears in several surahs. The clause about judging between people over what they differed in nearly always comes at the close of such a question, not in the middle.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage guards a prophet's honour without settling the historical question that divides communities. It says what God did with him. It says the dispute itself will be judged, and that the judging belongs to God. That shape suggests how believers might hold such questions in the meantime: open where the sources are open, and settled only where the text is plain.

crossReferences.why: Addresses the same contested end more directly, and says God raised him to Himself.
Uses the same verb for taking, in the account of Jesus answering on the Day of Judgement.
Ends another dispute between communities the same way, by deferring it to God's judgement.

studies.applyIt: There are questions you will not settle, including some that matter. This verse models what to do with them. State clearly what you do hold, name the disagreement as a disagreement, and leave the verdict where it belongs. Try that phrasing once this week on something you have been arguing about in circles.
studies.explainEasier: God tells Jesus that He will take him and lift him up to Himself. He will clear him of the people who refused him. On the last day God will settle what they argued about.

studies.title: In This World And The Next
studies.meaning: The sentence begun in the verse before splits into two outcomes, and this is the first of them. The punishment is described as reaching both worlds. Then the closing words rule out anyone stepping in. Early scholars note the pairing of the two worlds, which comes back across this surah. They read the phrase about helpers as denying the very thing an Arabian audience would look for first: not innocence, but someone with enough standing to speak up for you before God.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, closing the surah's account of Jesus. Next comes the passage comparing his creation with that of Adam. The wording repeats a phrase used earlier in this surah of a different group, and early commentaries note that habit of returning to its own phrasing. The passage speaks about a group marked out by refusal, not about any named people or time.

keyTerms.note: A particle that introduces one branch of a division and expects a matching branch to follow. Its presence signals that the sentence is only half finished, and the next verse supplies the other half.
The plural of one who comes to another's aid, from the same root used a few verses earlier of the disciples. The word that named loyalty in one scene names its absence in this one.
The adjective comes from a root meaning to tighten or bind hard. It describes intensity as constriction rather than as duration, a different image from the one the English suggests.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Nobody in Arabia stood alone before a claim. When a man was accused, his clan bargained and the elders stepped in. Blood money was raised by relatives who might not even like him. Guilt rarely met a person head on, because a network took the shock. So saying that someone has no helpers described a state almost unthinkable there, and worse than the penalty itself.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrase about having no helpers occurs earlier in this same surah. It comes there in a passage about those who kill prophets and those who call for justice. The surah uses the formula twice, in two quite different sections. It is one of many repeats that bind its long argument across changes of subject.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Consequence is placed in both worlds rather than all put off, which keeps the present morally serious. The sharpest words are the last ones. What is taken away is not comfort but anyone to speak on your behalf. That says something about how answering for what you do is shaped here. The decisive absence is not of pleasure but of anyone standing between a person and what they did.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical closing phrase about having no helpers, earlier in this surah.
Supplies the matching branch of the sentence: the reward given in full to the faithful.
Denies that speaking up for someone will be accepted or any help given on that day.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of your sense of safety comes from people who would step in for you: a manager, a relative, a friend with influence. That is real and worth being grateful for. Name one of them today and thank them. Then sit for a moment with the fact that the arrangement is temporary, which is what this verse is pointing at.
studies.explainEasier: God says that people who turn away from the truth will be punished. It will happen in this life and the next. No one will be able to help them or stand up for them.

studies.title: Wages Paid In Full
studies.meaning: The other branch of the sentence arrives. Those who believed and did good are paid their wages in full, using the same trading verb this surah applied earlier to the settling of every account. Then a clause is attached that seems to belong to the first branch rather than this one: God does not love the wrongdoers. Early scholars read that placing as deliberate, so that even a promise of reward closes on a limit. Then the next verse names what has just been recited.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, at the close of the surah's account of Jesus, just before the comparison with Adam. The verse after steps outside the story to describe it. Classical commentaries link that to the talks then going on in the city with a visiting Christian delegation. Naming the recitation as verses and as a reminder frames what came before as evidence, not as a story told for its own sake.

keyTerms.note: The trading verb for discharging an obligation completely, used earlier in this surah of the final reckoning. Applied to reward, it makes the promise a settlement rather than a present.
The word for a worker's pay, not for a gift. It implies something earned and owed, which is why the verb of full payment suits it and why the two are so often paired.
Two words: a reminder that brings something back to mind, and an adjective from the root for firm judgement. Together they name a text that recalls and decides in the same breath.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Paid work existed alongside slavery and family duty in seventh-century Arabia. Men were hired for a harvest, a journey, or a season of herding. The pay was agreed first and settled at the end. Fights over a withheld wage were common enough to be a known kind of grievance. Full payment on the agreed day was hoped for rather than assumed.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase naming this recitation as verses and a wise reminder occurs only here in the Quran. The surah places it at a hinge. It comes right after a long story and right before a comparison drawn from it. This is one of several points where the text pauses to describe itself in the middle of an argument.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Reward is described in the words of wages, not of favour. That makes it owed rather than merely hoped for. The closing words hold the whole promise inside a moral frame. Then the next verse does what this surah does again and again: it names its own material. The story just told is called a sign and a reminder, so its purpose is stated rather than left to be guessed.

crossReferences.why: Supplies the other branch of this divided sentence, the outcome for those who refuse.
Uses the same promise of wages paid in full, adding an increase from God's bounty.
Says the patient will be given their reward without any reckoning applied to it.

studies.applyIt: Think about work you have done that was never acknowledged, and notice the small resentment attached to it. The word used here is wages, not gifts. Try holding one unacknowledged thing this week as already owed and already recorded. Then see whether that changes how badly you need someone else to notice it.
studies.explainEasier: God says that people who believe and do good will get their full pay for it. Nothing will be held back. Then God says that what has just been read out are His own signs and a wise reminder.

studies.title: The Likeness Of Adam
studies.meaning: The argument is made by comparison, not by denial. Suppose a birth without a father shows something extraordinary about a person's nature. Then the first human being, made without either parent, would show more. The comparison works by scale: whatever is unusual in one case is more unusual in the other. No tradition has drawn that conclusion about Adam. Then the next verse closes the matter briefly, naming the truth as from God and warning against wavering.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. Classical sources tie this section to the Christian delegation from Najran. They had come to talk about the nature of Jesus. The comparison belongs to that talk. The surah has already given the news of his birth in terms of full honour. So the argument comes after the honour, not in place of it, and the commentaries stress that order.

keyTerms.note: Not a metaphor but a parallel case put forward for reasoning. The word introduces an argument by analogy, which is how early scholars read this verse as a whole.
The most ordinary material named in the Quran's accounts of human origin. Choosing it strengthens the point, since the more unusual creation began from the least remarkable substance available.
From a root tied to drawing back and forth, as milk is drawn from an udder. It pictures doubt as a swinging motion rather than a settled position a person has arrived at.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Argument by parallel case was the ordinary tool of Arabian dispute. A poet or a judge made his point by setting one situation beside another, then let the audience draw the line themselves. That was held to work better than stating the point outright. So the form of this verse would have felt familiar at once, even where its content was fought over.
studies.didYouKnow: The command Be, and it is, appears twice within thirteen verses of this surah. It is used once of Jesus and once of Adam. Those are the only two places the formula occurs in the whole chapter. Their pairing across such a short distance is the hinge this comparison turns on.
studies.theologicalSignificance: An unusual origin is treated as evidence about God, not about the one created. Creation by command is God's ordinary way of working. So the way a person came into being says nothing about their nature. The principle is applied to one question here, but its reach is much wider. It cuts the worth and standing of a human being loose from the circumstances of their arrival.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same command of Jesus twelve verses earlier, which is what makes the comparison land.
Describes Adam's creation from clay, and the breathing of spirit into him.
Addresses the same question directly, asking that nothing beyond the truth be said in religion.

studies.applyIt: The move this verse makes is worth borrowing. Rather than deny a claim, it sets a second case beside it and lets the comparison do the work. Next time you disagree with someone, try finding the parallel case instead of the counter-argument. It is slower, and it leaves the other person somewhere to stand.
studies.explainEasier: God says that Jesus is like Adam. God made Adam out of dust. Then He said Be, and Adam was there. Adam had no father and no mother at all.

studies.title: Come, Let Us Call
studies.meaning: When argument has run out, a different kind of settlement is proposed. Both sides are to bring their families and stand together. Then they call down God's rejection on whichever side is lying. What is staked is the striking part: not property, not standing, but the people each side most wants to protect. Early scholars record that the invocation never took place. The other party declined it and chose a negotiated settlement instead, and the sources treat that refusal as telling in itself.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, and this is among the best attested occasions in the surah. Classical sources agree that a Christian delegation from Najran came to the city and discussed the nature of Jesus at length. When that reached its limit, they were offered this shared invocation. The delegation stepped back from it and negotiated terms instead. The Quran records the offer, not the outcome.

keyTerms.note: From a root suggesting release and unrestrained pleading, used of praying with nothing held back. The form makes it mutual, an appeal both parties make together rather than one against the other.
The plural of the word for a self or soul. Read plainly it names each party's own persons, and early scholars discuss how widely its scope extends without reaching one settled answer.
Those who state what they know to be false, as distinct from those who are merely mistaken. The proposal targets deliberate falsehood, which is why sincerity on both sides is its condition.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Oaths were the final instrument of Arabian dispute. Where evidence failed, a man swore, and how serious the oath was depended on what he put at risk in swearing it. An oath taken with children present placed the whole family under whatever followed. So this proposal uses a known procedure and raises it to the most serious form available.
studies.didYouKnow: The invocation described here is one of the few proposals in the Quran that classical sources agree was never carried out. For early scholars the interest lies in the withdrawal, not in any event. A party sure of its position declined a test. It had been invited to help set the terms of that test.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The weight of a religious claim is put in what a person will stake on it. That is not an argument about evidence but about sincerity, and it assumes both sides truly believe God answers. The passage also sets a limit on arguing itself. Once knowledge has come, more argument is not the reply. What is offered instead is a proposal that would end the matter.

crossReferences.why: Sets out a comparable procedure of solemn invocation where ordinary evidence cannot settle a matter.
Puts a similar challenge to another community: wish for death, if you are truthful.
Gives the earlier instruction for the same situation, that the duty ends at conveying.

studies.applyIt: Notice the difference between believing something and being willing to stake something on it. You do not need a dramatic test for this. Ask what you would actually risk on one conviction you state often, and answer honestly. If the answer turns out to be nothing, that is worth knowing before somebody else discovers it.
studies.explainEasier: Some people kept arguing about Jesus even after the truth had come. God gave them a way to settle it. Both sides should bring their families and stand together. Then they should ask God to turn away from whichever side is lying.

studies.title: The Narrative Of Truth
studies.meaning: The long account closes with a summary in three parts. What has been told is the true narrative. There is no god but God. And God is mighty and wise. The order matters, because the story is presented as leading to that statement rather than decorating it. Then a short condition follows: if they turn away, God knows those who corrupt. Early scholars note that the answer to refusal is knowledge rather than punishment, which leaves the matter where it began.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, at the end of the surah's story about Mary and Jesus, just before the well-known invitation to a word held in common. Classical sources place this whole sequence in the discussions with the delegation from Najran. Its position matters: the summary comes after a long and honouring account, and before an appeal. It does not come at the end of a telling-off.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to follow a track. A narrative in Arabic is literally a following of traces, so calling this the true account claims accurate tracking rather than merely honest intention.
From a root meaning to be scarce and therefore precious, and also strong and hard to reach. It combines value with being out of reach, which is why English needs two words for it.
From a root meaning spoilage, used of food going bad and of an arrangement breaking down. It names damage done to something that was working, rather than wrongdoing in the abstract.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Family lines and tribal history were passed on by specialists whose standing rested on getting it right. A reciter caught inventing lost that standing for good. Arabic grew a set of technical words for judging how sound a chain of transmission was. So calling an account the true narrative there was a claim the audience knew how to test.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for narrative gives its name to a later surah. The Quran also uses it of the story of Joseph, calling that the most beautiful of accounts. The root's basic sense is following a track. It gives the verb used when the sister of Moses is told to follow her brother along the river.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A story and a statement of belief are put in one sentence here. An account of a family and two births is offered as an argument for God's oneness, not as a picture of it. The closing words are just as careful. Refusal is met with a statement about God's knowledge, which permits no human response. It leaves the judging where this surah always puts it.

crossReferences.why: Follows immediately with the invitation to a word held in common between communities.
Calls the account of Joseph the most beautiful of narratives, using this same word.
Closes Abraham's prayer with the same two names, mighty and wise, set side by side.

studies.applyIt: Try telling one story about your own life today in a way that ends where it actually leads, rather than where it is most flattering to stop. This verse closes a long narrative with the single claim the narrative was for. Most of us let stories trail off. Notice what yours would have to end on.
studies.explainEasier: This is the true story, God says, and there is only one God. He is strong and wise. If people turn away from that, God knows who is breaking things and spoiling them.

studies.title: Come To A Common Word
studies.meaning: An invitation is issued rather than an argument won. The proposal is held to three things: worship of God alone, joining nothing with Him, and no one among us taking others as lords beside God. That third clause turns the invitation inward as well as outward, naming a failure any community can fall into. If the invitation is declined, the reply given is not a rebuke. It is a statement of your own position.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. Classical sources report this verse in the letters sent to rulers beyond Arabia. The wording shows up in the letter to the Byzantine emperor kept in the early collections. Others tie it to the group from Najran that came to debate with the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). The two settings fit together, and early scholars report both.

keyTerms.note: The adjective means level or even, from the root for equality. It describes ground on which neither party stands higher, which is why the invitation cannot be read as a demand for submission.
The plural of the word used for God as Lord, here applied to human beings. It covers anyone whose word is treated as final, which is why early scholars read it as addressed to everyone present.
An imperative addressed to the ones declining. Instead of arguing further, the speaker asks them to be witnesses to his own position, which turns an opponent into a record keeper.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Diplomacy in that world ran on formal letters, memorised and carried by a single trusted rider, sometimes for weeks. They were read aloud to a court. A message had to state its business in one or two sentences. The messenger had to be able to repeat it, and a hostile audience could not easily twist it. This verse has that shape: short, quotable, and framed so refusing it costs the refuser more than the sender.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for a common word has had an unusually long public life. In 2007 it was chosen as the title of an open letter from Muslim scholars to Christian leaders. The name came straight from this verse. The letters that followed became one of the most widely read modern documents between faiths. Early scholars had already read the verse as a model for address rather than dispute.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The invitation names the least you can agree on, and refuses to inflate it. That is a discipline, not a concession. Including the clause about taking one another as lords puts the speaker under the same test as the person addressed. And the instruction for what to say when refused sets the terms of disagreement: state your position, ask for it to be witnessed, and stop.

crossReferences.why: Instructs argument with the People of the Book in the best manner, on shared ground.
Sets out the method: invite with wisdom and good instruction, and argue in the better way.
Gives a parallel declaration: our deeds are ours, yours are yours, and God will gather us.

studies.applyIt: In your next disagreement about belief, start by naming out loud what you and the other person actually agree on. Say it in one sentence, before anything else. Then stop and let them respond to that. The order in this verse is the whole method. Most conversations of this kind fail because the shared sentence is never said.
studies.explainEasier: The message to Jews and Christians is simple: let us agree on one thing. We all worship God alone. Nobody should treat any other person as if they were God.

studies.title: Arguing About Abraham
studies.meaning: The question is put as a matter of order in time. Abraham lived before either the Torah or the Gospel came down. So a dispute over which later community he belonged to asks what the dates cannot support. The argument is about sequence, not about doctrine. It ends by inviting the listeners to reason it through themselves. Early scholars note the tone: the address is direct, but the reasoning is offered rather than forced on anyone.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, where more than one community in and around the city claimed Abraham. The claim mattered because it carried authority over whose practice was the original. Classical commentaries report disputes of exactly this kind there. The surah's answer does not pick between the claimants.
