It points out that the labels being fought over came into being after the man they are applied to.

keyTerms.note: From the root for advancing a proof. The form used makes it reciprocal, a contest of claims, and the verb comes back several times in this section as the activity being questioned.
The passive of the verb for revelation descending. Using the passive keeps attention on the timing of the event rather than on who caused it, which is exactly what the argument turns on.
From a root meaning to tie or tether, the same word behind the term for a hobble on a camel. Reason in Arabic is the faculty that restrains, holding a person back from running loose.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Claims about ancestry were fought over in Arabia the way property was, and just as hard. Tribes traced themselves back to famous forebears. A claim that held brought precedence, better marriages, and a share in the care of the sanctuary. So arguments about who a distant ancestor belonged to were not about the past. They settled standing in the present, and everyone listening knew it.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran mentions Abraham in twenty-five different surahs, and only Moses is named more often. This surah names him again and again. He is the figure the Quran most often uses as common ground between communities. That is part of why the argument here is fought over him and not someone else.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a limit on how far a later label can be pushed backwards. A group formed around a book cannot claim a man who lived before it, even when it truly traces itself to him. The limit keeps the earlier figure from being taken over. It also says something wider: what a person was is not settled by who later claims him.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same question about several patriarchs, asking whether you know better than God does.
Gives the conclusion two verses later, describing what Abraham actually was.
Describes Abraham as a community in himself, upright, and not among those who associate.

studies.applyIt: Notice the shape of this argument: not a better claim, but a question about the timeline. The next time you argue about who owns a tradition, a phrase, or a founder, check the dates first. Do that before you weigh the merits. It settles more arguments than people expect, and it costs nothing to look.
studies.explainEasier: God asks the people of earlier books why they argue about Abraham. Their books came long after he lived. So those books cannot tell them which group he was in. God asks them to think it through.

studies.title: Neither One Nor The Other
studies.meaning: A line is drawn between two kinds of dispute. There is arguing about what you have some knowledge of, which the verse notes without approving. Then there is arguing about what you know nothing of, which it questions. After that the answer comes plainly: Abraham belonged to neither of the later communities. He is described instead by two words: one means turned away from every false object of worship, the other surrendered to God. He is not claimed for a third party; he is described.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, carrying on the address begun in the verse before. The fight over Abraham was live there. His name backed claims about whose practice was the first one. Classical commentaries describe the argument in general terms. They read the surah's answer as taking away the terms of the fight rather than deciding it. That is why the words used name neither side.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to lean or turn aside. It describes someone who has turned from every false object of worship toward God, and Arabia used it before Islam of people who kept to that alone.
The participle from the same root as the religion named earlier in this surah. Applied to a figure who long preceded any later community, it names a disposition rather than a membership.
The indefinite form is used twice, so the verse speaks of having some knowledge of a matter rather than expertise in it. That makes the contrast one of warrant rather than of qualification.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia before Islam remembered people who rejected the idols. They belonged to no community with a book. The word used here for upright attached to them in ordinary speech. So the audience had a living sense of what it named: someone clearly devoted to one God, and clearly outside the settled religious groups of the region.
studies.didYouKnow: The word rendered upright appears twelve times in the Quran, and most of those uses describe Abraham. It is never used as the name of a community, unlike the two labels this verse turns down. That is part of why it works here as an alternative to both of them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes a claim about what gives religious speech its warrant. Disagreement is not itself the fault; disagreement without knowledge is. Then it answers the original question by refusing both available labels. That suggests the categories communities sort themselves by may not reach back to the figures they are built on. What is offered instead describes which way he faced, not what he belonged to.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same claim by naming the upright way of Abraham, who associated nothing with God.
Calls him the one who named this community, carrying the description forward in time.
Describes a straight religion as the upright way of Abraham, spoken in the Prophet's own voice.

studies.applyIt: There is a specific discipline here: notice when you are arguing past the edge of what you actually know. Pick one topic you have opinions about and locate that edge honestly. Then, in the next conversation about it, say where the edge is, out loud. It is a small thing to say and unusually hard to do.
studies.explainEasier: God asks why people argue about things they do not know. Then He gives the answer plainly. Abraham was not a Jew and not a Christian. He simply turned away from false gods and gave himself to God.

studies.title: Nearest To Abraham
studies.meaning: Who has a claim on Abraham is answered by a test, not by a family line. The closest to him are the ones who followed him, then the prophet addressed here, then those who believe. Early scholars note that descent is not mentioned at all. The verse closes by naming God the guardian of the believers, which quietly replaces the whole frame of the dispute. What was being argued over was patronage, and those last words assign it.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, closing the short section that began with a question about arguing over Abraham. Claims of a link to famous ancestors carried real authority in the region, and communities there traced themselves to him. Classical commentaries read this verse as the answer to the argument set up two verses earlier. It puts a test in place of an inherited claim, one anyone can meet or fail.

keyTerms.note: A comparative from the root meaning to be close and to take charge. It covers nearness and the right that comes with it, so the verse answers a question about entitlement and closeness at once.
The verb of walking behind someone on a road. It names a relationship made by movement rather than by birth, which is precisely the shift this verse is making.
From the same root as the comparative that opens the verse. Ending on this word ties the two halves together: nearness to Abraham is answered by naming who is near to the believers.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Patronage was the structure of Arabian society. A client attached himself to a stronger party. That bond decided who defended him, who spoke for him, and where he stood in any gathering. Claiming a great ancestor was a way of claiming a patron who could never pull out. The last words of this verse speak to exactly the need that made such claims valuable.
studies.didYouKnow: The comparative that opens this verse and the noun that closes it come from the same root. So the argument and its answer are built out of one word. Turns of this kind, where a passage rests on one root in different forms, are a known feature of Quranic style. They are mostly invisible in translation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Belonging is redefined as following rather than descending. That makes a figure from history open to anyone and inheritable by no one. The effect reaches past the dispute at hand, since it removes any claim on God's favour held by right of birth. The closing words complete the move. They name the relationship believers actually have, and that is a gift rather than a claim.

crossReferences.why: Says the covenant with Abraham does not reach the wrongdoers among his own descendants.
Applies the same connection to the community addressed, calling it the way of Abraham.
Names God the guardian of those who believe, bringing them out of darkness into light.

studies.applyIt: Ask what you are counting on that you did not earn: a family reputation, a school, a community you were born into. None of it is bad to have. But this verse puts following where inheritance was, so pick one thing you have inherited and find the actual practice underneath it. Then do that practice this week.
studies.explainEasier: People argued about who Abraham really belonged to. God says the closest to him are the ones who followed him. That means this prophet and the people who believe. God looks after those who believe.

studies.title: They Only Mislead Themselves
studies.meaning: A wish is described, and then its effect turns around. Some among the People of the Book would like to lead the believers astray. What happens is that they lead themselves astray instead. The sharpest part comes at the end: they do not perceive it. Early scholars note the careful limit to a party rather than a whole community. The surah keeps to that limit and returns to it openly a few verses later.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, in the section that addresses the scriptural communities of the city directly. The surah is careful with its scope. It speaks of a group among them here, and describes an upright group among them a few verses later in warm terms. Classical commentaries keep that distinction. No particular occasion is reported, and the sources read it as a pattern rather than one episode.

keyTerms.note: A verb of affectionate wanting rather than of plotting. It names an inclination of the heart, which is why the verse can describe an intention without reporting that anything was done.
A word for a portion of a larger body, from a root meaning to go around. Its use here is a deliberate limit on scope, and the surah keeps to that limit consistently.
From the root behind the words for a poet and for fine awareness. It names subtle noticing, so the denial says the harm is not merely unadmitted but genuinely unfelt by them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A guide who misled a caravan in the desert did not walk a separate road home. He was on the same route, out of water at the same hour. The consequences of his direction reached him first. Everyone who had travelled understood that misdirection is not something you do to other people from a safe distance. The image behind this verse was a practical fact of the trade routes.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a party used here comes back through this surah, and not only of others. It later names two groups among the believers who almost lost heart before a battle. It names a group at Uhud caught up in their own concerns. The surah applies the same limiting word in both directions, which stops it becoming a label for one side.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The verse describes how a moral thing works. An attempt to damage someone else lands first on the one attempting it, and lands unseen. The first consequence of an intention sits inside the person who holds it, and arrives before anything at all reaches the target. The closing words about not perceiving are what make this serious. A harm you cannot feel is one you have no reason to stop.

crossReferences.why: Describes an upright group among the same community, reciting through the night and prostrating.
Uses the same reversal: they deceive only themselves, and they do not perceive it.
States the principle generally: an evil scheme encircles only the people who devise it.

studies.applyIt: Think of a time you wanted something to go badly for someone. Not acted on it, only wanted it. Notice what that wanting did to you while you carried it, and how little it did to them. The claim in this verse is not moral advice; it is a description of where the damage actually goes.
studies.explainEasier: Some people from the earlier faiths would like to pull the believers off the right road. But they only pull themselves off it. And they cannot even tell that this is happening to them.

studies.title: Truth Dressed In Falsehood
studies.meaning: Two questions are put in the same form, and both turn on one phrase: while you know. The first asks why signs are refused by people who are themselves witnesses to them. The second names two separate acts: mixing truth with falsehood, and hiding truth. It attaches knowledge to both. Early scholars observe that neither question asks whether the thing happened. The form takes it as given and asks for a reason, which leaves the answer with the hearer.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, part of the surah's direct address to the scriptural communities of the city. Classical commentaries link the passage to disagreements there about what the earlier scriptures held. They do not fix it to one episode. In this section the surah addresses a party, never everyone. It says so plainly a few verses earlier and comes back to it later.

keyTerms.note: The verb literally means to dress something in a garment. Mixing truth with falsehood is pictured as putting the wrong clothes on a thing, so it is still there and no longer recognisable.
From a root for holding something back within, used of suppressing knowledge, evidence or grief. It names withholding what one has rather than asserting what is false.
The verb covers seeing something firsthand and testifying to it. Its use sharpens the first question, since a witness who denies is doing something different from a stranger who disbelieves.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Testimony held a society together where almost nothing was written down. In a dispute over a debt, a sale or a killing, a witness was the whole evidence. A man known to have hidden what he saw lost his standing for good. Everyone knew the difference between lying outright and simply not saying what you knew. The second was harder to prove and did just as much damage.
studies.didYouKnow: The image of clothing truth in falsehood appears more than once in the Quran. The verb belongs to the ordinary vocabulary of dress. Arabic uses one root for a garment and for confusion. That lets the text describe a subtle twisting with a completely everyday word rather than a technical one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage names hiding as a wrong in its own right, apart from denial. Something can be kept accurately, held in full knowledge, and still be withheld at the moment it would count. Both questions say that those addressed know. So the failure named is one of will, not of understanding. That is where this surah has already placed division among people who share a text.

crossReferences.why: Names the same two acts together: do not clothe truth with falsehood, nor conceal it knowingly.
Traces division among scriptural communities to rivalry arising after knowledge had come.
Speaks of those who conceal what was sent down of clear proofs and of guidance.

studies.applyIt: Concealing is easier than lying and feels almost innocent. Think of one thing you know that would help someone if you said it, and that you have not said because saying it would cost you. You do not have to act today. Name the cost accurately to yourself first, because that is usually where the honesty is missing.
studies.explainEasier: God asks the people of earlier books two things. They turn away from His signs even though they can see them. They also mix the truth with lies and hide it, and they know they are doing it.

studies.title: Believe At Dawn, Refuse By Evening
studies.meaning: A tactic is quoted rather than described. Believe in the morning and reject by evening, the speakers say, so that the believers will turn back. The reasoning behind it is social. People known to have studied the scriptures reverse themselves in public, and others then conclude there was something in it worth reversing. Early scholars note that the passage exposes a plan simply by reporting it. The surah uses that method more than once in this section.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, in the surah's address to the scriptural communities of the city. Classical commentaries report the tactic as concerning the change in the direction of prayer, though they differ over the details. The surah puts it down to a group, not to everyone. The wording of the plan suggests a proposal made among a few people, not a position taken in public.

keyTerms.note: An idiom for its first part, the way a face is the front of a person. Arabic gives the day a face and an end, so the tactic is described as a body turning.
The counterpart to the opening phrase, closing the figure. The pairing marks out a single day, which is what makes the reversal conspicuous rather than gradual and unremarkable.
The verb for going back the way you came. It names the intended effect on others: not a refutation of anything, but a retracing of steps that had already been taken.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Changing religion in a tribal society was public, and it changed structures. It moved a person's alliances and altered who would defend them. It was noticed at once by everyone who mattered, because nobody changed religion in private. That is what makes the tactic here believable. A visible reversal inside one day would have been talked about across the whole city before nightfall.
studies.didYouKnow: This verse quotes a plan directly, in the words of those making it. The Quran does that in several places with the schemes of opponents. Early scholars note that reporting a private proposal in public was itself a kind of answer. The tactic depended entirely on nobody knowing it was a tactic.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage assumes that conviction spreads both ways. People take their bearings partly from what others do. That is a realistic account of how belief moves, and the passage does not condemn it. What it exposes is the deliberate use of it as a lever. The tactic also depends on religious commitment being visible, and the surah elsewhere treats that visibility as a strength rather than a weakness.

crossReferences.why: Describes wavering between two sides and belonging fully to neither, in similar terms.
Portrays those who profess belief without holding it, and the sickness in their hearts.
Continues the quoted speech, adding the instruction to trust only those of your own religion.

studies.applyIt: You are more influenced by other people's confidence than you think, and so is everyone around you. Pick one commitment you have quietly softened because somebody you respect seemed unimpressed by it. Reconsider it on its own terms this week, without reference to them. The tactic in this verse only works on people who have never done that.
studies.explainEasier: Some people made a plan. They would say they believed the new message in the morning, then say they did not believe it by evening. They hoped that would make the believers doubt and go back.

studies.title: Guidance Is God's Guidance
studies.meaning: Someone is telling his own people to trust no one outside their religion. God answers that advice with something much larger than the quarrel it came from. Guidance is God's guidance, so it is not a thing any community owns and hands around. Then comes the second answer: all grace is in God's hand, and He gives it to whomever He wills. Early scholars spend a long time on the words in between, because they can be read more than one way: it is not clear who is speaking there, or where the quotation ends.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, and the address begun one verse earlier is still running. The worry underneath it is a real one for any community with a long tradition: what we were trusted with might be handed to someone else as well. Classical commentaries say this passage meets that worry directly instead of brushing it aside. That is why the answer is about God's freedom to give, and not about anyone being unworthy.

keyTerms.note: The word carries the definite article, so it names guidance as one single thing rather than a quality a person might own. Tying it to God takes it off the list of what a community holds in trust.
The root means what is left over and above, an excess. It names a gift beyond anything owed, which is exactly why no party can stand up and claim it as a right.
A participle from the verb to be wide. It says God has room, and here that means giving to one party leaves nothing less on the table for anyone else.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wells, grazing land and trade routes were limited, and most goods were genuinely rival: what one tribe used, another could not. Standing worked the same way. Precedence was a fixed amount split among a small number of claimants, and everyone knew it. So hearing God described as vast pushed straight against the instinct of the room. The first listeners would have felt how strange that word was.
studies.didYouKnow: The last word about God in this verse says He has room, and the Quran almost always pairs it with knowing, as it does here. Early scholars read that pairing as a guard. Plenty does not mean handing things out carelessly. The giving is unlimited in how far it reaches and exact in where it lands.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God is described here as a giver who does not run low, and that changes the thing you are tempted to fight over. Guidance and grace are not shares in a fixed stock. They are gifts from someone with more than enough. So a community somewhere else receiving something takes nothing away from you, and the whole logic of religious rivalry loses its footing. This does not deny that revelation is truly given to particular people at particular times.

crossReferences.why: Says God singles out for His mercy whom He wills, answering a very similar reluctance.
Says plainly that guiding people is not the messenger's work to do, but God's alone.
Finishes the thought at once: He singles out His mercy for whomever He wills.

studies.applyIt: Notice the small drop you feel when someone outside your circle does well at something you care about. That reaction is assuming a fixed supply of good things. This verse ends by saying there is room. Try it once this week: when the feeling arrives, say the person's name out loud and one true good thing about what they did.
studies.explainEasier: Some people said to trust only those who follow your own religion. God answers that guidance comes from Him. Good things are in His hand. He gives them to whoever He wants, and He has plenty to give.

studies.title: Singled Out For Mercy
studies.meaning: The argument running through the verse before ends here in one line, and the line is about God rather than about anyone's claim. Mercy is assigned, and it is assigned to whomever He wills. The verb means to set something apart for one particular receiver, not to hand it out at large. Early scholars point out that no reason is ever offered for why this person and not that one. The dispute did not need one. Knowing where the decision sits was enough to settle it.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, at the close of a section answering a hard worry: that revelation might be given to people outside your own community. Two verses do the work together. The first says all grace is in God's hand. This one says it is placed deliberately. Classical commentaries treat the pair as the surah's answer to a long argument about which community holds what. Neither side walks away with a test to apply.

keyTerms.note: The root means to set apart for one particular case, the opposite of what is general. It describes a gift addressed to someone by name rather than scattered over a crowd.
From the root that also gives Arabic its word for a womb. The Quran uses this term for guidance, for revelation and for rain, so what is assigned here is deliberately left wide.
The root is connected to bone, so the sense is of something with mass rather than merely something large. It describes the grace as having weight, and not only reach.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Gifts in Arabia were public and specific. A chief handed things out at a gathering and everyone watched who received what, so a gift said as much about a relationship as it moved goods. Being singled out mattered more than the value of the thing itself. The verb in this verse belongs to that world, where the choosing was the part that carried meaning.
studies.didYouKnow: Three descriptions of God arrive one after another at the close of this short section: vast, knowing, and holder of immense grace. Ending a passage on God's names is a habit of the Quran rather than an accident. Early scholars read the particular names chosen each time as a summary of the argument just made.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Mercy here is specific, not merely general, and that changes what kind of thing it is. A mercy that reached everyone equally would be a feature of the world, like weather. A mercy assigned on purpose is an act, and an act has someone behind it with intentions. Those intentions are never explained. So the person who receives is left holding gratitude rather than an account of why he deserved it.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb of God singling out His mercy for whomever He wills.
Sets up this conclusion by placing all grace in God's hand, given to whom He wills.
Tells the People of the Book that grace is in God's hand, given out as He wills.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing in your life you did nothing to arrange: where you were born, a person who took an interest in you early, some capacity you simply have. Name it specifically rather than in general. The verb here means singled out, and the practice it suggests is working out what was addressed to you.
studies.explainEasier: God chooses who will receive His mercy, and He gives it to whoever He wants. What He hands out is very great. That choice belongs to Him alone, and no one else can make it.

studies.title: A Heap Of Gold, A Single Coin
studies.meaning: Two men can belong to the same community and be nothing alike, and this verse says so without flinching. Leave one of them a fortune and he hands it back. Leave the other a single coin and you will not see it again unless you stand over him. Then the verse names the belief that made the second man feel entitled: we are under no obligation towards outsiders. What is condemned is not so much the unpaid coin as the rule invented to excuse it. That rule, the verse says, is put in God's mouth knowingly.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, where the surah is speaking to the scriptural communities living in the city. Trust across those lines was ordinary daily business. Deposits, loans and goods moved between people who did not share a religion, because there was no other way to trade. Classical commentaries read this as describing a real pattern of conduct. They also hold to the even-handedness of the verse, which names the trustworthy man first.

keyTerms.note: From the root that gives Arabic its words for faith, for safety and for a deposit left in trust. To entrust someone is to make yourself safe with them, which is why the same root covers belief.
The same word used earlier in this surah for heaped-up wealth. Early Arabic dictionary writers argued over the exact quantity, but never over its sense of an enormous and unnamed sum.
The participle for standing, used of someone who stays there and will not leave. It pictures a creditor physically planted until he is paid, which is what recovery looked like without courts.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina had no bank and no bailiff. A trader leaving for a season handed his savings to somebody he judged safe, and the whole system rested on what people said about you. A man known to give deposits back drew business. A man who did not was left alone, though he could rarely be forced to pay. Standing over a debtor until he handed the money over was a shabby thing everyone had either done or watched.
studies.didYouKnow: The two amounts in this verse cannot actually be compared: an unmeasured heap of gold set against one named coin. Classical writers on style treat that as deliberate. Give the extremes and the listener fills in everything between them. The word for the larger sum turns up earlier in this same surah, inside a quite different argument.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Conduct and community are pulled apart here. The honest man and the thief are placed inside the same group, and the verse will not let either one stand for the whole. Then it goes further. Limiting your honesty to your own people is called a lie told about God. So the mistake in what a person believes comes first, and the mistake in what he does follows from it.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same refusal to generalise, describing an upright group inside the same community.
States the general rule: hand trusts back to the people they belong to.
Describes a deposit given without any written record, and calls for the trust to be discharged.

studies.applyIt: Notice whether your standard of honesty shifts with the person in front of you: a stranger, a large company, someone from outside your circle. It probably does shift a little, and the shift usually arrives with a reason attached. Pick one such case this week and hold yourself to the standard you would use with a friend.
studies.explainEasier: Some people of the earlier books will give back a whole pile of gold you left with them. Others will not give back one coin unless you keep asking. They think they owe nothing to outsiders.

studies.theme: The Love Between God and the Believer
studies.title: God Loves The Mindful
studies.meaning: A single word opens this verse and knocks over the claim just quoted. On the contrary: the debt is owed. What follows is not a rebuke but a description, and it is put positively. Whoever keeps his commitment and guards himself is loved by God. Early scholars notice the move from one awkward case to a general rule, and from a named group to anybody at all. A claim about who deserves your honesty is answered with a door left open to everyone.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, just after somebody has said that no debt is owed to outsiders. The surah's habit here is worth watching: it meets a narrow claim with a wide rule, not with a charge of its own. Early scholars point out that the reply names no community at all. That is what makes it a fix to the rule itself, and not an attack on the people who were using it.

keyTerms.note: A particle used only to overturn a negative statement, so a plain yes will not carry it. Its whole job is to contradict a denial that has just been said out loud.
From the root for completeness, used of paying a debt in full. Keeping a commitment is described as paying it right out, with nothing quietly held back at the edges.
The root means to take shelter behind something. It names people who move carefully because they are aware of what they are avoiding, not people who have reached a rank.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A promise in Arabia was enforced by nothing but reputation and kin. There was no registry, no contract law, and no authority that could compel a man across a tribal boundary. What held the whole system together was simple enough. A person's word was the entire sum of their credit, and everyone knew whose word was good. A promise kept was the currency the economy actually ran on.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah says what God loves and does not love more often than most chapters of the Quran do. The statements are scattered along its whole length rather than gathered in one place. That gives the surah a running commentary on character, laid alongside its arguments about belief and history.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God's love is attached here to a condition anyone at all can meet. The condition is a kept promise, not a membership and not a rite, which puts plain reliability among the things that matter most. The wording repays attention too. The verse does not say God loves the man who did this. It names a whole class of people. So the love reads as a settled leaning rather than a reaction.

crossReferences.why: Quotes the very claim this verse overturns, that no obligation is owed to outsiders.
Opens a whole surah with the instruction to fulfil commitments, before anything else is said.
Says a commitment will be asked about, treating the promise itself as something you answer for.

studies.applyIt: Think of a small promise you made recently and have quietly let slide, the kind nobody would ever chase you for. Do it today, badly if necessary, rather than well next month. The word here means paid in full, and small unpaid promises are the ones that decide what people can really rely on you for.
studies.explainEasier: God says that keeping your word does matter. Whoever keeps a promise and stays careful about right and wrong is loved by God. It does not depend on which group a person belongs to.

studies.title: Sold For A Small Price
studies.meaning: This verse treats a broken promise as a sale, and all its force sits in the price. What gets handed over is a covenant with God and a person's own sworn word. What comes back is called small, and it is never named. Four things follow, and three of them are withdrawals rather than punishments: no speech, no look, no declaring clean. Early scholars notice that the pain itself is mentioned last and briefly. It reads as though losing God's regard were the heavier half of the loss.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, in the run of verses about trusts and kept commitments. Early scholars report several occasions behind this one, all of them involving false oaths sworn to grab property or win a dispute, and the reports disagree on the details. So the sources take it as a general word about oaths sworn lightly. It landed in a world where a sworn word settled cases no evidence could reach.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary verb for purchase, used in the Quran for trading one thing away to get another. Calling this a purchase makes the person an active party who looked at the terms and said yes.
Left deliberately unmeasured. Early scholars say any price at all would be small against what is given up, so the word describes the exchange itself rather than the sum received.
An old word for a lot assigned to someone, from the root for creating and dividing up. It names not a reward but the share a person would have had, which is why its absence reads as loss.
The root covers growth and cleansing together. It carries the sense of pronouncing someone clean as well as making them so, so what is withheld here is vindication as much as washing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An oath sworn in front of witnesses closed a case. Where there was no document and no outside witness, a solemn oath was the last tool anyone had, and communities accepted it because the other option was violence. A man who swore falsely walked off with the disputed property. The whole system held together only because most people believed a false oath cost more than the goods were worth.
studies.didYouKnow: Two of the three withdrawals named here turn up together again in Surah 2, where God will not speak to certain people and will not declare them clean. That passage is about hiding revelation for a price. The Quran repeats clusters of denials like this, and adding the third item makes this the fullest form of them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: What this verse threatens is mostly the end of a relationship, not a penalty. Not being spoken to, not being looked at, not being declared clean: each one is a withdrawal of regard, and all three are listed before any mention of pain. So the weight of the loss sits somewhere other than where fear usually puts it. Your word given to God is treated as something that holds you in His view.

crossReferences.why: Names the same withdrawals, of those who hide what was revealed in exchange for a price.
Warns against using oaths as a tool of deceit, and calls the price a little thing.
States the positive form just before this: God loves the one who keeps his commitment.

studies.applyIt: Think about what you have actually traded your word for lately. Usually it is not money. It is convenience, or getting out of an awkward conversation, or looking better than you are. Name the price out loud in its real currency. This whole verse is about the exchange rate, and most of us have never once checked ours.
studies.explainEasier: Some people trade away their promise to God and their own sworn word for a small gain. They will have no share in the life to come. God will not speak to them or look at them.

studies.title: Twisting With The Tongue
studies.meaning: There is a way of misleading people that never quite tells a lie, and this verse catches it in the act. Some of them bend their tongues while reciting, so that what you hear sounds like scripture and gets taken for it. Then the denial comes twice over: it is not from the Book, it is not from God. Early scholars argue about what the twisting involved, whether a change of delivery, of wording, or of the sense, and they keep the whole range open. Nobody disputes how it works. It leans on the authority of a voice, not on a claim you could examine.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, where the surah is speaking to the scriptural communities of the city. Reciting the earlier scriptures there was a public act and a respected one. Early scholars tie this verse to live disputes about what those scriptures actually said. They read it as describing a practice rather than one particular day. The Quran keeps it narrow, as it does all through this section, and names only a party among them.

keyTerms.note: The verb for pulling something out of its straight line, used of twisting a rope or turning the head aside. Applied to tongues, it makes the distortion physical rather than merely an idea.
The plural of the organ, which in Arabic also means a language. Putting the fault in the tongue rather than in a text places it in the delivery, where a listener cannot inspect it.
A verb of counting and supposing, from the root for reckoning up. It names a guess made on thin information, which is exactly where anyone sitting and listening to a recitation stands.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Scripture in that world was heard far more often than it was read. Few people could check a text, copies were rare and costly, and authority sat with whoever was reciting. A trained voice carried its own weight, and a crowd listening to a language it did not fully command had no way to test what it heard. The weakness this verse names was built into how people met the Book.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb here for twisting shows up elsewhere in the Quran for people turning their heads away, and the same root gives Arabic its word for a bend in a road. The picture holds steady across all of them. Something that ought to run straight is being pushed off to one side without ever being snapped.
studies.theologicalSignificance: This names a kind of dishonesty that leaves every single statement standing. Nothing is denied, nothing is openly made up, and the false impression comes out of the delivery alone. Calling that a lie about God, rather than a lie about a text, sets a high bar for religious speech. You answer for the impression you created, and not only for the words you used.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same twisting of tongues, adding that it is a slander against the religion.
Speaks of writing a book with your own hands and calling it God's, for a small price.
Names the matching act a few verses earlier: dressing truth in falsehood and hiding it.

studies.applyIt: Notice the gap between saying something false and building a false impression out of true things. The second is far more common and much easier to excuse. Pick one time this week when you were accurate on the surface and misleading on purpose. Then go back and correct the impression, rather than the words.
studies.explainEasier: Some people twist their words while reading out loud. They make it sound like it comes from the holy book when it does not. They say it is from God when it is not, and they know.

studies.title: No One Given Scripture Would Say
studies.meaning: This verse is about something a prophet simply could not do. A man handed a book, sound judgement and prophecy would never turn round and ask people to worship him. Instead the verse puts words in his mouth: be people of the Lord. It uses a rare term for those who belong wholly to God, and then roots that condition in two very ordinary jobs, teaching scripture and studying it. Early scholars notice that what is offered instead of worship is a practice, not a rank.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. The surah is dealing here with the Christian community of Najran, and with wider arguments about how much a prophet or a teacher is owed. Early scholars report that the verse answers a blunt question. Could the obedience owed to God be handed to a prophet instead. The answer speaks of prophets in general and names no single one, as this whole section does.

keyTerms.note: From the root for making firm and for handing down a ruling. Named apart from the Book, it points to the knack of applying what you know, which owning a text does not give you.
A rare word built straight on the word for Lord. Early Arabic dictionary writers tie it to deep learning joined with devotion, and use it of teachers whose knowledge is turned toward God.
From a root meaning to wear away by passing over again and again, as feet wear a road into a track. Study in Arabic is smoothing something by returning to it, not taking it in once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Teachers in that world held real power over their students. Religious standing across the region ran through scholars who could read what most people could only hear, and a teacher's word settled how a whole community prayed and lived. The pull this verse describes was nothing imagined. Everyone listening knew of houses whose loyalty followed one learned man wherever he went.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for people wholly given to the Lord shows up only three times in the entire Quran, once here and twice in a later surah. Each time it names learned teachers among earlier communities. It is one of the rarest terms the Quran has for a kind of religious person, and nothing else quite matches it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A limit is set on religious authority from inside the office rather than from outside it. The very gifts that make a man worth following are what make a demand for worship impossible from him. The aim of teaching moves too. Those taught are meant to become people of the Lord themselves. So teaching is pointed at your standing on your own feet before God, not at leaning on the teacher.

crossReferences.why: Carries the same argument on: nor would he tell you to take angels and prophets as lords.
Shows Jesus asked about exactly this, and disowning it in the plainest terms available.
Describes a community taking its scholars and its monks as lords apart from God.

studies.applyIt: If you learn from someone, a teacher, a speaker, a writer, notice whether the effect is to send you toward the source or to keep you coming back to them. Both patterns are common enough. Test it this week by acting on one thing you learned from them without checking back in with them first.
studies.explainEasier: No one God gave a book and prophethood would tell people to worship him. He would tell them to belong to God instead. That is what teaching the book and studying it is for.

studies.title: Angels And Prophets Are Not Lords
studies.meaning: The same argument runs straight on. A man who could not ask to be worshipped could not tell you to take angels or prophets as lords either, so the ban reaches past his own case to every go-between there is. Then the verse closes with a question rather than a proof: would he order you to refuse God after you have given yourself to God. Early scholars notice that the question does the work an argument would otherwise have to do. You are meant to feel how odd it sounds.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, and this verse and the one before it are a single argument. Reverence for angels and for prophets was alive in several religious communities of the region, and the surah does not stop to list the forms it took. Early scholars read the verse as addressing the principle rather than any one practice. That matches the way this whole section speaks of prophets in the plural.

keyTerms.note: The plural of the word the Quran uses throughout for God as Lord. Its root covers owning, raising and ruling all at once, so taking someone as a lord means putting your affairs under him.
A verb for adopting or picking something up for your own use. It puts the act on the person doing it, rather than on any status the other party has claimed or asked for.
From a root meaning to cover or bury, used of a farmer covering seed with soil. Refusal in Arabic is pictured as covering something already there, not as failing to notice it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia before Islam treated go-betweens as a normal part of religion. Gods were approached through lesser figures, and some held that certain beings were partners of the high god, a belief the Quran takes up elsewhere. The first listeners understood the pull of a go-between straight away. They had only just walked out of a system built around one.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for lord turns up here in the plural, which is unusual, since the Quran normally uses it of God alone and in the singular. The plural shows up only a handful of times in the whole Book, and every time it sits inside an argument about go-betweens. The number of the word is part of the point.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Here God closes a door that religious history keeps pushing back open, where honour paid to a genuinely honourable figure slowly turns into something else. What is striking is how the door gets closed. Angels and prophets are not brought down an inch. Their standing is left completely intact, and only the direction of worship is fixed. That split between honouring someone and worshipping them is what this section rests on.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same plural word for lords in the call to a common word between communities.
Describes a similar arrangement, taking scholars and monks as lords apart from God.
Answers a similar argument, insisting Jesus was a servant on whom favour was placed.

studies.applyIt: Notice who you go to first when something goes wrong. Not who you believe in, but who you actually call. There is nothing wrong with having people you trust, and this verse brings nobody down. It only asks you to know the order, and the order shows in what you reach for first.
studies.explainEasier: A true prophet would never tell people to treat angels as their masters. He would not say that about other prophets either. He would not ask people to turn away from God after they had given themselves to God.

studies.title: The Covenant Of The Prophets
studies.meaning: God takes a pledge here, and He takes it from the prophets themselves rather than from the people who followed them. The terms are conditional. You have been given scripture and wisdom; if a messenger comes confirming what you hold, you will believe in him and support him. Scholars differ over whether the pledge binds the prophets in person or their communities through them, and the early commentaries keep both readings. The scene ends with their yes, a call to bear witness, and God naming Himself among the witnesses.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, and the argument that started with what a prophet could and could not say now closes. A live question sat underneath it in that city. Was accepting a later messenger a break with an older covenant, or one of the terms of that covenant. Early scholars read this verse as the surah's answer. Supporting a confirming messenger is written into the original agreement, not set against it.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to tie firmly, related to a trusted bond and to a knot. It names an agreement made secure, and is a stronger word than the ordinary Arabic one for a promise.
A word for a heavy load, or a tie that holds something down. It names a duty by its weight, and the Quran uses it elsewhere of burdens people ask to have lifted off them.
From a root meaning to settle and come to rest. Affirming in Arabic is letting a matter settle into place, so the question asks whether the terms have been taken as final.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Covenants in Arabia were sealed in public, and the people standing round were the whole of the enforcement. The two parties said the terms out loud. Everyone there was expected to remember them and to speak up if a dispute came later. A covenant with no witnesses was worth almost nothing. The scene here follows that shape exactly, down to the call for the parties to bear witness themselves.
studies.didYouKnow: God names Himself among the witnesses to His own covenant. That is a strange thing to find in any agreement, because a witness is normally a third party to it. Early scholars read it as a way of making the covenant heavier to carry. This surah reaches for the language of witnessing again and again, including in the disciples' prayer to be written among the witnesses.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God is shown running one long agreement, not a series of replacements. Each prophet had already accepted, in advance, that he would back a later messenger who confirmed what he held. That makes the handing on a term of the first covenant rather than a break in it. For you, that means recognising a later revelation is loyalty to the earlier one, and not a betrayal of it.

crossReferences.why: Recalls a covenant taken from the prophets, naming several of them one by one.
Describes a covenant taken from those given the Book, to make it clear and not hide it.
Speaks of a messenger found already described in what earlier communities held.

studies.applyIt: Think about a commitment you made in advance, before you knew what it would cost: a marriage, a job, a friendship, a faith. Promises like that are agreed under one set of conditions and tested under another. Name the one you are inside right now, and what it is actually asking of you today.
studies.explainEasier: God made a deal with the prophets. Each one was given a book and wisdom. If a later messenger came and agreed with what they had, they would believe him and help him. They all said yes.

studies.title: Willingly Or Unwillingly
studies.meaning: Turning away after you have said yes has a name, and the first of these two verses gives it. Then the second pulls the camera back as far as it will go, and asks whether some religion other than God's is really being looked for. Everything in the heavens and the earth has already surrendered to Him, willingly or not. Early scholars say that phrase is holding two things at once. Creation surrenders because it has no choice. People who choose surrender because they chose. Neither one is folded into the other.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, at the close of the section about the covenant of the prophets. The question asked here is put in general terms and aimed at no named group. Early scholars read the pairing as a typical move of this surah, which keeps stepping out from a particular quarrel to a frame as wide as the universe. They also note that the argument is drawn from creation rather than from scripture, so it stands on its own feet.

keyTerms.note: From a root used of a date bursting out of its skin. It names stepping outside a line rather than denying the line is there, so it describes conduct after an agreement, not before.
A pair of nouns naming the two ways of complying. Setting them side by side covers the whole range without saying which creatures fall where, which lets one phrase describe everything at once.
The same verb as the religion named earlier in this surah, used here of the heavens and the earth. One word for creation's surrender and for a person's is the move the passage turns on.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything in that world could be seen obeying something. The stars turned on a schedule navigators trusted with their lives, the seasons came round, the camel knelt when it was made to kneel. People were the obvious exception, the one part of the arrangement that answered back. Listeners living that close to the physical world would have felt the contrast the question rests on.
studies.didYouKnow: The pair of words for willing and unwilling shows up only four times in the whole Quran. Three of those describe the entire created order surrendering or bowing down, and one describes human spending. The phrase is nearly reserved for statements about creation as a whole, which is exactly the job it is doing here.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God's claim is grounded in something you can walk outside and look at, not in a text, which means it can be put to anybody. If everything else already surrenders, your question is not whether you will surrender to anything. It is whether you will do it knowingly. That gap between going along with something and agreeing to it is where the whole weight of your choice sits.

crossReferences.why: Says everything in the heavens and earth bows to God, willingly or unwillingly.
Reports the heavens and the earth answering that they come willingly when called.
Supplies the covenant that turning away, in the first of these two verses, points back to.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of your day you already spend going along with things you never chose: gravity, tiredness, needing to eat, other people's schedules. The question here is not whether you will surrender to anything at all. It is which of those you have ever actually agreed to. Pick one and agree to it on purpose today.
studies.explainEasier: Whoever turns away after that is going outside the line. Everything in the sky and on the earth already gives itself up to God, whether it wants to or not. And everything goes back to Him.

studies.title: We Make No Distinction
studies.meaning: The believers are told to say what they believe, and what they say is a long list on purpose. What was sent down here. What was given to Abraham and his line. What Moses and Jesus and the prophets received from their Lord. Then comes the line that carries the weight: we make no distinction between any of them. Early scholars read that as a refusal to pick and choose, taking one messenger and turning down the next. They do not read it as a claim that every prophet stands at the same rank.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, straight after the covenant of the prophets and what followed from it. The words are put in the community's own mouth, and they answer a running dispute in the city about which revelations count. Early scholars point out that almost the same sentence appears in an earlier surah. They read the repeat here as that creed being put to work inside the arguments this chapter has been making.

keyTerms.note: A word for the lines that came down from Jacob's sons, from a root tied to spreading out. It names a lineage as a whole rather than any one man, which keeps the list from becoming a roll call.
A strong verb for cutting a thing into parts. Denying it means refusing to sort the messengers into accepted and rejected, which is exactly the habit this verse is answering.
The participle from the root this surah uses for the religion God accepts. Putting it at the very end turns the whole list before it into an account of what that surrender is made of.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Alliances in Arabia were held or broken one clan at a time. You could be at peace with one branch of a tribe and at war with another branch of it. Picking and choosing was simply the shape of politics. So a refusal to separate, stated here about messengers, cut against a habit of mind the first listeners used on nearly every relationship they had.
studies.didYouKnow: Almost this same declaration appears twice in Surah 2. The wording shifts a little each time, and so does the person speaking. Comparing the three versions is a standard exercise in the commentaries. The small changes show one creed placed in different mouths and put to work inside different arguments.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Faith is defined here partly by something it will not do. Accepting some messengers and rejecting others is the same mistake whichever ones you keep, because it leaves you as the one doing the choosing. The list also gathers in figures that other communities call their own. That turns a statement of belief into a map of what you share with them, rather than a fence.

crossReferences.why: Gives almost the same declaration, with the same list and the same refusal to separate.
Describes those who believe in some messengers and reject others, and names it plainly.
Puts the same words in the mouths of the believers, adding that they hear and obey.

studies.applyIt: Read the list slowly and notice how many of these names belong to communities you may think of as other. The creed you hold already has them inside it. If you have ever talked about those communities as though they had nothing to do with you, read this verse twice before the next such conversation.
studies.explainEasier: The believers say out loud what they believe. They believe in God and in what He sent to them. They also believe what was given to Abraham, Moses, Jesus and the other prophets. They accept all of them without leaving any out.

studies.title: What Will Not Be Accepted
studies.meaning: The word translated Islam is the noun for handing yourself over to God. The verse says that anything else a person goes looking for as a religion will not be taken from him. Early scholars read the word against the surah's own earlier meaning of it, and against the list of prophets just given. On that reading it names the stance every prophet taught, not a group set apart from them. The verb for seeking matters too. It pictures a man going after some other way, not a man who never met this one.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, and the order of the verses is the point. First comes the creed naming Abraham, Moses and Jesus and refusing to separate them. This verse follows straight out of it, so early scholars insist the two be read together. The surah has already defined the word in question much earlier, in a passage about people splitting apart after knowledge had reached them.

keyTerms.note: A strong form of the verb to seek, describing a deliberate hunt. It names someone actively going after an alternative, not someone who has simply never been reached by anything.
The noun from the root for handing a thing over whole. This surah has already used it for what every prophet brought, and that is the sense early scholars carry into this verse.
A word out of trade, naming a merchant whose venture comes back worth less than it cost him. It describes how a deal turned out, not a penalty dropped on someone from outside.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Trade was how Arabians understood risk. A merchant put money into a caravan, and he either came back with a profit or came back short. The word for that shortfall was ordinary trading talk, nothing more. So calling the outcome of a whole life a loss was not name-calling. It was an accounting word, and it landed on people who had watched ventures fail.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for religion and the word for surrender both turn up earlier in this surah. They come together in a single verse that sets out how the two relate. Those passages sit more than sixty verses apart. The later one simply takes the earlier one as read. That is one way this surah builds a single argument across its whole length.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Everything here turns on what the central word means, and the surah took care to define it before using it this way. Read as handing yourself over to God, the claim is not that you need a label. It is that you need a posture. The list of prophets just given shows that same posture running through every revelation. So the verse stays as demanding as it sounds without turning into a question of membership.

crossReferences.why: Defines the same word earlier in this surah, as the religion accepted with God.
Supplies the creed just before it, naming every prophet without separating them.
Describes whoever hands his face over to God while doing good as having his reward.

studies.applyIt: The word at the centre of this verse means handing something over whole. Pick one area of your life you have held back, not out of defiance but because you never got round to it. Name it exactly. Then hand over the smallest decision inside it today, and notice what that actually feels like.
studies.explainEasier: God says that He will only accept one thing from a person. That is giving yourself over to Him. Anyone who looks for some other way will end up with nothing in the life to come.

studies.title: After They Had Believed
studies.meaning: God asks a question here rather than handing down a verdict, and the question is about guidance, not about punishment. How would He guide people who refused after believing, after testifying that the messenger is true, and after clear proofs had reached them. Early scholars notice that three layers of knowledge are stacked up before the refusal arrives. What is described is not a mistake but a turning back on what you already knew. The closing line widens it to anyone and gives the condition a name: wrongdoing.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. Early scholars report occasions involving people who walked out of the community and later wanted back in, though the reports vary in their details and in who they concern. Because they differ, the sources take this as a general word about reversing yourself after knowing better. They also give real weight to the verse a few lines on, which opens a door back.

keyTerms.note: A question about the way something could happen, not about whether it could. It asks by what road guidance would reach such a person, which leaves more open than a flat no would.
From a root meaning to stand out and be sorted from the rest. The word names evidence that has already done its work, so it describes clarity reached rather than clarity offered.
From a root for darkness, and in use for putting a thing where it does not belong. Wrongdoing in Arabic is misplacing, which is why one word covers injustice and setting others beside God.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Turning back in a tribal society was ruinous, and so it was rare. Leaving a community meant leaving its protection behind, and returning meant facing every person who had watched you go. People did it anyway, pushed by family, by debt or by fear. The first listeners knew of particular cases by name. That is part of why the surah takes the situation head on.
studies.didYouKnow: This passage runs to four verses, and the last of them turns the severity right around. That verse opens with a single word meaning except. The shape is a habit of the Quran, where long warnings are often closed by an exception, and this one names the people who turn back and put matters right.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The trouble here is placed in the person, not in God's willingness to help. Guidance is not described as held back in anger. It is described as having nothing left to work with, because everything guidance normally brings has already arrived and been set aside. Calling the state wrongdoing rather than error makes it about what you did with what you knew, not about what you managed to understand.

crossReferences.why: Turns this passage around three verses later, excepting those who repent and set things right.
Describes moving in and out of belief again and again, and what it does to guidance.
Separates a man forced to speak against faith from one who opens his chest to refusal.

studies.applyIt: Notice that this is a question and not a sentence, and notice where the passage goes three verses later, which is to an exception. If you are carrying something you think has put you outside the door, read to the end of the passage before you decide. Most people stop at the severity and never reach the line that follows.
studies.explainEasier: These people believed and then turned away from it. They had already seen that the messenger was telling the truth. They had seen clear proof of it. God asks how He could guide people who did that.

studies.title: Except Those Who Turn Back
studies.meaning: These three verses run from the heaviest words in the whole section straight into their reversal. First the penalty is named: shut out by God, by the angels and by all people. Then it is not lightened, and no one is given more time. Then comes a single word meaning except, and everything before it is suddenly limited. Early scholars point out that turning back on its own is not what gets named here. It is paired with putting things right, so an inward change is tied to a repair somebody could see.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, at the close of the passage about walking away after belief. Early scholars report that people in exactly this position did come back. They understood the exception as covering real cases, not as a polite form of words. The sources also read the order as chosen on purpose. The severity is said in full first, so that what follows cannot be taken as softening it.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to drive away and expel. The English word curse suggests a spell; the Arabic describes a distance opening up, being put outside rather than harmed by a formula.
A passive verb from the root for lightness of weight. It pictures the punishment as a load, so relief would mean carrying less of it rather than carrying it for a shorter time.
The verb for returning to a place you came from. Repentance in Arabic is a change of direction rather than a feeling, which is why this verse can pair it with a visible act.
From the root for soundness and for making peace between people. It names mending what got broken, and putting it here stops the turning from being a purely inward event.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Being driven out was the harshest thing an Arabian community could do to a person. It stripped away protection completely, and a man in that state could be killed with nobody answering for it. That is why exile was saved for the gravest offences. Coming back was possible, but it took a public act of repair, usually a payment. The wording of these verses sits right on top of that procedure.
studies.didYouKnow: The shortest word in this whole passage is the one that undoes it, the word meaning except, which opens the last of the three verses. Early scholars point out that the Quran often hangs such a clause off its severest statements, and always in the same place. It comes once the warning has been said in full.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God states a consequence at full weight and then, in the same breath, allows an exception to it. Holding both is the point, since either one alone would give you a false picture of Him. Pairing the turning with repair says something further about what He is asking. The way back is open, and it opens onto work rather than onto a declaration you make once.

crossReferences.why: Asks the question these verses answer, about guidance after knowledge was pushed aside.
States the widest form of the same promise, telling servants not to despair of God's mercy.
Joins repentance to good action, and describes bad deeds being swapped for good ones.

studies.applyIt: If you have decided something is past mending, notice that this passage names two things and not one: turning back, and repairing. The second is usually the part that has actually been dodged. Pick the smallest piece of repair open to you, something plain and doable this week, and do that one first.
studies.explainEasier: These people are shut out by God, by the angels, and by everyone else. Their punishment will not be made any lighter. But there is one way out of it. If they turn back and put things right, God forgives.

studies.title: Deeper Than A Single Turn
studies.meaning: The verses just before held a door open for anyone who turns back and repairs. This one describes a case where that door has shut. The wording is careful: refusal after belief, and then more refusal piled on top of it. Early scholars say the weight sits on those added layers, because what is named is not one reversal but a settled direction that keeps going. Several of them read the closing of repentance as belonging to the hour of death, when turning has become impossible rather than merely unwanted.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, immediately after the line that let in those who repent. The commentaries insist on reading the two together, since one opens what the other seems to close. The classical sources tie this verse to people who left the community and then kept walking further from it. The reports disagree about who and when, so the commentaries take the description as a general one.

keyTerms.note: A reflexive form of the verb to add, so the increase is something a person does to himself. It describes a build-up over time rather than one act, which is what sets this case apart.
The noun from the verb for returning. Naming it as a thing they own, their turning, points at something offered rather than at a mood, which is why scholars ask when it is offered.
From a root used of a traveller losing the road, and of a thing that has been mislaid. It names being off the path rather than fighting it, which is a very different picture from defiance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A traveller who took a wrong turn in the desert could fix it within the hour and be fine. The same wrong turn, held for a day, carried him past the wells he knew and out beyond his own memory of the route. Distance did the damage, not the first mistake. Every caravan traveller understood that an error grew costlier the longer you kept walking it.
studies.didYouKnow: This verse and the one before it sit side by side and pull in opposite directions. One lets repentance in. The other says it will not be taken. Early scholars treat that pairing as deliberate rather than as a snag in the text, and a good deal of the commentary literature is about how to hold the two together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God is drawing a line between one reversal and a direction of travel. What is put beyond acceptance is not a single act but a course that keeps being added to. So the danger here is built-up momentum, not the size of any one decision. Read beside the verse before it, the two together describe a door that stays open and a person who can walk too far to turn round.

crossReferences.why: Opens the door this verse seems to shut, for those who turn back and put things right.
Says repentance is not for those who keep going until death is at the door.
Describes faith arriving too late to help, once the consequence is already in sight.

studies.applyIt: The line drawn here is between a mistake and a direction. Look at something you have been doing that you already know is wrong, and ask honestly whether you are still at the first stage or have been adding to it for a while. Then turn now rather than later, because this verse is about distance.
studies.explainEasier: Some people believed, then turned away, and then went further and further away. Their turning back will not be taken any more. They have wandered right off the road and lost their way.

studies.title: The Earth Full Of Gold
studies.meaning: The biggest sum the language can build is named here, and then refused. Gold enough to fill the whole earth would not be taken as a ransom from someone who died refusing God. Early scholars notice that the verse never calls the gold worthless. It says the payment will not be taken, which is a statement about the deal and not about the metal. The closing words repeat a phrase used earlier in this surah, about having nobody at all to help you.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, closing the run of verses about turning away after belief. What is described is a state at the moment of death, not the state of any living person, and early scholars press that point hard. The argument turns on how final the state is, not on how harsh it sounds. No particular occasion is reported for it, so the sources take it as a general word following the discussion before.

keyTerms.note: A construction naming however much it takes to fill a thing. Applied to the earth it gives you the largest amount ordinary Arabic can say, without naming any number at all.
From the root for buying a captive back, a deal people across Arabia knew well. It assumes a world where almost anything at all could be settled for the right price.
Named exactly, rather than left as wealth in general. Gold was the one good whose worth held across borders and across generations, which is why it stands here for value itself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ransom was ordinary business. Captives taken in raids went home for a payment, blood claims were settled in camels, and even a life had a price on it. The system was practical rather than cold, since it kept feuds from eating whole tribes. In that world, hearing that a payment would not be taken was stranger than hearing the price was high. It meant stepping outside the system entirely.
studies.didYouKnow: The picture of the earth's fill of gold offered as ransom turns up elsewhere in the Quran with a twist. There, the wrongdoers would offer everything on earth and as much again beside it. The figure comes back in several places, and every time it describes a trade that cannot be made.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God is marking the edge of what can be bought. Almost everything in the first listeners' world could be settled with a payment, so the verse names the largest payment anyone could imagine in order to say that this is not that sort of matter. The difference is in kind, not in amount. That is why the line about having no helpers follows so naturally on its heels.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same picture, everything on earth offered twice over, and refused as ransom.
Denies that any ransom will be taken or any pleading accepted on that day.
Ends with the same phrase about having no helpers, earlier in this surah.

studies.applyIt: Notice how many of your problems you quietly solve with money or something like it: time bought, jobs paid away, discomfort handed to someone else. That is not wrong and it works. Then name one thing in your life that is genuinely not of that kind. Most people can find one, and most people avoid looking at it.
studies.explainEasier: Some people refuse the truth and die still refusing. If one of them tried to pay with enough gold to fill the whole earth, it would not be taken. Nobody will come to help them.

studies.title: Until You Give What You Love
studies.meaning: Two things happen here, and the first one lands on anybody who has ever given away what they did not want. You will not reach goodness until you spend from what you love, so what is being measured is your attachment and not the amount. Then the ground shifts to an old argument about food. Everything was allowed to the Children of Israel except what Israel held back from himself, before the Torah came down. And the challenge follows: bring the Torah and read it out, if you are telling the truth.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. Early scholars report that companions of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) answered the first verse the same day. They gave away the particular things they valued most. The reports name different people and different gifts, but they agree on the pattern. The second verse belongs to the surah's long argument with the scriptural communities of the city, about which food rules came first. It asks them to bring out the text itself.

keyTerms.note: A word for wide, open-handed good, from a root tied to open land. It covers devotion, kindness to parents and honest dealing all at once, which is why the Quran uses it as a summary.
The verb for laying out money, from a root also linked to a tunnel and to something running out. Spending in Arabic is pictured as draining away, not as passing to another person.
The ordinary verb for love, used here of things you own. It turns the condition from a quantity into a relationship, since two people giving the same sum are not doing the same thing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in Medina was specific and had names on it. A man did not own a portfolio. He owned a particular date grove, a particular well, a named horse. Everyone knew which property was whose, and which of a man's holdings he cared about most. So giving from what you loved was a public act, and the whole community could see exactly what had changed hands.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for goodness here anchors one of the best-known passages in Surah 2, where goodness is defined as a list of beliefs and practical acts rather than as facing a direction in prayer. The two passages define the same word from opposite sides. One does it by content, this one by cost.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God sets the condition inside the giver, not inside the gift. A donation that costs you nothing may still help somebody, and it is not called worthless, but it is described as not reaching the thing named. So what you were holding on to sits at the centre of the question. The verse then adds that God knows whatever you spend, which reaches the gifts nobody ever sees.

crossReferences.why: Defines the same word for goodness by a list of beliefs and acts, rather than by direction.
Warns against giving away the poor part of what you have, which you would not take yourself.
Describes people feeding others while loving the food, and wanting nothing back for it.

studies.applyIt: Look around the room you are in and find something you would rather not give away. That is this verse's measure, and it has nothing to do with the price tag. You do not have to part with that object. But give something this week whose absence you would actually notice, and see whether it registers differently.
studies.explainEasier: You will not be truly good until you give away something you love. God knows whatever you give. All food was allowed for the Children of Israel. The only things left out were the ones Israel gave up himself.

studies.title: The First House For People
studies.meaning: A warning, an instruction and then a claim about a place, all in three short verses. Anyone who invents things about God after that challenge is named a wrongdoer. Then the instruction: follow the way of Abraham, who leaned toward God and was not among those who set up partners. And then the ground shifts entirely, to the first house ever set up for people.
