Early scholars read that third verse as settling a question of who came first. It points past the argument to a building older than any side in it.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. Early scholars tie this passage to live arguments in the city about which sanctuary came first. The community had lately been told to turn toward Mecca in prayer, so the question was not academic. The surah's answer is about dates, not about winning a point. It matches the argument made earlier about the timing of the Torah and the Gospel next to Abraham himself.

keyTerms.note: A word for the whole practice a community follows, different from the word for religion used elsewhere here. It names a road walked by a group rather than loyalty owed to a person.
A name for the valley of the sanctuary, used only here in the Quran. Early scholars discuss how it relates to the familiar name, and link it to crowding and people pressing together.
The passive of the verb to place. Leaving the builder unnamed at this point puts the weight on how early the house stands in time, rather than on whose hands raised it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sanctuaries organised Arabian life. Trade fairs, truces and pilgrimage seasons all gathered around them, and the tribe that kept one drew income and standing from it. So a claim about which sanctuary came first was a claim about money as much as about religion. The first listeners heard this as a statement about where the real centre of the peninsula lay.
studies.didYouKnow: The name used here for the sanctuary's valley appears nowhere else in the whole Quran, and the familiar name appears exactly once, in a later surah. Early Arabic dictionary writers link the form used here to a root meaning to crowd or press together. They tie that to how thickly people stand around the house.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God rests the claim on dates rather than on merit, the same move the surah made about Abraham and the later scriptures. What is being said is that this house came first in time, and that its purpose was never narrow. It was set down for people, and it is called guidance for all beings. That makes it a sign rather than a possession, and the next verse goes on treating it that way.

crossReferences.why: Shows Abraham and his son raising the foundations of this same house, and praying over it.
Uses the same argument from dates earlier in this surah, about Abraham and the scriptures.
Describes the site of the house being shown to Abraham, with instructions for its use.

studies.applyIt: The argument here rests on what came first. Try that on something you inherited without ever asking: a family habit, a way of marking a season, a phrase you use all the time. Go and find out where it actually started. Knowing where a practice began usually loosens your grip on the version you were handed.
studies.explainEasier: God says to follow the way of Abraham, who turned to God alone. The first house of worship ever built for people stands at Bekka. It is blessed, and it is a guide for everyone.

studies.title: Whoever Enters It Is Secure
studies.meaning: The house is described by what stands inside it and by what happens to people who come. There are clear signs, and one gets named: the place where Abraham stood. Then comes safety. Early scholars read that in two ways at once, as the old inviolable safety of the sanctuary and as the safety of anyone who arrives there looking for God. The journey is owed to God by whoever can manage it, and being able is written into the same sentence. Then the last words turn unexpectedly gentle. God has need of nobody.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, inside the section arguing over which sanctuary came first. Early scholars place this verse before the community could get to Mecca at all, since the city was still shut to them. So the passage describes a journey its first hearers were not able to make. That timing is part of how the sources read it. The description arrived well ahead of the opportunity.

keyTerms.note: A noun of place from the verb to stand. It names the spot where a man stood rather than a monument, so the sign is a place marked by an act, not by anything built on it.
From the root that gives Arabic its words for faith and for trust. Safety and belief share a root, so entering the house safely and entering it in faith fall inside one word family.
From a root meaning to be rich and to do without. It says God gains nothing at all from any of this, which puts the whole practice on the side of the one performing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The sanctuary could not be violated, and that was the one dependable truce in Arabia. Men who would have killed each other on the open road stood side by side inside its boundary. Traders came to its seasons under a safety no tribe would break, and blood feuds paused at its edge. That security was the most valuable arrangement the peninsula had. Even those who kept idols in the house respected it.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for the standing place of Abraham shows up only twice in the Quran, here and in an earlier surah, where the instruction is to take it as a place of prayer. Both times it is fixed to this same sanctuary. Nowhere in the text is there any description of what it actually looks like.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The closing words are the ones that change everything. A journey is described that costs people real money and real time, and then God says He has no need of any of it. That takes the trade out of the picture. Nothing is being delivered to God, so whatever the journey does, it does inside the person who makes it. The safety promised at the house works the same way. It is received, not earned.

crossReferences.why: Names the same standing place and instructs that it be taken as a place of prayer.
Describes the call going out, and people arriving from every deep mountain pass.
States the same point in general: you are the needy ones, and God is free of need.

studies.applyIt: Notice the line about God having no need of any of it. Whatever you do today that you think of as religious, nothing is being handed over to anyone. It changes the taste of an act to remember that its whole effect lands on you. Hold one small practice today with that in mind and see what shifts.
studies.explainEasier: Inside the house are clear signs, like the place where Abraham once stood. Anyone who walks in there is safe. People who are able to make the journey owe this trip to God. God needs nothing at all from anyone.

studies.title: Why Turn Others Away
studies.meaning: God puts two questions to the People of the Book, and the second one cuts deeper than the first. Why reject the signs of God, when God is watching everything you do. Then the second: why turn people who have believed off God's path. Why look for a way to put a bend in it, when you can see the road yourselves. Early scholars notice the move from what a man does with his own belief to what he does to somebody else's belief. Both questions end by naming God as watching, not by naming a punishment.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, in the surah's address to the scriptural communities of the city. Early scholars tie this section to efforts made to unsettle the young community there. Old tribal quarrels were stirred up again. Doubts were raised about the new direction of prayer. The reports of single incidents disagree with one another, so the sources read these verses as describing a pattern rather than one day.

keyTerms.note: The verb for barring someone from a road, used of a physical block as much as of talking a person out of something. It names an effect on movement, not on opinion.
A noun for a bend or a warp, used of a stick that will not lie straight. Applied to a path it means putting a kink in it, so the road still goes somewhere, just not where it did.
The plural of one who testifies and one who is simply present. It is used of the people addressed, and in the singular of God two lines earlier, setting two kinds of witnessing side by side.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A road in Arabia could be spoiled without ever being closed. Move a cairn, fill in a well, or give a traveller a slightly wrong bearing, and a whole caravan ends up in country it cannot cross. Nobody had to block anything. Bending the route was the cheap and deniable form of obstruction, and every traveller knew how small a change it took.
studies.didYouKnow: Both verses end on God's awareness instead of on a threat, and they use two different wordings for it. One says God witnesses what is done. The other says God is not unaware of it. That second one is a double negative, which Arabic uses to say a thing harder than the plain positive would.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God separates refusing something yourself from stopping somebody else from reaching it. He gives the second one the longer question. So what you owe reaches past your own choices, out to the mark you leave on other people. Both questions land on being watched rather than on punishment. That leaves the weight where this surah usually puts it. You are seen, and the verse treats that as enough.

crossReferences.why: Names those who disbelieve and turn others from the path of God, joining the two acts.
Describes those who bar others from God's way and want it crooked, in very similar words.
Uses the same pair of verbs of people who bar from the path and want a bend in it.

studies.applyIt: There is a difference between not doing something yourself and making it harder for someone else. Think of a person in your life who is trying to get more serious about something good. Notice whether your reaction has made that easier for them or slightly more awkward. Then change one small thing about how you respond next time.
studies.explainEasier: God tells the messenger to put two things to the people of the book. They turn away from God's signs while God watches them do it. They also try to keep other believers off God's road.

studies.title: Who You Listen To
studies.meaning: The address swings round, and now it is the believers being spoken to. What they are warned about is not being argued with. It is going along. If you comply with a party of those given the Book, they will send you back after your belief. Early scholars point at the verb, which means returning a thing the way it came. They point too at the word party, since this surah keeps the warning off a whole community and on particular people. What is being described is influence, not force.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. Early scholars tie this verse and the ones after it to a single incident, when old hostility between the two main tribes of the city was stirred back to life on purpose. It came close to fighting between men who had made peace only a few years earlier. The reports agree on the shape of it while differing on details. The passage about holding to God's rope, three verses on, is read as the answer to it.

keyTerms.note: The verb for willing compliance, from a root meaning to do a thing readily. It describes going along with someone rather than being talked round by them, which is why the warning picks it.
From the root meaning to return a thing to where it came from. It pictures a reversal as a road walked backwards, rather than as a new place somebody has arrived at.
One of the limiting words this surah keeps reaching for. It holds the warning on particular people acting in a particular way, and off a whole community.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The two great tribes of Medina had fought a long and exhausting war before the community formed, and it had ended only a few years before. The grievances were fresh, the dead were still named one by one, and men who now prayed together had faced each other in the field. Reviving that memory took no invention at all. It only took somebody raising it at the right moment.
studies.didYouKnow: This warning opens a short passage that holds one of the most quoted lines in the whole surah, the one telling people to grip God's rope together and not to separate. The warning and the remedy stand only three verses apart. Early scholars read them as one piece, written to answer one incident.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God puts the danger in going along with people, not in hearing them out. You can listen to a case all the way through and walk off unmoved. Falling into step with someone is the thing that changes you. So who you follow matters in itself, before any claim of theirs gets examined. And the remedy the surah gives a few lines later is not a better argument. It is people holding on together.

crossReferences.why: Gives the answer three verses later: hold to God's rope together, and do not separate.
Shows people on that day saying they obeyed their chiefs, and were led off the path.
Describes regret over a companion who turned someone away after the reminder came.

studies.applyIt: Think about whose approval you actually adjust yourself for. Not who you admire, but who you would soften a position in front of. Everyone has someone. Name one, and remember what you last changed because of them. This verse is not asking you to cut anybody off, only to watch the thing working.
studies.explainEasier: God speaks to the believers here. If they go along with some of the people who were given the book, those people will pull them back. They would lose the faith they already have.

studies.title: Hold On Until The End
studies.meaning: How could you turn away, God asks, when His words are being recited among you and His Messenger is standing there. The question is a reproach, and the answer arrives in the same breath as a remedy. Whoever takes firm hold of God has been guided to a straight path. Then the bar goes up: revere God as He truly deserves. And it gets pinned to the hour of death, so the instruction is about lasting rather than about starting well.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. The classical sources tie this passage to one particular day. Somebody set out to reopen the old feud between the two main Arab clans of the city, reciting poetry about a battle they had fought before the migration. The reports describe men reaching for their weapons before the quarrel was cooled. These verses and the ones just after them came down into that scene, which is why they turn straight to unity.

keyTerms.note: The verb for gripping something to save yourself, used of clinging to a rock or a rope. It pictures a body in danger, not a mind agreeing, and it comes back two verses later as a command.
Literally the full due of being mindful of Him, a phrase that sets no measurable limit. Early scholars read it alongside a later verse telling believers to be mindful as far as they are able.
The instruction is not to die, but to be in this condition whenever death arrives. Arabic says that with one participle, which is why the line reads as a command about staying, not about dying.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The two clans being addressed had fought a war within living memory. Many men in that mosque had lost a father or a brother to the other side. Feuds in that culture were kept alive by recitation, and a poem naming a killing held the debt open for generations. One well-chosen verse recited in a marketplace could restart a conflict that had already cost hundreds of lives. That is exactly what these verses interrupted.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb here for taking firm hold comes back two verses later as a direct order. There the whole community is told to grip the rope of God together and not to divide. Early scholars read the pair as one motion. First one man's grip is described, then the same grip is made shared, with the incident behind them supplying the reason.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God sets the bar for reverence with no ceiling on it, and then ties it to endurance rather than to intensity. That moves the whole demand off peaks and onto keeping going. Fixing it to the hour of death, which nobody can put in a diary, means the only way to meet it is to be in that state all along. And what is offered for wavering is not more effort. It is holding on to something outside yourself.

crossReferences.why: Turns that one grip into a shared one, and names the feud these verses healed.
Tells believers to be mindful of God as far as they are able, read alongside the bar set here.
Shows Jacob giving his sons the same charge, not to die except in surrender to God.

studies.applyIt: Ask what you actually hold on to when things get hard: a person, a plan, a distraction. Name it honestly, without deciding yet that it is wrong. Then pick one moment in the coming week, when the difficulty lands, to reach for prayer first instead. The word here is about grip, and grip is trained by repeating it.
studies.explainEasier: God asks how people can turn away when His words are being read to them. Hold on to God and you stay on the right road. Stay that way right up to the end of your life.

studies.title: The Rope And The Pit
studies.meaning: One command arrives in two halves: hold on together, and do not break apart. The word for holding is the same one used for gripping a rock above a long drop. Then comes the reason, and it is a memory rather than an argument. You were enemies, He joined your hearts, and by that favour you became brothers. The last picture is a ledge above a fire pit and a hand pulling you back from it. That turns the old hostility into a disaster you survived, not an awkward chapter you have moved past.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, and this is one of the more firmly reported occasions in the whole surah. The classical sources describe someone reviving the memory of a battle fought between the city's two main Arab clans before the migration. They describe the anger it raised in men who had been reconciled only a few years earlier. These verses came down into that gathering. The word brothers named a relationship those same men had lately been fighting against.

keyTerms.note: A rope let down to someone below, and in Arabic also a pact of protection between tribes. Early scholars gloss it as the Quran, as the covenant, or as both, and keep the range open.

A reflexive form, so the splitting is something the group does to itself. Arabic marks that in the verb, which makes this a warning against self-inflicted breakage, not against being broken by others.
The verb for making things familiar and joining them into one, related to the word for composing a book. It describes closeness created rather than a truce imposed, which is the claim being made.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina before the migration had been a town at war with itself. Its two main Arab clans had fought for years, and the last big battle sat inside the living memory of most adults in the mosque. Alliances with the town's other communities had shifted all through it. Men praying in the same row had killed each other's relatives. So the word brothers here was not warm language. It named a recent and unlikely fact.
studies.didYouKnow: A rope let down to you had a precise legal sense in Arabia. When a strong tribe offered protection to a weaker one, the agreement was described in exactly this language. Early scholars note that the picture therefore binds both sides. Whoever holds the rope is tied by the pact as well as saved by it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God takes the credit for the peace, not the men who made it, and that turns any later division into ingratitude as well as a political mess. He also reframes a town making up as a rescue, which raises the stakes a long way. And there is only one rope. So what holds you together is not a deal struck between you. It is what each of you has a hand on.

crossReferences.why: States that no wealth on earth could have joined these hearts, and that God did it.
Names believers as brothers, and makes reconciliation between them the response.
Gives the single person's version of the same grip, in the verses just before this one.

studies.applyIt: Think of one relationship in your community that was repaired and has quietly started fraying again. A branch of the family, a group of friends, people at your mosque. Do the small unglamorous thing this week, the message or the visit, before the fraying hardens into a position. This verse calls division a fire, and you have been pulled back from it once already.
studies.explainEasier: Hold on to God together and do not split apart. Remember that you used to be enemies. God brought your hearts together and made you brothers. You were at the edge of a fire and He pulled you back.

studies.title: A Group That Calls To Good
studies.meaning: There should be a group among you with three jobs: calling people to what is good, urging what everyone already recognises as right, and holding them back from what is wrong. The order is not accidental, since the invitation comes before either instruction. Those who do this are named as the ones who come out well. Then the warning arrives by contrast, pointing at communities that split up and argued after clear evidence had reached them. So what is dangerous here is the splitting, not the not knowing.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. These lines come straight after the verses that healed a quarrel between the city's two main Arab clans, one that nearly turned into fighting. Early scholars read the placing as the building half of that episode. Having stopped the community from breaking apart, the passage hands it a job to do. The reference to those who divided after clear proofs came is usually read as pointing at earlier communities, not at any group in the town.

keyTerms.note: A group held together by a shared purpose rather than shared ancestry. The Quran uses it of nations, of religious communities, and once of a single man, so its size is set by its job.
From the root for knowing. It names good that a society already admits is good, which roots the work in shared ground rather than in a standard nobody has heard before.
The mirror construction, from the root for denying or failing to recognise. The pair makes moral work a matter of reminding people what they know, not of importing something foreign.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina had no police force and no standing court. Order was kept by clan elders, by public reputation, and by ordinary men willing to speak up in a market or a courtyard when something was wrong. A community that would not correct itself had nothing else to fall back on. So handing this work to a group inside the town described something the first listeners already lived. It was the line between a working settlement and a lawless one.
studies.didYouKnow: The paired words for recognised good and rejected wrong come together in nine verses of the Quran, and the pairing became the standard name for a whole field of Islamic writing on conduct. Early scholars argued over the grammar of this one verse. Some read the group as a special part of the community, others as the community itself. Both readings are still held.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God makes moral work shared and organised rather than leaving it to each person's private conscience, which turns the health of a community into a religious matter. Putting the invitation first sets the tone for all of it. The work starts by calling people toward something, not by stopping them. And the failure named is splitting apart after the evidence was clear. So staying together is treated as a condition for the work, not a prize for finishing it.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same three tasks to the community as a whole, brought forth for humanity.
Sets out how the calling is done: with wisdom, good teaching, and the better argument.
Names urging one another to truth and to patience as what saves people from loss.

studies.applyIt: The next time you see something wrong in a group you belong to, start with the first of the three jobs rather than the third. Say what the better thing would look like before you say what is wrong with the present one. It is slower and it works more often. This verse puts the invitation first for a reason.
studies.explainEasier: Some people in every community should call others to do good. They should speak up against wrong. Do not be like the groups who broke apart and argued after the truth was made clear to them.

studies.title: Faces On That Day
studies.meaning: A whole day gets described through nothing but faces. Some are bright, some are darkened, and not a word is said about what caused either. Then the darkened ones are addressed with a question that is really a reminder: did you refuse after your belief. Early scholars point out that the picture comes straight from everyday Arabic. A bright face means relief and being proved right. A darkened face means grief and disgrace. So what is happening is not a verdict being read. It is a condition becoming visible.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, after the call to hold together and the warning about breaking apart. Early scholars read these faces as the outcome of the argument that came before them. The question put to the darkened faces uses wording the surah has already used, about refusing after belief. No occasion is reported for it. The passage does its work as the close of a long run of verses.

keyTerms.note: A verb of colour change, used in Arabic for a face lit up by relief or joy. It describes brightness rather than skin, and the same root is used of eyes gone dim with weeping.
The matching verb. In Arabic a face going dark names grief, shame or dread, and the Quran uses the same idiom of a man handed news he did not want to hear.
The verb for tasting, used of meeting something directly and in person. It makes the consequence known from the inside rather than watched from outside, which is why it is chosen here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Faces did the work of documents in Arabia. Judgements were handed down in gatherings, and a man's outcome was read off him as he walked back to his people, before he had said a word. Everyone there knew what a returning face meant. In a place with no written verdicts, the face was where a decision became public. That is why this picture needed no explaining at all.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses this exact pair of colour verbs for faces in a later surah, where they describe people who lied about God. It uses the darkening idiom elsewhere too, of a man told that he has a daughter. So the image belongs to plain Arabic speech long before it belongs to any scene of judgement.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God shows you an outcome without showing you a trial. What surfaces on that day is a condition made visible, not a sentence being announced, which suggests the state was already there and is only uncovered. That is a very different picture from a courtroom where the result is still in doubt. The question put to the darkened faces fits it. They are asked to recognise something, not informed of it.

crossReferences.why: Gives the other half at once: bright faces are inside God's mercy, and they stay there.
Describes faces on that day shining and looking, and others drawn and braced for disaster.
Sets bright laughing faces beside faces covered over with dust and darkness.

studies.applyIt: Faces give people away long before words do. Spend a day noticing your own. Look in a mirror after a hard conversation, or in a dark screen. Not to judge what you see, only to notice what it already tells anyone looking. This passage assumes a life becomes visible in the end, and some of that showing starts early.
studies.explainEasier: On that day some faces will be bright and some will be dark. The dark ones will be asked if they gave up their faith after they had it. Then they will taste what follows.

studies.title: God Desires No Injustice
studies.meaning: The other half of the scene comes in a single clause, and the wording puts it in space rather than in feeling. The bright faces are inside God's mercy, and they stay there. Mercy is a place you are in, not a mood someone is having. Then the view pulls back twice. These are the signs of God, recited to you in truth, and God wants no injustice for anybody. And everything in the heavens and on earth is His, with every matter going back to Him.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, closing the long stretch that ran from the warning about division through to the faces. Early scholars treat these three verses as a summing-up of everything argued since the surah began talking to the scriptural communities. They state the principle underneath all of it. Then they put the whole business back in God's hands and leave it there.

keyTerms.note: A preposition of containment. Mercy is entered and stayed inside, which turns a quality into a location, and the Quran uses the very same construction of the gardens.
The phrase covers truth, reality and what is owed all at once. Reciting with it means the content is accurate and the reciting is properly done, and early scholars keep both senses.
A passive verb with a plural noun covering affairs, commands and situations. Nothing is said about who does the returning, so the process stays open and only the destination is named.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything in Arabian life went somewhere in the end to be settled. Disputes went to a judge, debts went to a reckoning, a caravan went to its destination. Nothing was simply left hanging, because an unsettled matter meant danger that carried on and on. So the idea that all affairs go somewhere to be decided was not a lofty thought. It described how their world already ran.
studies.didYouKnow: The line saying that all matters return to God appears several times in the Quran, and every single time it comes at the end of a passage, never at the start of one. Early scholars notice that placing. The phrase works as a way of closing something rather than opening it. It marks where an argument has finished.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The middle verse is the one that carries the other two. Straight after a scene of judgement, God says He wants no injustice for anyone at all, which makes everything just described the outcome of what people did rather than something wished onto them. And that line sits between the scene and the statement that everything belongs to Him. So His ownership can never be read as power used on a whim.

crossReferences.why: Gives the other half of this scene, the darkened faces and the question put to them.
Says God does not wrong anyone by the weight of an atom, and multiplies whatever is good.
Repeats the same principle in other words: God wills no injustice for His servants.

studies.applyIt: Take one line out of these three verses and sit with it: God desires no injustice for anyone. If you carry a suspicion that things are stacked against you, hold that line for a minute rather than arguing with it. You do not have to settle anything today. Notice only whether you actually believe it, and answer that honestly.
studies.explainEasier: The people with bright faces are inside God's mercy, and they stay there. These are God's signs, read out truly. God wants nothing unfair for anyone. Everything belongs to Him, and everything goes back to Him.

studies.title: The Best Community And Its Conditions
studies.meaning: Being called the best community sounds like a compliment until you read the rest of the sentence. Three things come attached: you urge what is good, you forbid what is wrong, and you believe in God. Early scholars read those as the grounds of the ranking, not as trimming on it. The opening verb is in the past tense, and scholars differ over whether that means the community was this in God's knowledge from the start, or is being reminded what it was brought out to do. Then the last line refuses to write off everybody else.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. Much of this surah deals with how the community got on with the People of the Scripture in the city, and with its recovery after the defeat at Uhud. The verse sits in a run of passages setting a community held together by a shared job against one pulled apart by rivalry. Early scholars report no single agreed occasion for it, and read it inside that argument.

keyTerms.note: From a root for a mother or a source. It names a body of people tied by something they share, a direction, a calling, a moment in time, rather than tied by blood.
A passive verb for being drawn out or made to appear, used elsewhere of crops pushed up out of soil. The community did not make itself. It was raised for a purpose.
Literally the known, the familiar. It covers what plain human sense already sees as decent, so the good being urged is nothing exotic. It is what people admit when they are honest.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In Medina a person's standing came off the family line. Which clan, which alliance, how many fighting men could be called out for a quarrel. Rank was inherited and then defended with poetry and raids. Now Meccan emigrants, Medinan hosts and clans lately at war with one another were told their rank lay in what they did rather than in who they came from. That was a genuinely strange arrangement.
studies.didYouKnow: This verse is fenced with qualifications on both sides. Its own last clause says that some of the People of the Scripture do believe. Three verses later the surah says outright that they are not all alike, and describes a group among them who recite through the night and bow down. The generalisation is never left standing alone.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God ranks a community by what it does, not by what it is. That means the ranking can be lost as easily as it was given. The order of the three things is worth noticing too. Two duties toward other people come before belief is named at all, so faith is shown running out into public life rather than sitting off to one side. And the closing line keeps the whole claim from hardening into contempt.

crossReferences.why: States the same commission as the job of a group inside the community, a few verses back.
Calls the community a middle nation set as witnesses over people, in the same language.
Corrects any sweeping reading at once, naming an upright group among the People of the Scripture.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing this week that you would normally let pass: a rumour repeated in a group chat, a colleague talked about unfairly. Say something, briefly and without heat, and then let it go. This verse ties the community's worth to small interventions exactly like that, made by people who would rather have kept quiet.
studies.explainEasier: God tells this community they are the best one raised up for people. But that comes with a job. They tell people to do good, warn them away from wrong, and believe in God.

studies.title: No Harm Beyond Insult
studies.meaning: God puts a ceiling on what your opponents can actually do to you. The harm, He says, will reach no further than words that wound. And if it comes to fighting, the result is named before it starts: they turn and run, and nobody comes to their aid. Early scholars read this as reassurance given at one particular moment, not as a standing rule about every future encounter. They also notice the word chosen for the harm. It covers annoyance and injury of the kind that never reaches anything vital.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, right after the passage calling this community one raised up for the good of people. Early scholars place these verses in a stretch of real pressure from groups in and around the city. They read them as spoken to people who had good reason to feel outnumbered. The reassurance belongs to that setting, and the surah turns shortly afterwards to a battle that went badly.

keyTerms.note: A word for harm that stings and wounds without destroying. The Quran uses it of insult, of discomfort and of small injury, so it names a kind of damage rather than a degree of it.
An idiom for running away, built on the word for a back. Arabic describes a retreat by what the pursuer sees, which lands harder than the plain word for flight would.
The passive of the verb for coming to someone's aid, from the root used earlier in this surah of the disciples. The passive leaves the helper who never arrives completely unnamed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Insult was a weapon in Arabia, and a serious one. A satirical poem could damage a tribe's standing for a generation, and poets were hired to do exactly that. So being told that opposition would go no further than words was no small comfort to those listeners. Words were the thing they feared most after the sword, and sometimes ahead of it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for harm turns up more than twenty times in the Quran, covering things as different as verbal abuse, physical discomfort, and the wound left by a boastful gift. Its range is wide enough that early Arabic dictionary writers define it partly by what it leaves out. It is damage that does not destroy.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God draws a line around what opposition can reach, which is a different promise from saying none will come. The insults and the irritation are conceded outright, and the claim is only about where the damage stops. That is a particular kind of comfort, and an honest one. It neither denies that the thing hurts nor lets the hurt settle the question for you. You are left free to feel the sting without drawing a conclusion from it.

crossReferences.why: Says plainly that you will hear much hurt, and ties it to patience and being mindful.
Tells the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) to let their hurt go, and rely on God.
Names giving with no reminder and no hurt after it as the giving that keeps its reward.

studies.applyIt: Someone will say something to you this week that stings and changes nothing at all. Notice the gap between how much it hurts and how much it actually does. Those two amounts are almost never the same, and the whole comfort of this verse lies in keeping them apart. Name the second one out loud. It usually turns out to be small.
studies.explainEasier: These people cannot really do you any harm. All they can do is say things that sting. If they fight you, they will turn round and run away. And no one will come to help them.

studies.title: Except By Two Ropes
studies.meaning: Humiliation and hard living are described here as having settled over a community in the past, like a tent pitched over them. The causes are named right inside the verse: refusing God's signs, killing prophets, disobedience and going too far. But two exceptions sit in the middle of it, and both are called ropes. One comes from God and one comes from people. Early scholars read them as a covenant with God and a bond of protection or treaty with other human beings. So the way out is named in the same breath as the condition.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, in a stretch of the surah that keeps moving between describing and qualifying. Early scholars read this as an account of a past state tied to named conduct, and not as a permanent verdict on any people. The very next verse says plainly that they are not all alike, and describes an upright community among them. The sources treat that next line as part of how this one is to be read.

keyTerms.note: A passive verb used of pitching a tent over a place. The picture is of something set up above and around people, so the state is a covering rather than a quality they own.
The word for a rope, used in Arabic for a covenant or a deal of protection. The same picture turns up a few verses earlier, where believers are told to grip God's rope together.
From the root that gives Arabic its word for the poor and for stillness. It names being unable to move or improve your position, rather than poverty counted as a bare sum.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Protection deals were the fabric of Arabian security. A group with no treaty was exposed everywhere it went, and a group with a bond could travel and trade in safety. People spoke of such deals as ropes and as ties. Everybody knew that the gap between a safe life and an exposed one was often one arrangement with a stronger party.
studies.didYouKnow: The picture of a rope shows up twice inside ten verses of this surah. Once it is God's rope, which believers are told to hold on to together. Once it is here, as the exception to a described condition. The same everyday word carries a promise in one place and an escape route in the other.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God names causes here rather than declaring what anyone is, and that is exactly why the next verse can say they are not all alike. Read together, the two say something about how consequences work. Conduct gets named, its effects get described, and the description is stopped before it can harden into a label. The two ropes do the same work from inside this verse. A way out is left standing.

crossReferences.why: Follows straight after and says they are not alike, naming an upright community among them.
Uses the same picture of a rope from God, as what believers are to hold to together.
Describes the same condition and names the same causes, in an earlier surah's account.

studies.applyIt: Notice that this verse names causes and then, one line later, refuses to let the description turn into a label. That is a discipline worth borrowing. When you catch yourself explaining a whole group by a pattern, say the next sentence as well: they are not all alike. Say it out loud, and mean it about one specific person you know.
studies.explainEasier: This community was covered over with shame and hard times. The verse says why: they refused God's signs and they killed prophets. But two things could still protect them. A bond with God, and a bond with other people.

studies.title: They Are Not All Alike
studies.meaning: Four words at the start of this verse take back the sweep of everything before it: they are not alike. What comes next is warm all the way through. Among the People of the Book there is an upright community, and they recite God's verses through the hours of the night, and they bow down. Early scholars note the word for upright, which pictures something standing firm. They note the choice of the night hours too, because that puts the practice where nobody is watching. Nothing in the description is hedged.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, immediately after a passage describing a condition and the conduct behind it. Early scholars treat that placing as the whole point of the verse. It stops the description before it from being spread over everybody. Some sources tie it to members of the city's scriptural communities who had joined the young community. Others read it more widely. Nobody disputes the praise itself.

keyTerms.note: A word for evenness, used of a level surface and of two things of the same measure. Denying it says the members of a group cannot be swapped for one another, which is a claim about variety.
A noun for a body of people joined to a participle meaning standing. The picture is standing firm and standing in prayer at once, and early scholars keep both senses in view.
A plural noun for the stretches the night falls into. Naming them in the plural suggests reciting spread right across the night, rather than one vigil kept at a fixed hour.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The night belonged to whoever chose to take it. Lamps were expensive, oil was rationed, and most households went dark soon after the evening meal. So anyone reciting through the hours of darkness was burning a costly resource and losing sleep before a working day. It was the least visible and most expensive kind of devotion, and nobody would know unless a neighbour happened to hear.
studies.didYouKnow: This verse opens one of the Quran's most direct refusals to generalise, and the passage it starts runs for three verses of praise with no conditions attached anywhere. The word for community used here is the same one the surah used a few verses earlier for the believers themselves. Both groups end up under one word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God refuses the sweeping statement for the sake of getting it right, not for the sake of manners. A group's conduct has just been described. At once the text says the group is not all one thing. That treats even a fair criticism as unfinished without this line. The praise that follows matters too. It is given for acts anyone would call devotion, and no test of membership is attached to it.

crossReferences.why: Describes the condition this verse qualifies at once, one line earlier in the surah.
Closes the surah by describing those among the People of the Book who believe with humility.
Describes those nearest in affection to the believers, and their tears on hearing revelation.

studies.applyIt: Find one group you hold a settled opinion about, and think of a specific person inside it who does not fit. Not as a clever exercise: an actual person with a name. Hold both facts at the same time, the pattern you noticed and the individual who contradicts it. The whole method of this verse is insisting that both stay in the sentence.
studies.explainEasier: Not everyone in a group is the same. Among the people of the book there is a group that stands firm. They read God's words during the hours of the night. And they bow down low in prayer.

studies.title: Quick To The Good
studies.meaning: The praise keeps going and turns into a list of what these people actually do. They believe in God and the Last Day. They urge what everyone recognises as right and hold others back from what is wrong. And they hurry toward good deeds. That verb for hurrying is the striking one, because it carries competing inside it, not merely doing. Then a guarantee: whatever good they do will not be denied them. Early scholars notice these are exactly the qualities the surah gave its own believing community a few verses back.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, inside the passage that refuses to lump the People of the Book together. These two verses finish a picture that began with an upright group reciting through the night. The qualities named are the same ones the surah has already handed to the believers, word for word. Early scholars read that repeat as chosen rather than accidental, and as the point the passage is making.

keyTerms.note: A passive participle from the verb to know. It names what a sound conscience already recognises, so the good being urged is familiar rather than newly imposed from outside.
The matching term, from a root meaning to find a thing strange or to deny it. Wrong is what that same conscience refuses, which pairs the two words as recognition and its opposite.
A form of the verb to hurry that carries competition in it. It describes eagerness measured against other people, so the good is chased rather than merely carried out.
From the root meaning to cover over, used elsewhere in this surah of refusing signs. Applied to a reward it means a deed being covered up and left unacknowledged by anybody.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Being known for what you did was the currency of a small town. A man who acted well in a public matter expected it to be remembered, and a slight went unforgotten for a generation. Being denied credit for something you really did was one of the deepest injuries in that world, worse in some ways than losing property. A name could not be rebuilt by working harder.
studies.didYouKnow: The two verbs for urging good and holding back wrong travel together as a fixed pair all through the Quran. This surah hands that pair to its own believing community a few verses earlier. Here the very same formula is used of a group among the People of the Book. That is one of the most deliberate touches in the whole passage.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God attaches the guarantee to what people do, not to where they belong. Good done will not go unacknowledged, and the doer's community is never once mentioned. Set beside the same description of the believers a few lines earlier, the effect is hard to miss. The qualities themselves are what count. And the closing line says God knows the mindful, which puts the reckoning out of reach of human sorting.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same three qualities of the believing community, a few verses earlier in this surah.
Describes prophets racing toward good deeds and calling on God in hope and in awe.
Tells everyone to compete in good works, wherever it is that they turn.

studies.applyIt: Pick the good thing you have been meaning to do and keep pushing back. The verb here is about racing, and the enemy of racing is delay, not laziness. Do the smaller version today rather than the better version next month. Notice how much of the delay was really about wanting it to look impressive.
studies.explainEasier: They believe in God and in the last day. They tell people to do good and to stay away from wrong. They rush to do good things. Whatever good they do will be counted for them.

studies.title: Said Again, Ending Elsewhere
studies.meaning: Money and children are the two things people bank on, and this verse says neither will stand between anyone and God. Then it names where such people belong: they are the people of the Fire, and they stay in it. The surah said almost exactly this a hundred verses earlier, but closed on a different picture, on fuel rather than on company. Early scholars point out that the chapter restates its own wordings at intervals and changes the ending each time. They read the change as a mark of how far the argument has travelled in between.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, immediately after the passage praising an upright group among the People of the Book. The placing is chosen. A warm description is followed at once by a warning, and the warning is aimed at a group defined by refusal rather than at any community. Early scholars treat that pairing as this surah's way of stopping either statement from being carried off on its own.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for a close associate or a travelling companion. Arabic uses it for those tied permanently to a place or a state, so the phrase describes belonging, not location.
From a root meaning to persist and to last without changing. It describes duration without alteration, which is why the same word covers both the garden and the fire in this surah.
Named with the definite article, as a known thing and not as a description. The Quran usually names it this way, assuming the hearer knows what is meant rather than introducing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Belonging in Arabia was said in exactly this shape. A man was named as one of the people of a valley, a well or a tribe, and that phrase told you where he could travel safely and who would answer for him. Being called the companions of something said who you were, not where you happened to be. The first listeners heard the line in that register.
studies.didYouKnow: This verse repeats an earlier one in the same surah almost word for word, and only its closing picture changes. Surah 3 does this several times, bringing back a wording after a long stretch of other material. Those repeats are one of the ways the chapter holds a long and wandering argument together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God puts this warning directly after praise of people outside the community, and neither one is handed out by group. The verses before praised with no conditions attached. This one warns without naming anybody at all. In both cases what settles the outcome is described purely in terms of what a person does and what a person refuses. That is the position this surah keeps returning to.

crossReferences.why: States the same claim almost word for word earlier in this surah, closing on another picture.
Supplies the praise of an upright group that this warning follows immediately.
Repeats the same formula about wealth and children being no help against God.

studies.applyIt: Notice how the surah alternates: praise, then warning, then praise again, never letting either one settle into a verdict about a group. If you tend to read scripture hunting for confirmation about who is in and who is out, this stretch is built to make that hard. Read the four verses around this one in order.
studies.explainEasier: Some people turn away from God. Their money will not help them when they stand before Him. Their children will not be any help to them either. They belong to the Fire, and they will stay there.

studies.title: A Wind With Frost In It
studies.meaning: God draws a picture for money spent with nothing real behind it. It is like a wind carrying bitter cold that reaches a standing crop and kills it. The detail that stings is what was lost. Not seed, but a harvest, something already grown and days away from cutting. Early scholars point to the last line, which turns the whole loss inward. God did not wrong them. The wrong was already standing in that field, because the owners are described as having wronged themselves before the wind ever arrived.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, in the stretch describing those set against the community. Early scholars link this picture to money spent to buy a name or to buy an edge. That takes in money spent on campaigns against the young community itself. The Quran names no occasion for it. The sources take the comparison as a general one, since its point is about what stands behind an act and not about who paid.

keyTerms.note: A word for fierce cold, from a root also linked to a long grinding sound and to tying something tight. It names cold that grips, not just a temperature that has dropped.
The word for worked ground and what grows on it, used earlier in this surah among the things people love. It carries the labour that went in as well as the crop that came up.
The object is put before the verb, which Arabic does for emphasis. The word order insists that the party wronged and the party doing the wronging are the very same people.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A crop lost late was the worst loss there was. Seed that failed cost you a season's seed. A standing harvest killed days before cutting cost the seed, the water, the labour and the whole year's food. Frost was the particular fear on higher ground, arriving in a single night with no warning at all. Everyone farming knew families ruined in exactly that way.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the tilled field in this picture turns up earlier in this same surah, sitting in the list of things made attractive to people. The Quran often puts one word to work twice inside a chapter in different roles. Here a single word names both something loved and something destroyed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The failure came before the disaster did. A wind destroys the crop, but God says the wrong was already done, and done by the owners to themselves. That makes the loss a revealing rather than a punishment. What happens shows what the spending actually was all along. An act done for the wrong reason was never carrying the weight its owner believed it carried.

crossReferences.why: Compares a gift given for show to soil on a rock washed bare by heavy rain.
Compares the deeds of those who refused to ashes blown apart by wind on a stormy day.
Describes deeds turned into scattered dust once they are finally brought forward.

studies.applyIt: Think of something good you did recently and ask honestly what you were hoping would come of it. Not to spoil it, and not to decide you should stop. Just notice the answer. This picture is about what stands behind an act, and that is usually easier to see in a small case than in a large one.
studies.explainEasier: What these people spend is like a freezing wind. The wind hits a field of grain that is ready and kills it all. God did not treat them unfairly at all. They did the harm to themselves.

studies.title: Confidants From Outside
studies.meaning: The word translated friends here means the lining of a garment, the layer that sits against your skin. So this is about your inner circle, the people close enough to hear what you never say in public. The warning is against letting people into that circle who want you harmed. The description is exact. They will not stop short of ruining you, and they would be glad to see you strained. Hostility has already slipped out in what they say, and what stays hidden is worse. Then it closes: the signs have been made plain, if you use your reason.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, at a time when the community's plans and private business were of real interest to groups set against it. Early scholars read this as being about private counsel, not about ordinary dealings with neighbours. They point out that the Quran elsewhere calls for kindness and fairness toward anybody who has not fought the community. The wording of this verse draws that same line by itself.

keyTerms.note: The word for the inner lining of a garment, the layer against the skin. Used of people it names close confidants, so the warning is about access rather than about acquaintance.
A noun covering corruption, confusion and losing your senses. It names damage that spoils how a thing works, rather than damage that destroys the thing outright.
From a root for being strained or pushed into difficulty, used of a bone breaking after it had started to set. It names distress that comes from pressure, not from one blow.
A strong form from the root for hatred. It is described as having already surfaced in speech, which is what lets a listener work out that more of it is being held back.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a city the size of Medina, a household's private business travelled at the speed of one conversation. Plans for a journey, a marriage being arranged, a debt falling due, the movements of a caravan: all of it was worth something to somebody. Nothing was locked away. Who you spoke freely in front of was the whole of what a family or a town could do to guard itself.
studies.didYouKnow: The word here for an inner circle comes straight out of the language of clothing, where it names the lining that sits against the body. Arabic uses its opposite number for the outer face of a garment. The pair gives the language a neat way of telling what is close and hidden from what is put on show.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God separates the people you deal with from the people you confide in. The warning falls only on the second group, and ordinary dealings are left alone. Who gets into a community's private counsel is treated as a matter of judgement, not of good will. And the verse ends on reason rather than on orders. You are meant to understand the instruction, not just carry it out.

crossReferences.why: Instructs kindness and fairness toward those who did not fight you over religion.
Carries straight on, describing an affection that runs in only one direction.
Uses the same word for an inner circle, in a passage about who is taken into confidence.

studies.applyIt: There is a difference between who you are kind to and who you tell things to. Most people manage the first carefully and the second by accident. Think about the last thing you were genuinely worried about, and who ended up hearing it. Ask whether that list was chosen, or was just whoever happened to be nearby.
studies.explainEasier: God tells the believers not to let people who wish them harm into their closest circle. Those people want to see them in trouble. Their dislike already shows in what they say. What they hide is worse.

studies.title: You Love Them, They Do Not
studies.meaning: Loving people who do not love you back is named here, and the believers are not blamed for it. You accept the whole of scripture, and they do not accept in the same way. Then comes a scene played in two rooms. Warmth when they meet you. Fingers bitten in rage once they are alone. What the messenger is told to say next is short and uncomfortable: die in your rage. Early scholars read that as a statement about how useless such anger is, and not as a curse laid on anyone.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, carrying on from the verse before about who gets let into a community's confidence. Early scholars place these verses among groups in the city whose public manner and private opinion did not match. The reports about named individuals disagree, so the surah keeps to the general description, as it does all through this section. The weight lands on the gap between the two rooms.

keyTerms.gloss: they bit their fingertips at you
keyTerms.note: A physical idiom for rage that has found nowhere to go. Arabic uses it of frustration turned back on yourself, and the noun names the very tips of the fingers, not the hand.
Early Arabic dictionary writers mark it off from ordinary anger as the inward heat that has not yet come out. It names the feeling itself rather than anything done because of it.
Literally the owner or the substance of the chests. The phrase names not only the contents but the settled leaning under them, which is why translators reach for the word heart.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Public courtesy was required in Arabian society, and it told you very little. Hospitality was laid on for people you fully meant to fight. Greeting a man warmly in the market said nothing about what you said of him at home. Everyone understood that the two levels ran alongside each other. What was rare was any way of knowing which one you were standing in.
studies.didYouKnow: The gesture of biting the fingers in rage shows up in only one other place in the Quran, where a wrongdoer bites his hands in regret on the Day of Judgement. Both times a body is turning its frustration back on itself. Both moments are ones where nothing at all can now be done about the cause.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God allows an affection that is not returned, and He never tells anybody to pull it back. What gets corrected is not the love but the misreading of the situation. The believers are handed the truth instead of a change of heart. Then the last line moves the whole matter into God's knowledge. That is how this surah usually closes a description of what people are hiding.

crossReferences.why: Introduces the same group one verse earlier, warning against taking them into confidence.
Uses the same gesture of biting the hands, in regret this time rather than in rage.
Says earlier in this surah that God knows what the chests hold, hidden or shown.

studies.applyIt: There is probably someone you like more than they like you. That is ordinary, and it is not a failure on either side. This verse does not tell the believers to stop caring. It tells them to see the situation accurately. Try holding both facts about one relationship this week, without cooling the warmth and without pretending.
studies.explainEasier: You care about these people, but they do not care about you. When they meet you they say they believe. When they are alone they bite their fingers in anger. God knows what is in every heart.

studies.title: Their Scheming Will Not Reach You
studies.meaning: First the pattern gets named, and most people recognise it. Your good fortune upsets them, and your bad fortune pleases them. Then comes a condition, and it is not a tactic. If you endure and stay mindful, their scheming will not harm you at all. Early scholars notice that nothing whatsoever is said about countering the plan. The protection offered is tied entirely to how the threatened person behaves. And the closing line says God encompasses what they do, which is a claim about reach rather than about revenge.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, at the close of the short passage about confidants and hidden hostility. Early scholars connect it to the period around the hard day at Uhud, when the community's setbacks were watched closely by people hoping for them. The surah turns to that battle in the very next verse. So this instruction sits immediately before an account of a real defeat.

keyTerms.note: A verb of light contact, used of one thing brushing another. It is used here of good fortune, while a much stronger verb carries the misfortune, a difference early scholars notice.
A verb for hitting a target, stronger than the one used of good fortune in the same sentence. The pairing suggests trouble arrives with more force than ease ever does.
A noun for a plan laid quietly, from a root also used of straining and of a trick. It names the arrangement itself, not anything eventually carried out through it.
A participle from the verb to surround, used of a wall enclosing a place. It describes knowledge as containment, so nothing they do lies outside the line of it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a city where everyone's fortunes were public, pleasure at a rival's setback was a known social fact. A failed harvest, a lost caravan or a marriage broken off was discussed everywhere within days. There was nowhere private in which to fail. Living well under that kind of watching was a practical problem, and people faced it constantly.
studies.didYouKnow: The two verbs for good and bad fortune in this verse are deliberately unequal in force. One means to touch lightly. The other means to strike a target. The Quran uses that imbalance in several places, and early scholars read it as matching how differently the two things are actually felt.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God ties your safety to how you behave, not to anything you do about the threat. That takes security out of the result of a contest and puts it inside the person who is exposed, which is a large claim. What makes a scheme harmless happens in the target and not in the plan. And naming God as encompassing keeps the scheme fully in view without letting it decide anything.

crossReferences.why: Joins the same two qualities, patience and mindfulness, to hearing much hurt from others.
Says God does not guide the scheming of the treacherous through to what it aimed at.
States that an evil scheme closes in only on the people who thought it up.

studies.applyIt: Someone is probably pleased about a setback of yours right now. You cannot do anything about that, and trying to is exactly what this verse declines to recommend. Instead, name the two things it does ask for, endurance and staying mindful, then pick the smaller of the two and work on it today.
studies.explainEasier: When something good happens to you, it upsets them. When something bad happens, they are glad about it. But if you hold on and stay careful, their plans cannot hurt you at all.

studies.title: The Morning You Went Out
studies.meaning: The account of the hardest day the community had faced does not begin with the fighting. It begins with a morning, with leaving home and putting men into position. Then two admissions land quickly. Two groups among the believers almost lost heart, and in that same moment God was their protector. Then a reminder of the earlier victory, won when they were weak. Then an instruction that ends on being thankful. Early scholars notice that the story of a defeat opens by recalling a win.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, opening the surah's long account of the battle at Uhud in the third year after the migration. A force came up from Mecca to avenge what it had lost at Badr, and the Muslim force went out to meet it beyond the city. The classical sources agree on the broad shape of the day. That includes the near-withdrawal of two groups before the fighting, which the Quran records here without softening it.

keyTerms.gloss: you set out in the morning
keyTerms.note: A verb tied to the early part of the day, from the root that gives Arabic its word for tomorrow. The hour is inside the verb rather than added alongside it.
From a root meaning to settle someone in a place, used of finding lodging for a traveller. Applied to a battle line it means putting each group where it is meant to stay.
A dual verb from a root covering weak resolve and lost nerve. The dual form is exact, naming two groups and no more, which is why the report cannot be spread any wider.
The plural of a word for someone lowly or powerless. Used of the earlier battle, it concedes the community's own weakness rather than saying anything about its opponents.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A battle in that world was often decided before contact rather than during it. Position, high ground and the discipline of holding a line counted for more than numbers did. A force that broke formation was usually finished. Men fought beside their own relatives, so one group pulling back exposed families as well as flanks. Putting men in position that morning was the most important work of the day.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran names the battle of Badr outright in this passage, and it is one of very few places where it names a battlefield at all. Most of its references to particular events describe them without giving them a name. That makes this naming unusually direct, sitting inside the account of a later and much harder day.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The line about the two groups who nearly faltered is the one to sit with. God says in the same breath that He was their protector. A failure of nerve is written down and not denied, and the bond is not described as broken by it. That sets up everything the rest of this section does. The account can afford to be honest about weakness, because the argument never depended on hiding it.

crossReferences.why: Recalls Badr earlier in this surah, describing the two parties and the sign in them.
Describes the appeal for help at Badr and the reinforcement sent as reassurance.
Carries this account on, describing the moment the line broke and giving the reason.

studies.applyIt: Notice how this opening is built: before describing a bad day it recalls a good one, and how weak they were before that. When something goes wrong this week, try starting your account of it in the same place, with what went right before and how thin the margin really was. It changes what the difficult part means.
studies.explainEasier: Remember the morning you left home to place the believers for battle. Two groups nearly gave up, but God kept them safe. God had already helped you win at Badr when you were weak.

studies.title: Three Thousand Sent Down
studies.meaning: What reaches the frightened men here is a question, not a declaration. Is it not enough for you that your Lord reinforces you with three thousand angels sent down. Early scholars differ over which battle the number belongs to, some reading it of the earlier day at Badr and others of the day this passage describes. The sources record the disagreement and leave it open. What nobody disputes is the shape of it. Reassurance comes as a question, which leaves the hearer to do the answering.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, inside the account of the battle at Uhud. Early scholars differ over whether the promise reported here belongs to that day or to the earlier victory at Badr. Both readings are preserved in the major commentaries, along with the evidence for each. The Quran itself does not settle it. The surah moves straight on to a further promise of help, this time with conditions.

keyTerms.note: From the root for being enough, the same one behind the phrase God is enough for us later in this surah. It asks about what will do, not about what anyone would like.
From a root meaning to stretch or extend, used of a supply line and of ink drawn up from a well. Help is pictured as reaching out to you rather than simply dropping in.
A passive participle stressing that the help descends rather than merely turns up. Early scholars note that the same root runs through this surah's whole vocabulary for revelation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Numbers in Arabian warfare were known and counted with care. Before a fight, scouts reported how big the other force was, and men then did their own sums about whether to stand. Three thousand was more than most armies the peninsula had ever put in one place. Naming it named an amount outside anything they had seen, while still speaking in the terms a fighter thought in.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran gives an actual count of angels in only a handful of places, and two of those concern battles fought by this community. Everywhere else, angels are described as present with no figure attached at all. That makes the counted reinforcements in this surah and in Surah 8 unusual inside the text.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God reassures by asking rather than by declaring, which hands the work of believing back to the person who is afraid. No guarantee is issued. The help is also described as already on its way rather than pledged for later, since the verb has it under way. So fear is met with information about the present, not about the outcome. That is a very different comfort from a prediction.

crossReferences.why: Describes the appeal at Badr and a thousand angels sent one after another as the answer.
Raises the number in the very next verse, on two conditions that are stated plainly.
Speaks of forces nobody could see, sent down at a moment when numbers had failed.

studies.applyIt: Notice that this is a question. When you are afraid you probably ask for reassurance. You rarely stop to answer whether what you already hold would be enough. Try that today with one specific worry. List what you actually have in hand, then answer the question honestly instead of going straight on to ask for more.
studies.explainEasier: The believers were told that their Lord was backing them up. He sent down three thousand angels to help them. They were asked whether that was not enough for them.

studies.title: If You Hold And Guard
studies.meaning: The answer to that question comes back in one word: on the contrary. Then the promise is extended, and this time it carries conditions. If you hold fast, if you stay mindful, and if they come at you all at once, the help rises to five thousand marked angels. Early scholars discuss the word describing them, which points to some distinguishing mark, and they keep more than one explanation of it. The conditions are the part that repays attention. Unseen help is tied to what the people receiving it actually do.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, still inside the account of the battle at Uhud and its promise of help. Early scholars differ over whether the five thousand were sent, and many read the attached conditions as not met that day. The sources keep both sides of the discussion carefully. The surah's own later account of the battle describes exactly the failure of nerve those conditions name.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to boil over, used of water and of a sudden surge. It describes an attack arriving all at once with no pause, which is why translators reach for suddenly.
A participle from the root for marking, the same one used earlier in this surah of branded horses. Early scholars explain it as marked in appearance, or as marking out their targets.
From the root covering binding and holding back. In a battle it means keeping your position under pressure, which is exactly what the surah later says was not done.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Discipline decided fights in that world. A line that held under archery could beat greater numbers. A line that broke up to collect plunder lost the field. Commanders repeated their position orders over and over, because everyone knew how fast a formation came apart once men started thinking for themselves. The conditions in this verse are stated in the words of exactly that problem.
studies.didYouKnow: The number here climbs from the verse before it, three thousand to five thousand. The rise arrives carrying conditions that the first figure never had. Early scholars treat that wording as chosen on purpose, not as decoration. Much of what they say turns on whether the larger help was ever actually sent.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God ties unseen help to what people do without turning it into a wage. Endurance and mindfulness are named as conditions, not as causes, and the help stays His to give. That keeps two things together which come apart easily. One is the assurance that support is real. The other is that what you do while waiting for it genuinely matters.

crossReferences.why: Asks the question this verse answers, about whether the first reinforcement would do.
Describes the moment later in this surah when holding fast gave way, and what followed.
Ties a promised advantage in battle to the state of the people receiving it.

studies.applyIt: The two conditions here are endurance and care. Both are unglamorous, and both get practised beforehand rather than summoned on the spot. Pick one situation you know is coming, and decide now, in writing if that helps, what holding your position is actually going to look like when it arrives.
studies.explainEasier: If you hold your ground and stay careful, they may still rush at you. Your Lord will then send even more help. Five thousand angels with clear marks on them will come down to your side.

studies.title: Only Good News For You
studies.meaning: God says plainly what the angels were for, and it was not military. He made it good news for you, and He made it so your hearts would settle. Then the point lands with no hedging on it: help comes only from God. Early scholars read this as heading off a natural mistake, because a promise of thousands of angels invites the thought that the numbers are what does the work. The verse says the numbers were for the hearts. The outcome was never a matter of counting.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, closing the passage about angels inside the account of the battle. Early scholars treat this verse as the key to the two before it, since it says what the promise was actually for. The surah's bigger argument about that day is being set up right here. The community's confidence had to rest somewhere other than on an advantage they could see.

keyTerms.note: From the root behind announcing glad tidings, and behind the change that comes over a face at good news. It names the message, not the thing announced, which is the very line this verse draws.
From a root describing ground that is level and still, and a heart at rest. It pictures reassurance as settling rather than as excitement, a quieter image than the English suggests.
From the root for coming to someone's aid, the same one used of the disciples earlier in this surah. It names help given, so victory is something received rather than achieved.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Morale was treated as a real weapon in Arabian warfare. Commanders spread word of allies coming, of fresh men on the road, of losses on the other side. A force that believed it was backed fought differently from one that did not. Everyone knew that what men believed about their numbers counted for as much as the numbers themselves.
studies.didYouKnow: The line saying victory comes only from God appears twice in the Quran, here and in Surah 8. Both times it sits inside an account of a battle. Both times it lands right after a mention of angels sent as reinforcement. That repetition, in settings so closely matched, is one of the tightest parallels between the two surahs.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God separates what did the work from what was given to steady you. Thousands of angels are described as sent for the sake of the hearts, and never as the thing that decided the day. That keeps unseen help from being counted up like a resource. It guards against two mistakes at once: leaning on visible strength, and leaning on invisible strength as though it were the same sort of thing.

crossReferences.why: States the same thing in nearly identical words, after the reinforcement at Badr.
Says later in this surah that if God helps you, nobody at all can overcome you.
