studies.historicalContext: This came down in Medina after the battle at Uhud. Leaving a position that day had itself been tied to the taking of spoils. The early sources report a suspicion going round about something missing from the collected goods, and they read the verse as the answer to it. Reports of the item differ. So early scholars treat the occasion as clear in outline and unsure in its details.

keyTerms.note: A precise term for removing something from shared property before it is handed out. Arabic has a word of its own for it, which tells you how familiar the problem was in that world.

keyTerms.gloss: he will bring what he took
keyTerms.note: The verb means to come or arrive, so the picture is a person carrying the item into the gathering. Nothing is said about its weight, and early scholars note that the carrying is the point.
The trading word used earlier in this surah for a debt settled completely. Its return here puts both the taking and the reckoning into the language of accounts kept and closed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Spoils were gathered into one place and shared out by an agreed method, and the whole system rested on nothing leaving the pile first. A man who took an item early gained something small and put the arrangement at risk. Everyone knew that. Everyone also knew how easy it was to do in the confusion after a fight.
studies.didYouKnow: Arabic has a verb just for taking from shared property before it is divided, and it is not the ordinary word for theft. The Quran uses it only in this surah. That a word exists for this alone shows how much a fair division of spoils mattered to holding a fighting force together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage answers a suspicion by stating what a prophet is, rather than by denying one charge. That is worth noticing, because it makes the defence about the office instead of about the word of one man. The picture of carrying the item into the gathering does something too. A hidden act becomes an object you can see. That is how the Quran usually shows a covered thing finally uncovered.

crossReferences.why: Addresses the division of spoils directly, referring the whole matter to God and the Messenger.
Instructs that trusts be given back to those they belong to, and that judgement be just.
Uses the same verb for being paid in full, of every soul on a day beyond doubt.

studies.applyIt: The exact failure here is taking a little from something held in common: an expense claim, a shared resource, time billed but not worked. It is always small, which is what makes it easy. Pick one such thing and put it back this week, quietly. Nobody needs to know, which is rather the point.
studies.explainEasier: A prophet would never take things in secret. Anyone who does will have to carry what he took on the Day when everyone stands up again. Then each person gets exactly what he earned, with nothing taken away.

studies.title: Not The Same At All
studies.meaning: A question is asked that answers itself. Is the one who went after the approval of God like the one who came away carrying His anger. Then comes a very short verse that is easy to pass over: they are degrees with God. The wording is unusual. It does not say they have degrees; it says they are degrees. Early scholars read that as tying people to their rank, rather than having a rank handed to them from outside.
studies.historicalContext: This came down in Medina, in the stretch that follows the battle at Uhud. What people did on that single day had varied enormously. Early scholars tie the pairing to it, since the passage comes straight after a line about taking from the spoils. The question and the words about degrees are read together, and they name differences the day itself had made plain.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form of the word for contentment, used earlier in this surah among the rewards of the mindful. It names the regard of the giver rather than any particular gift given.
The verb means to return bearing something, used of a traveller coming home with a load. Displeasure is pictured as a thing carried back rather than as something sent after a person.
The plural of the word for a step on a stair. Saying that people are degrees, rather than that they have them, collapses the gap between a person and their standing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rank in Arabian society came from birth, from wealth and from the name of your line. You could see it in where a man sat and in when he was allowed to speak. Everyone in a gathering knew the order. A verse saying that people are their own degrees before God cut right across that, because standing there was inherited rather than built by anything you did.
studies.didYouKnow: The wording that people are degrees, rather than that they have them, turns up in a similar form elsewhere in the Quran. Early scholars of grammar ask whether a word has been dropped out. Most of them read the gap as meant, since the shorter form ties the person to the rank more tightly.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Standing before God is treated here as something a person becomes, not as something handed out, and the odd grammar is what does that. It fits the argument this surah has been making, that a hard day showed people what they already were. The two paths are worth holding side by side as well. One is named by what it goes after. The other is named by what it comes back carrying.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same wording of the believers, saying they are degrees with their Lord.
Names the approval of God earlier in this surah, among things better than what is loved here.
Says for all there are degrees according to what they did, and God is not unaware.

studies.applyIt: The passage asks a question and waits for you to answer it. Take one thing you did this week and ask honestly which of the two descriptions fits: going after approval, or coming away carrying something. Most days hold both. Naming which was which is the whole exercise, and it takes a minute.
studies.explainEasier: A person who goes after what pleases God is not the same as a person who ends up with God angry at him. They are not on the same level. God sees exactly what each one does.

studies.title: A Messenger From Among Themselves
studies.meaning: The favour is named, and then it is spelled out. A messenger was raised up from among the people themselves, and he recites the signs to them, purifies them, and teaches them the Book and wisdom. The phrase about being from among themselves carries real weight, because it makes the messenger a neighbour instead of a visitor. Then the verse closes by naming what came before, and calls it plain straying, with nothing softened.
studies.historicalContext: This sits in Medina, inside the account of what followed the battle at Uhud. Early scholars notice where it falls. A community that had just failed is reminded of what it was given, not of what it did. The three tasks listed here also turn up in the prayer Abraham makes over the sanctuary in an earlier surah, and the scholars read this verse as the answer to that prayer.

keyTerms.note: A verb for granting a benefit, from a root also tied to cutting off. In its good sense it names an unearned gift, and the Quran uses it of favours nobody could have claimed as a right.
Literally from their souls. The phrase makes the messenger one of them in origin and in kind, not simply someone present among them, and that is what early scholars draw out of it.
From a root covering both purity and increase. It names cleaning and growing as one process, so what is taken away and what develops share a single verb.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Authority in Arabia was local. A man listened to someone whose family he knew, whose line he could recite, and whose conduct he had watched for years. An outsider carried no weight whatever he said. So being from among themselves was not a detail of biography. It was what made it possible for him to be heard at all.
studies.didYouKnow: The same three tasks named here, reciting, purifying and teaching, appear in the prayer Abraham makes over the sanctuary in an earlier surah. He asks that a messenger be raised from among them to do exactly these things. Early scholars read the two passages as request and answer, and they note that the order is not the same.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation comes here through somebody the people already knew. It did not arrive as an event nobody could relate to, and that changes how it is taken in. The three things named are ordinary and can be repeated: reciting, purifying, teaching. The verse also calls what came before plain straying, with nothing added to soften it. That keeps the favour from being read as something the community had earned.

crossReferences.why: Records the prayer of Abraham for a messenger who would do these same three things.
Repeats the same three tasks almost word for word, of a community without scripture.
Describes the messenger as from among yourselves, grieved by whatever distresses you.

studies.applyIt: Notice the order in this verse: recited to, then purified, then taught. Most people run it backwards and begin with the learning. Try a week on the first item instead, reading a short passage aloud often, without studying it. Then see whether the third one lands any differently.
studies.explainEasier: God did the believers a great kindness. He sent them a messenger who was one of their own people. He reads them the words of God, makes them clean, and teaches them the Book. Before that they were clearly lost.

studies.title: It Is From Yourselves
studies.meaning: A question is quoted and then answered in four words. After a disaster the community asks how this happened, when they had dealt out twice as much on an earlier day. The answer is short and not at all flattering: it is from your own selves. Then the next verse says the same event came by the leave of God, and names what it was for. Early scholars hold both statements together. What the people did and what God allowed describe one event from two angles, not two rival explanations.
studies.historicalContext: This belongs to the account of the battle at Uhud in Medina. The comparison points back to the earlier day at Badr, where losses on the other side ran to roughly double what the community suffered here. Early scholars note that the question quoted was asked in earnest. A community helped once could not see why it had not been helped again.

keyTerms.note: From the verb to hit a target, so a disaster is named by its accuracy rather than by its size. The same root runs through this surah's whole vocabulary for what befalls people.
A dual form meaning double, pointing back to the losses dealt out at the earlier battle. Its presence is what makes the question reasonable rather than merely sulky.
Literally from with yourselves, a phrase for something starting in a place rather than merely sitting there. It names where what happened came from, not just where it landed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Tribes kept exact counts of their losses. Everyone knew how many had fallen on each side of a fight, and those numbers set what was owed and where a feud stood. So the comparison this verse makes was one its hearers could check for themselves. That is part of why the question felt so pressing to them.
studies.didYouKnow: These two verses give two different answers to the same question, and the Quran sets them side by side without smoothing them together. One names what the people did. The other names the leave of God. Early scholars treat that pairing as the answer itself, not as a problem to be solved.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Responsibility is laid on the people, and yet the event never leaves the hands of God. The passage does that simply by stating both. So neither easy way out stays open. You cannot blame the circumstances, and you cannot use a decree as an excuse. The purpose named in the second verse is that the believers be known, which puts the disaster to work. That changes what it was rather than explaining it away.

crossReferences.why: States the rule more generally: good reaching you is from God, and ill from yourself.
Says whatever strikes you is for what your own hands earned, and much is pardoned.
Gives the detailed account of what came from themselves on that particular day.

studies.applyIt: The community here asks a fair question and gets a short answer, and the answer holds no comfort at all. Comfort arrives later in the passage, not in place of it. Next time something goes wrong, answer the how question honestly first. Then go looking for the comfort.
studies.explainEasier: When you were hit hard, you asked how this could happen, even though you had hit them twice as hard before. The answer is that it came from you. God let it happen so it would show who really believes.

studies.title: Said With Their Mouths
studies.meaning: A group is described by an invitation and by the answer they gave it. They were told to come and fight, or else to help hold the enemy back. They replied that if they knew how to fight they would have followed. The verse does not argue with the excuse. It notes where they stood that day, then says something general about them: they say with their mouths what is not in their hearts. Early scholars point to the closing line, which says God knows better what they hide and never names it.
studies.historicalContext: This comes from the account of the battle at Uhud in Medina, where a large part of the force turned back before any fighting began. The early sources describe an exchange on the road: they were urged to keep going, and they refused. The Quran reports their words and its own judgement without naming anybody. Early scholars keep to that same restraint.

keyTerms.note: From a root tied to a burrow with two exits, used of a creature that goes in by one and leaves by the other. The picture is an arrangement built for escape rather than for living in.
A verb for repelling something, offered here as an alternative to fighting. Its presence widens the invitation, so the refusal cannot be read as turning down one particular role.
A comparison rather than a label. The verse says they were nearer to refusal than to faith that day, which measures a distance instead of settling them into a category.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Excuses on the road were common and mostly accepted. A man could turn back for a sick relative, a debt, or a doubt about the plan, and nobody usually pressed him on it. The excuse quoted here is a different kind. It claims not knowing how, rather than a duty waiting at home. Anyone who knew these men would have seen through it.
studies.didYouKnow: The root behind the word for playing a double part is linked in Arabic with a burrow that has a second opening. A small desert animal digs it that way so it can escape if the first one is blocked. Early Arabic dictionary writers keep that picture. It shapes the term: not a lie, but an exit made ready in advance.
studies.theologicalSignificance: This measures rather than labels. It says that on that day they were nearer to one thing than to another, which leaves the position open and names a direction instead of a fixed state. Its last move is one the surah makes elsewhere too. What they hid is never spelled out, and knowing it is left to God. That stops a description from hardening into an accusation.

crossReferences.why: Quotes another excuse for staying behind, saying their tongues say what is not in their hearts.
Describes a journey turned down, with an excuse the passage says they knew to be untrue.
Describes another group on the same day, wrapped up in themselves and hiding their thoughts.

studies.applyIt: The excuse quoted here claims inability rather than unwillingness, which is the commonest shape an excuse takes. Listen for it in your own next few days: I would, but I do not know how. Sometimes it is perfectly true. See if you can catch one occasion this week where it is the polite version of something else.
studies.explainEasier: Some men were told to come and fight for God, or at least help hold the enemy back. They said they would have come if they knew how to fight. That was not true. God knows what people keep hidden inside.

studies.title: Do Not Suppose Them Dead
studies.meaning: This passage answers a taunt. The men who stayed home said the dead would still be living if they had listened, and the reply is not an argument but a challenge: then keep death away from yourselves, if what you say is true. Then comes a correction of how you are meant to think of the fallen. Do not suppose they are dead. They are alive, with their Lord, and provided for, which puts them in the present tense.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina, just after the battle at Uhud. A body of men had turned back before the fighting, and afterwards they said of the dead that they would have lived if they had taken the same advice. Early scholars tie these verses to that remark. Some seventy of the community were killed that day, and nearly every household in the city had lost someone or was nursing someone wounded.

keyTerms.note: A verb for repelling something coming at you, used of pushing back a flood or an attacker. Turning it towards death makes the challenge physical, as if death were a force you could block.
The plain word for living people, with nothing softened about it. It is given without qualification, and early scholars are careful to say the life meant is real while its manner is not disclosed.
A passive verb in the ongoing present, the same word used of daily food in this world. It answers the practical worry of families left behind about people they can no longer feed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The dead of Uhud were buried on the field, two and three to a grave, in the clothes they fell in. Their families could walk out to the hill from Medina in an hour, and they did. Widows and mothers had lost the men who brought in the harvest and defended the wells. Grief there was public and loud, with formal mourning that could run for months.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran corrects the language people use about those killed in the way of God twice, here and at 2:154, and the wording is not the same. This passage rules out supposing them dead. The earlier one rules out saying it, and adds that the reader has no perception of the life in question.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The taunt assumes that staying out of danger is what keeps a person alive, and the reply does not argue that point. It hands the claim back as a test the speakers cannot pass, which shows they never quite believed it themselves. Then the second verse moves the question somewhere else. Whether someone is alive turns out not to be settled by what the people watching can see.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same correction earlier in the Quran, adding that the living are simply not perceived.
Carries on the review of Uhud, answering people who thought staying home would have changed things.
Answers the same instinct: death reaches people wherever they are, even in fortified towers.

studies.applyIt: If you have lost someone, try saying their name today in the present tense, in one ordinary sentence, the way you would speak of a person who has travelled. This passage is not asking you to feel less. It is asking you to notice how much of grief rests on a tense you chose without thinking.
studies.explainEasier: Some people who stayed home said the dead would still be alive if they had listened. God answers: then stop your own death, if you can. Those killed for God are not dead. They are alive with Him.

studies.title: Glad For Those Behind Them
studies.meaning: The description carries on from the verse before, and the striking thing is which way their attention runs. They are delighted with what they have been given. Then they are glad for the ones who have not yet joined them, the people still behind. Their joy is not for themselves alone; it reaches back to people still living. Early scholars point to the verb for receiving good news, which is used twice across these two verses.
studies.historicalContext: These words came in Medina, in the passage about those killed at Uhud, and they were spoken to a community burying its own. Early scholars read the section as comfort for the bereaved, since it describes the dead as taken up with the people they left. That direction is what the sources stress. Grief usually runs the other way.

keyTerms.note: A participle from the root for gladness, used in the Quran at times of a gladness that turns into vanity. Here it takes the bounty of God as its object, which fixes the sense securely.
A form of the verb for glad tidings that carries seeking or welcoming. It names the receiving of news rather than its announcement, which is why it suits those who have already arrived.

keyTerms.gloss: does not let go to waste
keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to lose or mislay something. It denies loss rather than promising increase, which is a quieter reassurance than a promise and a more exact one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The dead were buried fast, often on the field itself, and families often never saw the body. What relatives wanted most was news: how he died, whether he suffered, whether he was afraid. Riders brought those accounts back to the city and were pressed for every detail. These verses arrive into a community waiting for exactly that kind of report.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase saying they will have no fear and will not grieve turns up more than a dozen times across the Quran. It is always said of people in the care of God. Here it is said not of the dead themselves, but of the living they are glad about.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The dead are described as still attentive to the living, which turns the usual shape of grief around. The bereaved are being told that the people they mourn are glad about them. And the passage closes on a denial rather than a promise: it says the reward is not lost. That meets the exact fear of a community whose effort had just ended in a setback.

crossReferences.why: Opens this passage, saying not to think those killed in the way of God are dead.
Says the same thing more briefly, that they are alive though you do not perceive it.
Closes the surah with the same assurance that the work of a worker is never let go to waste.

studies.applyIt: Notice which way the attention runs here: from the ones who have arrived, back towards those still travelling. If you are grieving someone, try holding that direction for a moment instead of the usual one. You do not have to believe anything new to try it. See what changes in the shape of the missing.
studies.explainEasier: They are happy with what God has given them. They are also happy for the ones they left behind, who have not come yet. Those people have nothing to fear and nothing to be sad about. God will not waste what they did.

studies.title: They Answered While Wounded
studies.meaning: A group is described by one action taken at the worst possible moment. They answered the call of God and the Messenger after the wound had already reached them. Nothing is said about what they did next. The answering itself is the whole of the praise. Then the reward is tied to two qualities rather than to the act: doing well, and being mindful of God. Early scholars read that as widening the promise past that group, to a state anyone could be in.
studies.historicalContext: This came down in Medina. The early sources tie the verse to the day after the battle at Uhud, when the community was called out again to follow the force that was pulling away. Many of the men who answered were wounded from the day before. The march ended without any fighting at all. The sources note that, since the praise attaches to the answering rather than to a battle.

keyTerms.note: A form of the verb to respond that carries answering a summons. It names the reply rather than whatever followed it, which is why the praise can rest on the response alone.
The same word used earlier in this surah of the wound that reached both sides. Its return here ties the verse straight to the account of the battle rather than leaving the setting general.
From the root for beauty and excellence, so doing well means doing a thing finely rather than merely correctly. The Quran uses it of a quality of action rather than an amount of it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wounds in that world were treated with whatever was to hand: cautery, honey, cloth. A man cut the day before could barely hold a shield, and everyone knew it. Setting out again with untreated injuries was visible to the whole city, because the column left in daylight. The praise here describes something the community actually stood and watched.
studies.didYouKnow: The march this verse refers to ended with no fighting at all, since the other force had already moved on. So the praise goes to men who set out wounded and came home having done nothing. Few places in the Quran praise a response so clearly apart from its result.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Here the worth of an act is split from what the act achieved, and a response that produced nothing is praised. Then it goes further. The reward is tied to qualities rather than to the episode, so the praise is not shut up with the men who went. A piece of historical praise never becomes a closed record. It turns into a description anyone can fit.

crossReferences.why: Carries on the account, giving the words those who answered said when warned about the enemy.
Describes earlier communities who did not weaken at what struck them in the way of God.
Says nothing suffered on such a journey is lost, but is written as a good deed for them.

studies.applyIt: The praise here goes to showing up wounded and achieving nothing at all. If you have been waiting to feel recovered before going back to something you value, notice that this verse does not wait for that. Go back this week in whatever state you are in, and let the response itself be the whole of the act.
studies.explainEasier: These people answered God and the Messenger even after they had been hurt. They went out again while they were still sore and tired. God has a great reward for the ones among them who do good and stay careful of Him.

studies.title: God Is Enough For Us
studies.meaning: Fear is handed to them as information, and it has the opposite effect. The report is accurate, since an army really has gathered. Their answer is not to deny the danger but to change what the danger is measured against. The two words they reply with are a reckoning and a title: God is enough for us, and He is the best one to entrust affairs to. Early scholars point out that their faith increased rather than merely held.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. This looks back to the days just after Uhud, when wounded men were called out again to follow the Meccan army as it withdrew. Early scholars connect the verse with warnings brought to the Muslims that a larger force was gathering to finish them. Reports differ on who carried the warning, so the verse is usually read for the response it records rather than for the messenger.

keyTerms.note: From the root for counting and reckoning. The word does not say God will help; it says the account already balances, so nothing more needs adding to the side they are on.

keyTerms.gloss: the trustee, the one relied on
keyTerms.note: A term from ordinary business for the agent you hand your affairs to, whose decisions bind you. Calling God this puts reliance into the language of delegation rather than of feeling.
Placed as the object of a verb meaning to increase, so faith is treated as a quantity that can rise and fall. The grammar assumes a thing with degrees, not a line you either cross or do not.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: News in Arabia travelled by rider and by rumour. A caravan arriving from the north could carry a report that changed the plans of a town by evening. There was no way to check a claim about an army two days away except by sending men towards it. Whole settlements decided on the word of one traveller. That is why the standing of the person speaking mattered so much.
studies.didYouKnow: Early scholars keep a report from Ibn Abbas that this same sentence was spoken by Abraham when he was thrown into the fire, and again by the community on the occasion of this verse. The words occur in this exact form only here. The root itself turns up across the Quran with other pronouns.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Reliance is presented here as a judgement rather than a mood. The believers do not report feeling calm. They state a sufficiency and give God a title drawn from law and trade. That makes trust something a frightened person can do without first stopping being afraid. The passage also lets fear be a real report about real danger, and puts all the change into what the danger is set against.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same fear from the other side, that nothing reaches a person outside what God has written.
Uses the same word for sufficiency, promising that God is enough for whoever relies on Him.
Addresses the Prophet with the same wording, God is enough for you and those who follow.

studies.applyIt: Next time bad news arrives, notice the gap between the report and your reaction to it, and put one sentence into that gap before you do anything else. It does not have to be long. The point is that the danger and your response are two separate things, and only one of them is yours.
studies.explainEasier: People told them a big army was coming and tried to scare them. It made them trust God more instead. They said: God is enough for us, and He is the best one to look after us.

studies.title: Fear Me, Not Them
studies.meaning: The men who marched out despite their injuries came home with favour and profit, untouched, having gone after what pleases God. Then the frame widens. The threat that had frightened them is put down not to the enemy but to Satan, working through people who follow him. What comes next is a redirection rather than a denial. Fear is not abolished; it is pointed somewhere else. Scholars read the words about Satan and his allies in more than one way.
studies.historicalContext: This belongs to the aftermath of the fighting at Uhud in Medina. Early scholars connect these verses to the march the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) called for right afterwards. Wounded men went out again to a halt on the Mecca road, and the opposing army never came back. Other reports connect them to an appointed meeting near Badr the following year that was not kept. Both settings fit the wording.

keyTerms.note: From a root for satisfaction and acceptance. It names not a gift given but God being pleased, which early scholars treat as the highest thing the Quran promises, above the gardens themselves.

An intensive form of the verb to fear: to work fear into someone. Early scholars read the object in more than one way, either that he frightens you of his allies or that he makes his own followers fearful.
A wide word covering injury, misfortune and wrong at once. Its indefinite form under a negation sweeps the whole category, so the claim is that not one instance of harm reached them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rumour travelled the Hijaz faster than any army. A traveller arriving at a Medinan well could say that Mecca had regrouped and was coming back, and by evening every household knew. There was no way to check it. Families with wounded men had to decide overnight whether to send them out again on the word of a stranger. This passage describes that kind of night.
studies.didYouKnow: The opening words here repeat, exactly, a phrase used three verses earlier at 3:171. There it describes what those killed at Uhud rejoice in. Here it describes what the survivors came home carrying. One short phrase holds a promise in one place and its fulfilment in the other.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Fear gets split in two here. One kind answers a power you can see and count. The other is owed to a power you cannot. By naming the first as the work of Satan, the passage treats being frightened as something done to a person, not as a plain fact about their situation. And it makes the other kind of fear a mark of belief. Courage and faith end up on one footing, instead of courage being left to a person's nature.

crossReferences.why: Records what the believers said when the same rumour reached them, just before this passage.
Calls the scheming of Satan weak, which is the other half of the claim made here.
Describes messengers who fear no one but God, the same redirection of fear stated as a rule.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time a piece of news makes your chest tighten, and before you act on it ask who is telling you and what they gain from your alarm. Most frightening reports arrive with no way to check them. You do not have to talk yourself out of the feeling. Just hold it for an hour before you let it decide anything.
studies.explainEasier: They came home safe, with good things from God, and nothing bad had touched them. They had gone after what pleases God. It was only Satan trying to make them afraid of his friends. Do not fear them. Fear God.

studies.title: Not Yours To Grieve Over
studies.meaning: These lines speak to someone watching other people fall away, and they refuse the assumption underneath the grief. Speed is the picture: they are racing into denial, as though hurrying somewhere. The reply is that nothing they do reaches God at all. What is actually at stake is their own share of what comes after. Then it is put as a trade, faith handed over and its opposite received, which makes the loss theirs and gives it a price.
studies.historicalContext: This falls in Medina, in the stretch after the setback at Uhud. The strain showed up people who had joined the community without really believing, and who now moved away openly. Early scholars read the address as comfort for the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), whose grief over refusal is described elsewhere in the Quran. No single occasion is reported with confidence. The setting is a community sorting itself out under pressure.

keyTerms.note: A form of the verb to hurry that carries a sense of competing. The same word appears at 3:114 for people racing towards good deeds, so one image serves two opposite directions.

A word from the language of dividing things up: the portion that falls to you when something is shared out. It treats the Hereafter as an estate where everyone has an allotment, and says theirs is empty.
Trading vocabulary. The verb means to purchase, so denial is what they paid for and faith is what they handed over. The Quran uses this frame again and again for choices that cannot be undone.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The market in Medina ran mostly on swaps rather than coin: dates for cloth, a camel against a debt. Everyone knew the feeling of making a trade and seeing later what they had given up. Traders would argue for days about whether a swap had been fair. Putting belief into that language let a listener feel the deal in his hands rather than think about it from far off.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for racing appears earlier in this same surah, at 3:114, in exactly the same form. There it describes people who hurry towards good works, and they are praised for it. The word itself is neutral. Only the direction of travel differs, and the surah lets the two lines stand a few pages apart.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage says plainly that people turning away does God no damage at all. That sounds obvious, and it clears away a whole kind of worry. If refusal cannot hurt the one refused, then standing up for religion is not the rescue of someone weak. It also draws a line under what the watcher is answerable for. Grief that assumes you could have stopped another person from choosing is grief about something that was never yours.

crossReferences.why: Names the same grief and its force, warning the Prophet not to destroy himself over people's refusal.
Uses the same buying image for the same exchange, adding that the trade returned nothing.
States what lies under this passage: the need runs one way, so refusal costs God nothing.

studies.applyIt: Pick one person whose choices have been weighing on you. Say plainly to yourself which part of it was ever in your hands and which part was not. Then do the small thing that is still yours, a message or an invitation or one honest sentence, and stop at the edge of what you can actually reach.
studies.explainEasier: Do not be sad about people who rush to turn away from God. They cannot hurt God at all. They are giving up faith and taking something worthless in its place. A painful punishment is waiting for them.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Long Life Is Not Approval
studies.meaning: This verse answers a conclusion people draw from what they can see. Someone denies God, does well, and the delay starts to look like approval. The passage grants the delay and refuses that reading. Extra time is not a reward; it only makes the record longer. Early scholars are careful with the words about increase, noting that Arabic can use this form for a result rather than for a purpose. And the last word calls the punishment humiliating, not merely painful.
studies.historicalContext: This came down in Medina, among the passages after Uhud that speak to a community whose opponents looked untouched. The leaders of Mecca had gone home whole, and their trade carried on. Early scholars report no particular occasion for it. They place it inside a running argument about how to read success in this world. The surah picks that argument up again at its close, warning about being impressed by wealth.

keyTerms.note: The verb means to extend time and to let out slack. Arabic used it of a tether paid out to a grazing animal, so the picture is rope given rather than a penalty cancelled.
An emphatic negative of the verb to reckon or calculate. It addresses a conclusion somebody has worked out alone, which is why the reply corrects a piece of arithmetic rather than a stated claim.
Built from the root for lowliness, so it names punishment that shames rather than only hurts. Three verses in a row here close with the same noun for torment and three different adjectives.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A debtor in Arabia could be given more time, and a creditor who put the date back was doing a favour with a limit on it. Everyone understood that a delayed debt was still a debt. An extension could turn into a trap if the debtor kept borrowing inside it. Listeners had watched families sink further during a grace period they had asked for themselves.
studies.didYouKnow: From verse 176 to 178 the same word for torment closes three verses in a row. Each time a different adjective follows it: great, then painful, then humiliating. The far end of the surah is built the same way. The two verses that promise reward, 195 and 198, each close with a noun, then the words from God, then a clause about what is with Him.
studies.theologicalSignificance: This verse will not let what you can see stand as a verdict, and that protects two people at once. It stops the comfortable from reading their comfort as approval. It stops the struggling from reading hardship as rejection. It also treats time as neutral rather than kind. What a person does with an extra ten years is what decides what those years were. Judgement is put off here, not called off.

crossReferences.why: Asks the same question about wealth and children and gives the same answer, that extension is not favour.
Names the gradual drawing-on this verse describes, and adds that the delay is deliberate.
Sets the same brief enjoyment against what follows it, in a single short sentence.

studies.applyIt: Think of an area of your life where nothing has gone wrong for a long time. Try not to read that as a verdict on how you are living. Ask instead what the last quiet year was used for. Name one thing you would do differently if this stretch of ease were a loan of time rather than a wage.
studies.explainEasier: People who turn away from God sometimes get a long, easy run. That is not God being pleased with them. The extra time only lets them pile up more wrong. In the end a shameful punishment is waiting for them.

studies.title: The Sorting You Cannot See
studies.meaning: God will not leave the community as it is, undivided. Events will separate what is sound from what is spoiled. But the separating happens through what people do, and nobody is handed a list. Knowledge of what is hidden stays with God, and where any of it is given out it goes to messengers He chooses. So the sorting is real, and its results are not visible to the people being sorted. The verse ends by asking for belief rather than for information.
studies.historicalContext: This came right after Uhud in Medina, where the battle had done exactly what the verse describes. Men who marched out turned back before the fighting. Others held their ground and were killed. Early scholars read the verse as an answer to a wish: that the insincere had been picked out in advance, which would have spared the community its losses. The reply is that the picking out is what the events were for.

keyTerms.note: The verb for sorting a mixed heap into its kinds, used of grain and of coins. It assumes the two are already different and merely mixed, so the sorting shows rather than makes.
A word for what is clean, pleasant and fit to use, applied to food, water and land. Its opposite here means foul or spoiled, so the pair comes from produce rather than from law.
Everything out of reach of the senses, not only the future. With the article it names a whole domain rather than one fact, which is why the denial is about access and not about any single item.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Threshing was a sorting job everyone had watched. Grain was beaten loose from the stalk, thrown up into the wind and let fall, and the light part blew away while the heavy part landed in a heap. Nobody could tell by looking at an unthreshed sheaf how much of it was chaff. Doing the work was the only way to find out, and it needed a wind.
studies.didYouKnow: This verse changes person in the middle of a single clause. It speaks of the believers from outside, in the third person, and then without a break says what you are upon. Arabic rhetoric has a name for that turn. It treats it as a way of pulling listeners inside a sentence that began as a description of somebody else.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage pulls apart two things people often run together. God knows who is sincere. That does not mean anybody else can. The one is granted fully and the other denied flatly, and that denial is what makes suspicion useless between people. It also gives hardship a job that is neither punishment nor accident. Difficulty is how a claim turns into a fact.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same principle as a question: whether people expect their claim of faith to go untested.
States the same holding back of the unseen, with the same exception made for a chosen messenger.
Uses the same phrase about separating the foul from the good, in the setting of another battle.

studies.applyIt: Think of a stretch of difficulty you are in now, and ask what it is sorting rather than what it is punishing. Do not answer for anybody else. Write one line about something that has become clearer to you about yourself since it began: a habit you did not know you had, a fear you had not named.
studies.explainEasier: God will not leave the believers all mixed together. Hard days show who is true and who is not. He does not hand you a list of what is hidden. He tells His messengers what He wants them to know.

studies.title: Collared With What You Kept
studies.meaning: This verse corrects a sum people do in their heads. Holding back feels like keeping, so it reads as a gain. The passage says it is a loss. Then it gives the picture that makes the loss visible: what was hoarded is fastened round the neck on the Day of Resurrection. Early scholars differ on whether the collar is the wealth itself changed, or a punishment shaped like it. The closing words take away the whole premise. God inherits the heavens and the earth, so nothing was ever held for good.
studies.historicalContext: This came down in Medina. The long section on the aftermath of Uhud turns here to money, and early scholars read the verse broadly rather than tying it to one episode. Some connect it to holding back knowledge of earlier scripture instead of wealth, since the verses just after it deal with concealing. Others keep it general. Medina at this point was under real strain, with an immigrant population living on what its hosts had.

keyTerms.note: The verb names a settled habit rather than a single act: a standing unwillingness to let go. The verse attaches it not to wealth in general but to what God gave them of His bounty.
Built from the word for a neck-ring. The same root gives the word for what a person is able to bear, so the picture is a load fastened where it cannot be put down.
The term from estate law for what passes to heirs when somebody dies. Applied to the heavens and the earth, it turns every owner into a temporary holder and God into the one who remains.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in Medina was mostly visible and mostly heavy: date palms, grain stores, camels, silver weighed out. You could read a household's standing from its walled garden. So hoarding was not a private act, since neighbours could see which stores never moved. Burial was quick and plain. The distance between a full storehouse and a wrapped body was something people watched close inside a single day.
studies.didYouKnow: The classical collections keep a report from the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) about hoarded wealth. In it the wealth comes on the Day of Resurrection as a serpent that seizes the man who kept it, and this verse is recited as its basis. The picture is already in the wording. The verb here is built on the word for a ring worn at the neck.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Ownership is treated here as a claim that reality does not support. What a person has is described as given, and the closing words name God as the one to whom everything comes back. Between those two statements, hoarding looks less like a moral failing than a mistake about the facts. And no instruction to give is issued anywhere in the verse. What gets taken apart is the reasoning that makes holding on feel sensible.

crossReferences.why: Extends the same picture, with hoarded metal heated and applied to the body that kept it.
Traces stinginess back to the assumption of self-sufficiency that the closing words here remove.
Names people as successors to what they hold, the same relation the inheritance clause implies.

studies.applyIt: Look at one thing you are holding that you have not used in a year: money set aside for no purpose, a tool, a coat. Do not resolve to become generous. Just decide today where that single item goes, and move it this week. The point is the specific object, not how you feel about it.
studies.explainEasier: Some people hold back the good things God gave them and think that is best for them. It is not. What they held on to will be hung round their necks on the Day when everyone rises.

studies.title: A Sentence God Heard
studies.meaning: The passage opens with hearing rather than with a reply. A remark had been made, that God is the needy one and its speakers are the rich. The first thing said back is simply that it was heard. Then the remark is joined to something far older, the killing of prophets. The two are treated as one turn of mind separated by centuries, not as two unrelated crimes. And the closing words shut off any complaint about the sentence. What is met is what the hands sent ahead.
studies.historicalContext: This came down in Medina. Early scholars connect the remark to a taunt made in the city, aimed at the way the Quran describes charity as a loan given to God. They do not agree on the exact wording, or on who was there. They record it as one particular occasion rather than as a general description. The verses around it carry on a long exchange with those in Medina who held earlier scripture.

keyTerms.note: The plain past tense, put first in the sentence for weight. The answer to a remark made in private is not an argument but a statement that it arrived, which changes what kind of thing the remark was.

The verb for entering something in a register or a contract. Its future prefix makes the recording a promise, so the words are handled as an entry to be produced later rather than an insult to be answered now.
An intensive form, not the ordinary word for unjust. Early scholars discuss the force of the intensive here and read the denial as ruling out injustice altogether, not just its extreme degree.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputation in Medina was made and unmade by things said in courtyards. A cutting line about a rival could cross the town before the evening meal, and poets were paid to make them. Nothing could be taken back once enough people had heard it. Feuds were kept alive for generations by single sentences nobody ever wrote down.
studies.didYouKnow: The whole of the second verse here appears again, word for word, at 8:51, and a slightly changed form of it appears at 22:10. The phrase denying that God wrongs His servants uses the same strong form everywhere it occurs. In every case it stands at the very end of a verse, never inside one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two claims are set against each other here. The remark treats need as something that could attach to God, and the passage does not argue the point; it records it. What follows says more. Joining a sentence spoken in Medina to the killing of prophets centuries before treats contempt as one thing running across time. And the final denial makes the record itself, rather than any verdict imposed from outside, the thing that decides.

crossReferences.why: Contains the language of lending to God that early scholars say this remark was answering.
Reports a similar saying about God and handles it the same way, quoting it before replying.
Joins the same two charges, a saying about God and the killing of prophets, in one sentence.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you said about God in a bad week, out loud or only in your head. The point of this passage is that it was heard, not that it was unforgivable. Say the truer sentence now, in your own words, without deleting the first one. Notice how differently the two sit in the same mouth.
studies.explainEasier: God heard the people who said that He was poor and they were rich. Their words are being written down, along with the prophets they killed. What they get in the end is what their own hands sent ahead.

studies.title: The Sign They Asked For
studies.meaning: A condition is quoted and then pulled apart by its own history. The demand is for one particular sign: an offering that fire comes down and eats up. It is presented as something already agreed with God. The reply does not deny that such signs were ever given. It grants them, and then asks what happened to the messengers who brought them. The argument turns on a fact rather than a rule. The condition had been met before, and the outcome was killing, so it was never the real obstacle.
studies.historicalContext: This came down in Medina, inside a long exchange with those in the city who held earlier scripture. The sign named was known from their own tradition, where fire coming down on an offering marked that it was accepted. Early scholars treat this as a demand reported from particular speakers, not a general one, and no single occasion is agreed. They read the reply as aimed at the argument itself rather than at any person.

keyTerms.note: The verb for entering a binding agreement, used of treaties between tribes. Putting it here makes the demand sound like an obligation already contracted rather than a preference, which is why the reply goes after its history.
From the root meaning to draw near. The word names the offering by its purpose, closeness, rather than by what is offered, and it occurs only three times in the whole Quran.
Plural of a word for whatever makes a thing evident. It covers miracles, arguments and plain scripture together, so the reply refuses to grant that only one kind of sign should count.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sacrifice was ordinary and public. An animal was brought, killed and shared out, and everyone there could see whether it met the standards of their own tradition. So setting a visible test for a prophet was not a strange request. It asked for the kind of proof a market or a tribal meeting used every day, put to a question neither could settle.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for an offering occurs three times in the Quran and nowhere else. One is in the account of the two sons of Adam at 5:27. There two offerings are brought and only one is accepted. The other is at 46:28, where it names not an offering at all, but the gods people took as a way of drawing near.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage turns down a familiar move: setting a condition for belief that is really a way of putting it off. It grants that the sign was given, then points at what followed. That makes the demand defeat itself, without denying that God gives signs. What it suggests is that resistance to a message is rarely about evidence. Whoever names a proof will usually find another reason once it arrives.

crossReferences.why: States as a rule what this verse argues from one case, that supplied proof does not compel belief.
Records the same pattern of messengers denied and killed that the reply here appeals to.
Lists a similar set of conditions set for a messenger, and the answer he was told to give.

studies.applyIt: Notice a condition you have set for yourself: the point at which you will start praying properly, or reading, or making the call you owe someone. Ask honestly whether meeting it would change anything. If the answer is no, do the smaller version of the thing today, and stop waiting for the condition to arrive.
studies.explainEasier: Some people said they would only believe a messenger who brought an offering that fire came down and burned. The answer is simple. Messengers did bring that before, with clear proofs, and those people killed them anyway.

studies.title: You Are Not The First
studies.meaning: This is the shortest kind of comfort. It offers no explanation, only a precedent: if you are being called a liar, so were the ones before you. Then the verse names what those earlier messengers carried, clear proofs, written pages, and a scripture that gives light. That raises the point instead of softening it, since they were not denied for want of credentials. Early scholars read the three items as one gathering rather than three separate books, listing the range of what had already been brought and refused.
studies.historicalContext: This closes a stretch in Medina where demands and charges are quoted and answered one after another. The community had just taken losses at Uhud, and in the city it was under steady attack in words. Early scholars report no special occasion for the verse. They read it as the comfort that follows the argument before it, spoken straight to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him).

keyTerms.note: Plural of a word for something inscribed, from a root meaning to write firmly or to build in courses. Translators render it as psalms, but it names the form a text takes rather than one particular book.
An active participle: not lit, but lighting. The scripture is described as a source of light rather than something lit up, and it is the same word the Quran uses of the moon.
A passive intensive form. The claim was not merely doubted; the man carrying it was accused. That is why the comfort offered concerns a person rather than an argument.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a society that kept its records in memory, calling a man a liar was the worst thing you could say. Contracts, debts and family lines all rested on what people testified. A man whose word failed once lost his standing in every later deal. The charge made in Mecca and Medina was aimed right there: not at the claim, but at the man as a witness.
studies.didYouKnow: The three items listed here appear together in this order only twice in the whole Quran. One is here. The other is at 35:25, where the sentence around them is almost a copy of this one. The two surahs are otherwise unlike each other in length and setting, and the repeated sentence does the same comforting work in both.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The verse puts the problem in the hearers rather than in the evidence, and it does that by history instead of by assertion. It also says something about prophecy as a job. Being denied belongs to the work; it does not mean anything has gone wrong. For a reader, that pulls apart two things people mix up all the time: whether a message is true, and how it was received.

crossReferences.why: Repeats this sentence almost word for word, with the same three items in the same order.
Adds what the earlier messengers did about being denied, which this verse leaves unsaid.
Makes the precedent plain: even the accusations themselves are inherited from earlier arguments.

studies.applyIt: The next time you are misrepresented, hold off on correcting the record straight away. Sit with it for a day. Notice how much of the sting comes from the accusation and how much from being unable to answer it. Then decide calmly whether answering would change anything for anyone other than you.
studies.explainEasier: If people call you a liar, that is nothing new. Messengers before you were called liars too. They came with clear proofs, with written pages, and with a book that gives light, and people still turned them down.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: The Enjoyment Of Delusion
studies.meaning: This verse says three hard things in a row, and each one is a kindness. Every soul will taste death, so the thing you fear most is not a trap set for you alone. It is the road everyone walks. You will be paid in full on the Day of Resurrection, so nothing you did was wasted, even if nobody paid you here. And winning is defined modestly: pulled clear of the Fire, let into Paradise. The last line does not call this life worthless. It calls it goods that mislead, which early scholars read as a comment on its scale rather than its reality.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. This part of it answers people made bitter by loss, and by the taunts that followed Uhud. The words are addressed to everyone, and early scholars report no particular occasion for them. But where they fall matters. They arrive among verses about the dead, about wealth held back, and about mockery, and they answer all three with the same measure.

keyTerms.note: A participle, not a verb. Death is something the soul tastes rather than undergoes, which makes it an experience passed through and leaves the one tasting still there afterwards.
A doubled form suggesting repeated small tugs rather than one movement. The passive keeps the reader from being the one doing it, and the picture is of someone edged away from a place they were near.
Trade vocabulary for provisions or wares carried for a journey, useful and real but not the destination. The word is used elsewhere of a traveller's kit and of goods lent for a while.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A caravan merchant carried two kinds of load: the trade goods he would sell, and the provisions he would eat on the way. The second kept him alive and was gone by the end. Nobody confused the water skins with the profit. Arabic used one word for both the wares and the travelling supplies, and this verse puts the whole of worldly life in the second group.
studies.didYouKnow: The sentence about every soul tasting death occurs three times in the Quran, at 3:185, 21:35 and 29:57, and something different follows it each time. Here it is repayment on the Day of Resurrection. In the second it is a test of good and bad. In the third it is a return to God.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Payment in full is put off, and that one move changes everything. If accounts are settled here, then every wrong left unpaid and every effort left unrewarded is a lasting injustice. If they are settled later, the present is a partial statement and not a final one. The passage also sets the bar for success very low and very firmly. Not rank, not honour. Simply being moved clear and let in.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the line about every soul tasting death, and follows it with testing by good and bad alike.
Expands the closing image, comparing worldly life to plants that dry out and crumble.
Calls this life amusement and the final home the real life, in a Meccan surah.

studies.applyIt: Look at your calendar for the coming week and find the item you are most anxious about. Ask what will be left of it in ten years, and answer honestly rather than piously, because some things will still matter. This verse is not flattening the difference. It is asking you to actually make it.
studies.explainEasier: Everyone will die one day. You get what you earned on the day everyone is raised. Anyone kept away from the Fire and let into the Garden has won. This life can trick you.

studies.title: Tested And Spoken Against
studies.meaning: This is a forecast, not a threat. Three things are named ahead of time: loss of property, loss of people, and a steady flow of insult arriving from two directions. Saying it beforehand takes away the surprise, which is the whole point. The response asked for comes as a pair, holding on together with mindfulness of God, and then the verse lifts that above merely coping. What is described is not survival but a course of action counted among the things that take resolve.
studies.historicalContext: This came in Medina, in the years after the emigration. The community was poor, had just been beaten at Uhud, and lived beside groups that opposed it in speech long before anything else. Property left behind in Mecca was not coming back. Early scholars read the verse as general preparation rather than an answer to one incident. They place it before the harder instructions of the later Medinan surahs.

keyTerms.note: The verb means to test by trial and also to wear a thing out by using it. It carries two emphatic markers here, front and back, which is the strongest way Arabic has of saying something will certainly happen.

A word for injury that stops short of real damage: an insult, a nuisance, a wound to dignity. Naming it apart from loss of life and property keeps small steady hostility from being dismissed as nothing.
The noun for a settled decision, the point at which wavering stops. The phrase it forms here counts certain courses of action among the things that need that decision made.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The emigrants reached Medina with almost nothing. Many took work carrying water or labouring in the date gardens of their hosts. Their houses back in Mecca stood full of other people. Meanwhile mocking verse about them went round, made to be memorised and repeated. Insult was a public trade in Arabia with its own paid experts, and a family could be mocked in poetry for a generation.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase that closes this verse counts something among the matters that take resolve, and it occurs three times in the Quran. Each time it describes patience. Here it follows persecution. At 31:17 it appears in a father's advice to his son. At 42:43 it describes forgiving someone after being wronged.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Advance notice is treated here as a kindness in itself. Nothing about the trial is softened. What is taken away is the second layer of suffering, the belief that hardship means something has gone wrong. The verse also puts insult in the same list as death and lost property, refusing to rank suffering by how dramatic it looks. And the response it asks for is active rather than merely endured.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same forecast with a longer list, and adds the words the tested are told to say.
Ends with the same phrase about resolve, attached there to patience over whatever befalls a person.
Instructs the Prophet on what to do with the abuse this verse says will certainly come.

studies.applyIt: Count the criticisms you took this week that were about you rather than about your work. Then notice how much of your energy went towards them. Holding on here is not silence; it is refusing to let the smallest hostile voice set the agenda for your day. Choose one you will stop rehearsing in your head.
studies.explainEasier: You will be tested through your money and through your own lives. You will hear plenty of insults from people who were given scripture before you and from those who worship idols. Hold on and keep careful of God.

studies.title: Thrown Behind Their Backs
studies.meaning: The pledge described here is a duty to speak: make the scripture plain to people, and do not hide it. Then the failure is reported twice, in two pictures. One is bodily, putting a thing behind you where nobody can see it. The other is commercial, a sale at a bad price. Early scholars note that the pledge is about passing the scripture on, not about believing it. So what is condemned is holding back what was known, not being wrong about it.
studies.historicalContext: This came down in Medina, inside a run of verses spoken to those in the city who held earlier scripture and were disputing the new message. Early scholars read the pledge as one taken from every group that was given a revelation, not as a single event. Some tie the verse to arguments about what earlier scripture held. They also record the view that the warning reaches anyone later trusted with knowledge.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to tie firmly. It is the strongest word for an agreement in the Quran, used of treaties and of the pledge taken from prophets, and it suggests a knot rather than a spoken promise.
The verb for tossing something aside carelessly, the way a date stone is discarded. It is not the word for refusing or for losing, which is what makes the phrase about their backs so sharp.
The price is not called wrong but small. That leaves the charge a matter of judgement rather than of law, and the phrase returns whenever the Quran describes something valuable traded away.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Knowledge in that century was carried by people, not on shelves. A man who could recite family lines or read out a contract held a place that rested on his being the only one who could. Scribes and scholars were consulted and paid, and their standing rose as what they held grew rarer. Making everything plain to everybody would have cost them something real.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about selling for a small price comes up across the Quran, and each time what is sold is a revelation or a pledge given to God, never an ordinary good. Two of those places are in this surah. One is here. The other is twelve verses later at 3:199, where it describes people who refuse to make the sale.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Plain speaking is made a duty attached to knowledge, not a favour done to others. Receiving revelation is described as taking on a duty to people outside the circle that got it. So hiding it counts as a broken pledge, not merely as holding back. It also implies that what they held cannot be turned into standing without loss. That is exactly what the picture of the price says.

crossReferences.why: States the same offence directly, naming concealment after clarification as the thing condemned.
Joins the same two elements, hiding scripture and selling it cheaply, inside a single sentence.
Describes people from the same communities who refuse this exchange, keeping the charge from becoming blanket.

studies.applyIt: If you know something that would help someone and have not said it, a name, a route through a process, a warning, send it today. Notice honestly whether some part of you enjoyed being the one who knew. That small pleasure is what this verse describes, long before anything is actually sold.
studies.explainEasier: God took a promise from the people who were given the scripture. They were to make it clear to everyone and not hide it. They dropped that promise behind them and sold it for a small price. It was a bad trade.

studies.title: Praised For What They Did Not Do
studies.meaning: Two appetites are set side by side and treated as one condition. One is being pleased with what a person has actually done. The other is wanting credit for what they have not. The sentence will not let the second pass as a small vanity. It puts it under the same warning as the offences around it. Then the next verse answers the question this raises, about who can grant or withhold praise, by naming the one to whom everything belongs.
studies.historicalContext: This came down in Medina. The early sources keep an exchange in which the verse is explained two ways. One is about people who stayed back from a campaign, then came with excuses and expected thanks. The other is about people asked what their scripture contained, who held it back and let themselves be praised as though they had answered. Early scholars record both readings, and neither pushes the other out.

keyTerms.note: The verb for open delight. The Quran uses it approvingly elsewhere, so the fault named here is not the pleasure itself but where it has been attached, which the words after it supply.
From a root meaning both to win and to be delivered. The same root gives the word for success used across the Quran, so escaping and winning are one idea in Arabic.
Ownership with authority behind it, not bare possession. Putting it straight after a passage about reputation sets the whole economy of human praise inside something that does not depend on it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Standing in Arabia was built up in public and remembered aloud. What a man did was recited at gatherings, sometimes by relatives and sometimes by paid poets, and reputations outlived the people who earned them. There was no written record to check a claim against. A man who spoke well of his own share in a raid, in front of the right listeners, kept that credit for good.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for rejoicing used here is not condemned everywhere in the Quran. At 10:58 people are told to rejoice, in that case at the grace and mercy of God. At 28:76 a wealthy man is told not to. The word carries no verdict of its own, and each passage is decided by what the rejoicing has been attached to.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage names a failure that leaves no visible trace. Nothing was stolen and nothing checkable was said. A person simply accepted an impression they knew to be false. By putting that under a serious warning, the passage treats the inner accounting as the real one. The verse that follows then removes the audience: if everything belongs to God, a reputation held on false terms is held nowhere at all.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same appetite working inside a good deed rather than in place of one.
Names display as the fault in an act that is outwardly correct, the same turn described here.
Gives a case of wanting to be seen doing what one is not actually doing.

studies.applyIt: Recall a compliment you accepted this month that was slightly more than you had earned, where you let a wrong impression stand because correcting it felt awkward. You do not need to go back and fix it. Just name it to yourself accurately, once. The discomfort of doing that is the entire exercise.
studies.explainEasier: Some people are pleased with what they did, and they also love being praised for things they never did. They should not think they will get away with it. A painful punishment is waiting. Everything belongs to God anyway.

studies.title: Signs For Those Who Think
studies.meaning: The signs are said to lie in two things: the making of the heavens and the earth, and the turning of night into day. Change that never stops is set beside the structure itself. The next verse describes who reads those signs, and it does so by posture rather than by learning. Remembering God in every position runs together with reflecting, and the two arrive at a conclusion spoken as a prayer: none of this was made for nothing.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina, and these lines close it. They come after long sections on Uhud and on debate with the People of the Scripture. The verses step back from all of that to the plainest evidence there is, which can be seen from anywhere. The classical collections keep reports of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) reciting them when he rose at night. Many read the passage as the summing up of the surah rather than an aside.

keyTerms.note: From a root for succeeding and taking turns, the same root behind the word for a successor. It names night and day as replacements for one another, not merely as two different things.
The plural of the word for the kernel inside a shell, the soft part of a date stone or a nut. Understanding is named as the pith of a person rather than an extra fitted to them.
A form of the verb that implies effort applied to yourself and kept up over time. It is not a flash of insight but a deliberate turning over, and the grammar keeps it ongoing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Before clocks and street lighting, the sky was the instrument everyone used. Caravans crossed the desert at night by the stars. Herders read the season from where the sun came up on the ridge. Dates for debts and pilgrimages were set by the moon. Watching the sky was not contemplation for these listeners. It was navigation, timekeeping and weather forecasting, done by people who could not afford to be careless about it.
studies.didYouKnow: What begins here as looking at the sky turns into a prayer that runs for four verses, one of the longer unbroken prayers in the Quran. It ends with a plea not to be disgraced on the Day of Resurrection. The verse right after it opens with the answer from God, replying to the request rather than leaving it hanging.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Evidence for God is put where anyone can reach it, which makes the argument open in a particular way. No text, no teacher and no language is needed first. The passage also joins two things usually kept apart. Remembering is devotional and reflecting is intellectual, and here the same people do both at once, in every posture. What they arrive at is about purpose, not about mechanism.

crossReferences.why: Lists the same signs at greater length, adding ships, rain and the movement of the winds.
Carries on the prayer these thinkers speak, from the plea about the Fire to the last request.
Turns the same reflection inward, asking whether people have thought about themselves.

studies.applyIt: Go outside tonight for two minutes without your phone and look up. Do not try to feel anything. Just find one thing you can actually see, a single star or the edge of the moon, and stay with it long enough to be bored. This passage describes people who did that often enough that it changed them.
studies.explainEasier: Look at the sky and the earth, and at how night turns into day. There are signs in that for people who think. They remember God standing, sitting and lying down, and say none of this was made for nothing.

studies.title: We Heard A Caller Calling
studies.meaning: The prayer moves from a fear to a claim and then to a request. Disgrace, not pain, is what is named first about the Fire, which tells you what these speakers dread most. Then they state their one credential, and it is deliberately small: they heard someone calling, and they answered. Nothing about their merit is offered. Three requests follow, using two different words for wrongdoing, and early scholars discuss those two without settling whether they are distinguished or joined for weight.
studies.historicalContext: This closes a surah that has argued, comforted and instructed for nearly two hundred verses before it turns to prayer. It belongs to Medina, and early scholars place the section late in that period. They treat it as a summing up rather than an answer to any incident. The speakers are the people described a few verses earlier, thinking about the making of the heavens and the earth.

keyTerms.note: The verb for public humiliation rather than private pain. Naming this first says that what these speakers fear about the Fire is exposure, and the same root returns two verses later as a request.
An indefinite noun: someone calling, not a named person. The vagueness is doing work, since the speakers describe their own moment of belief by the sound that reached them rather than by who made it.
A plural from a root meaning breadth and dutifulness, especially towards parents. It names people whose goodness is wide rather than merely correct, and the closing verses of this surah use it twice.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A caller was a working office in that world. Someone with a strong voice climbed to high ground and called out news, an assembly, a lost camel, a summons to prayer. Everyone within earshot then had to decide what to do about a voice whose source they could not see. That daily experience is what this prayer uses to describe becoming a believer.
studies.didYouKnow: The prayer runs unbroken from 3:191 to 3:194. Every sentence in those four verses is addressed to God, and the same words for our Lord are used five times. The classical collections report that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) would rise at night, look at the sky, and recite the closing verses of this surah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer shows a posture rather than a formula. It offers no achievements, only an answer to something heard, and then asks for what it has no claim to. Response first, request second, and merit never: that is the shape of prayer the Quran keeps coming back to. It also treats forgiveness and good company as one thing. What is asked for at the end is not a place but people.

crossReferences.why: Closes another long surah with a prayer in the same voice, asking rather than claiming anything.
Opens the prayers of this surah with the same address and the same worry about not lasting.
Ends another prayer with the same request, to die in the company of the righteous.

studies.applyIt: Say these two lines tonight in your own words, and stop at the part where the speakers explain why they believe. They mention nothing they achieved. Try saying your own version of that sentence, naming the moment or the voice that reached you, without adding anything at all about how you have done since.
studies.explainEasier: Our Lord, anyone you put in the Fire has been shamed. We heard someone calling us to believe in you, and we believed. So forgive our sins, wipe away our bad deeds, and let us die among good people.

studies.title: The Promise You Never Break
studies.meaning: A long prayer ends by asking for something already guaranteed, and that is the interesting part. The speakers ask for what was promised through the messengers. None of it is in doubt. Then they give their reason as a statement about God rather than about themselves. The one genuinely open request is the other, not to be disgraced.
